Document title: Online Tutoring, School Performance, and School-to-Work Transitions: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
Document description: This discussion paper investigates the effects of a one-on-one online tutoring program in Germany on both academic performance and school-to-work transitions. The program, operated by the nonprofit organization Lern-Fair, uses a web-based platform to connect university student volunteers with disadvantaged secondary school students in need of academic support. The study conducted a randomized controlled trial with 839 adolescents with low school performance, whose baseline characteristics were collected through a nationwide survey. The results show that online tutoring improves math grades, particularly among students with no other tutoring at baseline. Additionally, non-academic track students in the treatment group with no other tutoring at baseline were more likely to start vocational training and less likely to remain in the post-school transition system. The study finds no evidence that the online tutoring affected behavioral or socioemotional skills, such as grit or mental well-being. The findings contribute to the broader literature on the effects of tutoring programs and suggest that online tutoring can generate lasting benefits for low-performing students that extend beyond school performance.

Document title: The Relationship Between Earnings and Sexual Orientation: First Evidence from China
Document description: This study provides the first evidence on the labor market outcomes of lesbian, gay, and bisexual people in China using data from the 2020 Chinese Private Life Survey. The study finds that gay men earn significantly less than comparable heterosexual men, with the largest penalties in rural areas among gay men reporting exclusive same-sex attraction. Lesbian women tend to earn more than heterosexual women, but the differences are small and mostly insignificant. The estimates for bisexual men and women are uniformly insignificant. The study explores possible mechanisms, including labor market discrimination, labor market skills, household specialization, China's hukou registration system, and China's one-child policy. The evidence is most consistent with the specialization channel, suggesting that gay penalties and lesbian premiums are concentrated among gay men and lesbian women who specialize more and less in housework, respectively.

Document description: This report evaluates the Dutch government's annual policy on entrepreneurship and innovation for the period between 2020 and 2025, commissioned by the Ministry of Economic Affairs. Document title: Long-Term Effects of Group-Based Agricultural Support Amid COVID-19 Shocks in Nepal
Document description: This paper examines the long-term effects of agricultural support in western Nepal and whether support enhanced farmers' resilience to coronavirus disease (COVID-19) disruptions. Agricultural support programs in Nepal aim to transform smallholder farming from subsistence-based production toward more commercial, market-oriented systems. The programs offer support in the form of subsidized inputs, productive assets, credit, and technical training to improve productivity and incomes. The unique aspect of agricultural support in Nepal is that assistance must be channeled through formal agricultural groups, such as farmer groups or cooperatives. The COVID-19 pandemic created a sudden and severe disruption to agricultural markets and rural livelihoods in Nepal. The paper contributes to the literature on agricultural transformation and resilience in low-income settings by providing rare evidence on the long-term effects of agricultural support programs in a subsistence-dominated context. The study uses a four-year panel dataset that tracks farm outcomes before and after program implementation. The findings suggest that support led to substantial improvements in crop productivity, value, sales, and income. The effects are largest for support including training, asset subsidies, or credit, and support focused on higher-value products. The support provided between 2018 and 2022 had large effects in offsetting the negative impacts of COVID-19 restrictions, whereas support provided up to 2018 had a persistent effect in improving resilience to COVID-19 shocks.

Document title: Inflation and the joint bond-FX spanning puzzle
Document description: The document discusses the joint bond-FX spanning puzzle, where inflation is found to be an unspanned predictor of both bond and exchange rate returns. The authors generalize the yield spanning condition to non-linear models and exchange rates, and provide evidence that this condition is violated. They find that high inflation is associated with low subsequent bond returns but high dollar returns, and that this relationship holds after controlling for the information already embedded in the current shapes of U.S. and foreign yield curves. The authors also explore the mechanisms through which inflation predicts bond and dollar returns, and present a simple model that offers intuitive insights into these findings.

Document title: Trade sanctions
Document description: The document analyses the effectiveness of trade sanctions imposed on Russia following its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The authors use a novel dataset on export sanctions against Russia, covering 35 sanctioning countries and relating to around 6,000 ten-digit product codes observed in Russian customs data. They find that export sanctions banned 36% of all country-product varieties that Russia imported before the war by value, constituting one of the largest trade shocks in recent memory. The authors also find that imports of sanctioned country-product varieties fell dramatically after the war's onset, decreasing by 55% relative to nonsanctioned flows. The decline was sharp and grew over time, reaching nearly 72% by the end of the study period in December 2023. The authors conclude that import sanctions have generated substantial and persistent economic pain, challenging narratives that sanctions are merely symbolic or easy to circumvent.

Document title: Climate Laws and Green Finance: The Value of Legal Commitment
Document description: This document explores the impact of climate laws on sustainable investment. It uses a difference-in-differences design to analyze the effects of climate laws on the share of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) mutual fund holdings. The study finds that enshrining a climate commitment in law redirects capital toward green assets and that legally binding climate commitments lead to a substantial increase in the share of ESG holdings in total mutual fund assets. The effect is driven by laws setting net-zero emission reduction targets, which increase the ESG share by about 5 percentage points over 5 years. The study also finds that the effectiveness of climate laws depends critically on the economies' institutional capacity and that the adoption of net-zero laws mobilizes additional green finance equivalent to about 1.8% of gross domestic product within 5 years from adoption through mutual fund portfolios alone. Document description: The clean energy transition is increasingly dependent on a narrow set of critical minerals sourced and processed in a handful of countries. These minerals, such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper, and rare earth elements, underpin the deployment of low-carbon technologies central to climate action. Achieving net-zero emissions by mid-century will require the rapid and massive deployment of clean energy systems, which in turn will drive up demand for these critical minerals. Innovation can substantially reshape the elasticity of both supply and demand, and this review aims to chart the landscape of innovation that can mitigate the critical minerals challenge. The authors focus on particular applications central to the clean energy transition, such as renewable energy systems and electric vehicles, and span the value chain from mining and processing to manufacturing, usage, reuse, and recycling. They identify key technologies and gaps across the critical minerals value chain and showcase real-world examples of innovations that reduce primary demand or expand the supply of critical minerals. The authors also assess emerging policy challenges and opportunities for governments to foster innovation across the critical minerals value chain.

Document title: Rigging the Scores: Corruption through Scoring Rule Manipulation in Public Procurement Auctions
Document description: Corruption in public procurement auctions is a pervasive issue that undermines governments worldwide, distorting markets, stalling economic growth, and eroding public trust. Public procurement is especially vulnerable, with bribes in this sector accounting for a significant share of total corruption. Corruption in procurement involves illicit practices to manipulate contract awards for goods, services, and works, resulting in inflated costs and placing undue burdens on taxpayers and businesses. This challenge is particularly acute in developing countries, where weak institutional frameworks and inadequate accountability exacerbate the problem. Open scoring auctions are widely adopted to curb corruption, but this paper finds that corruption remains prevalent even within this procurement format. Procurement officers can collaborate with firms to manipulate scoring rules, ensuring predetermined winners, while corrupt firms submit noncompetitive bids to meet minimum bidder requirements. The paper introduces model-driven statistical tools to detect such corruption, identifying a corruption rate of 65 percent. Firm-level analysis reveals that local, state-owned, and less productive firms are favored in corrupt auctions. The paper explores policy implications, including the implementation of anonymous call-for-tender evaluations, which could improve social welfare by 10 percent by eliminating suspicious rules and encouraging broader participation.

Document description: This document explores the impact of Russia's economic shock in the early 1990s on its society and democratic values. Document title: Navigating the sea of natural real interest rate estimates
Document description: The document discusses the natural real interest rate and its role in monetary policy. The author reviews the literature on estimating the natural real interest rate and its drivers, highlighting significant uncertainty and variability in estimates. The challenges in achieving consensus on the natural real interest rate are mostly due to differing methodologies and model assumptions. Understanding these sources of uncertainty is essential for shaping future monetary policy, especially in a low interest rate environment where conventional policy tools may be limited. The author notes that there is little consensus in the academic literature on the current value and future direction of the natural rate, complicating policy decisions. The natural rate is the real interest rate consistent with full employment and stable inflation, and it serves as a conceptual anchor for assessing the stance of monetary policy. The author reviews various approaches for deriving the natural rate, resulting in widely differing estimates. The bulk of the variation stems from methodological aspects rather than from statistical uncertainty within a given model.

Document title: The global allocation of extractive windfalls
Document description: This paper studies the geographic allocation of extractive multinational enterprises' profits generated by commodity price shocks. The authors combine new administrative data on the worldwide activity of MNEs with exhaustive oil, gas, and mining production data at the firm level. They find that extractive MNEs allocate a third of their profits in non-extractive countries, and that profitability and effective tax rates display a U-shaped relationship in this sector. The authors identify the allocation of windfall profits by leveraging differences in the product specialization of extractive firms and commodity price changes, and provide evidence of overbooking of windfall profits in low-tax countries. They also estimate the magnitude of shifted windfall profits using consolidated data on publicly listed firms and find that windfall profits represent 66% of total positive increases in profits. Finally, the authors study the implications for fiscal windfalls in resource-rich countries and find that a 1% increase in oil, gas, and mining commodity prices increases fiscal windfalls by 1.01%, with a larger elasticity in the mining sector compared to the oil sector.

Document title: Signaling, screening, or sunk costs? Experimental evidence on how prices affect agricultural technology adoption in East Africa
Document description: This discussion paper explores how prices affect the adoption of new agricultural technologies in East Africa. The authors conducted a field experiment with smallholder farmers in Uganda and Ethiopia, distributing seed trial packs of recently released crop varieties. They found that willingness to pay for the seed trial packs is a strong predictor of subsequent use and adoption of the promoted variety, indicating a screening effect. However, paying for the seed does not always increase use through sunk cost mechanisms, and in some cases, payment even reduces use. The study suggests that modest positive prices can help target likely adopters without discouraging use, provided they remain low enough to avoid negative sunk cost effects. The findings have important implications for how pricing strategies can be designed to promote technology adoption in low-income settings.

Document title: A Decade of the BEPS Initiative
Document description: The Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) Project was designed to address concerns that the international tax system had not kept pace with the realities of the modern global economy. Concerns over double non-taxation and erosion of corporate income tax bases became more acute following the financial crisis of 2008-2009 and its associated fiscal pressures. In response, in 2015, the package of measures to counter BEPS was published (the BEPS Package), containing 15 BEPS Actions that sought to bring more coherence, substance, transparency and certainty to the international tax system. The BEPS Project led to an important change to the international tax policymaking landscape with the establishment of the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS (the Inclusive Framework). Launched in 2016 following a call from the G20, the Inclusive Framework brings its members – currently more than 145 jurisdictions – together to ensure the comprehensive implementation of the BEPS Package and to establish a level playing field in efforts to update the global tax architecture. This led to discussions under BEPS Action 1 on addressing the tax challenges arising from the digitalisation of the economy and the Two-Pillar Solution to Address the Tax Challenges Arising from the Digitalisation of the Economy (the Two-Pillar Solution). This report discusses the progress made in implementing the BEPS Package and its economic impact over the past decade. Progress with the Two-Pillar Solution, which was developed after the release of the original BEPS Actions, is beyond the scope of this report. The report highlights significant progress in implementing the four BEPS Minimum Standards, those measures whose implementation by all relevant jurisdictions is needed to avoid negative spillover effects across jurisdictions. Of the 15 BEPS Actions, four were deemed to be minimum standards. The results achieved with respect to the four minimum standards are outlined below: BEPS Action 5 (Harmful Tax Practices): More than 300 preferential regimes have been examined by the Inclusive Framework, and almost all the regimes that were found to pose BEPS risks have been amended or abolished, with only a few regimes still under review. BEPS Action 6 (Prevention of Tax Treaty Abuse): Over 95% of the agreements concluded by Inclusive Framework members (covering most of the global tax treaty network) are compliant or on track to become compliant with the Action 6 minimum standard. BEPS Action 13 (CbCR): 120 Inclusive Framework members have enacted Country-by-Country (CbC) legislation, covering nearly all large multinational enterprise (MNE) groups, and almost 4 650 bilateral relationships facilitate exchanges among nearly 100 jurisdictions. BEPS Action 14 (Mutual Agreement Procedures (MAP)): Over 500 treaties have been modified to include effective MAP provisions; access to MAP is now available in most eligible cases and MAP agreements are often effectively implemented. Many jurisdictions are closer to resolving MAP cases within an average of 24 months.

Document description: This paper examines how housing market overvaluation affects the transmission of monetary policy. Document title: Hand-to-Mouth Banks: Liquidity Constraints and the Marginal Propensity to Lend
Document description: This policy brief introduces the Marginal Propensity to Lend out of Deposit inflows (MPLD), a measure of how banks respond to unsolicited deposits. The analysis uses U.S. bank data from 1995-2021 and finds that before the Global Financial Crisis, the average U.S. bank lent out nearly every dollar of new deposits. Since the onset of Quantitative Easing, the average MPLD has declined to 0.35, reflecting looser liquidity constraints. The study also finds that differences across banks remain large, with institutions with thin cash buffers and fragile funding structures continuing to behave 'hand-to-mouth'. The findings have implications for monetary policy design, quantitative tightening, and the debate on central bank digital currencies. The analysis suggests that liquidity supply still matters, and that targeted credit support may be more effective than blanket liquidity injections. The study also highlights the importance of recognizing the heterogeneity in MPLDs for designing effective policies.

Document title: World Trade Report 2025: Making trade and AI work together to the benefit of all
Document description: The World Trade Report 2025 explores the complex relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and international trade, and how this relationship may shape inclusive growth. The report examines the opportunities and challenges of AI and trade, and how domestic policies can shape the trade and AI relationship to favour inclusive economic growth. It also looks at the central role the World Trade Organization (WTO) can play in ensuring that AI supports broad-based growth. The report suggests that trade can be a powerful enabler for an inclusive AI transformation, but that this potential can only be realized if we act deliberately, by closing digital divides, investing in workers, and promoting regulatory coherence. The report also highlights the need for greater international cooperation to make trade and AI work for all. The report uses a new AI Trade Policy Openness Index (AI-TPOI) to provide valuable evidence on trade policies shaping the development and diffusion of AI. The report concludes that the effects of the development and deployment of AI are raising concerns that many workers, and even entire economies, could be left behind, and that this exclusion has much to do with today's tensions around trade.

Document title: Command and Can’t Control: Assessing Centralized Accountability in the Public Sector
Document description: This document examines the effectiveness of a command-and-control management approach in the public sector, specifically in the education administration of Punjab, Pakistan. The approach relies on centralized decision-making and oversight, with officials expected to follow centrally determined directions or face punishment. The authors study the implementation of this approach in Punjab, focusing on the assessment of its accountability effects. They collect data on administrative activity, including teacher presence, student attendance, functional school facilities, and student test scores. The authors find that the intensity of accountability in the command-and-control scheme had no substantive impact on targeted school or student outcomes. They also find that officials did not respond to punishments at all, and that the program was maintained despite its lack of effectiveness. The authors suggest that the persistence of the program may be due to a naive examination of before-after comparisons, which can yield a strong positive effect of the program.

Document description: The document discusses the impact of divorce laws on women's welfare, particularly in cases of separation. Document title: Revisiting Adam Smith and the Division of Labor: New Evidence from U.S. Occupational Data, 1860–1940
Document description: This paper reevaluates Adam Smith's theories regarding the division of labor, market size, innovation, and productivity using novel U.S. occupational data from 1860 to 1940. The authors document a significant increase in occupational diversity during this period, noting that job titles became more specialized over time while generic roles declined. They find strong evidence that occupational specialization grows with the extent of the market, is facilitated by technological innovation, and is linked to higher labor productivity. The study also highlights the role of organizational changes and innovation spillovers during the Second Industrial Revolution in driving these trends. By analyzing census data and patent records, the researchers demonstrate that larger markets and industries foster greater specialization, which in turn boosts value added per worker. These findings confirm the enduring relevance of Smith's insights in the context of an industrializing economy characterized by large firms and rapid technological change.

Document title: The R&D and innovation effects of ﬁrm-speciﬁc trade opportunities
Document description: This paper explores how firm-specific trade opportunities affect R&D investments and innovative activities. The author uses Swedish register data to investigate how international trade in the form of export and import opportunities affects firm-level R&D investments and innovation outcomes. The results show that firm-specific export and import opportunities have large positive effects on a wide range of firm-performance measures. Increased trade opportunities of either type affect firm growth in terms of sales, value-added, and overall employment. The employment effects do not appear to be limited to low-skilled production workers; the impact on high-skilled employees is proportional to the overall employment effect. The author finds a positive relationship between opportunities to export and R&D spending, R&D employees, and product and process innovation. In contrast, a rise in the opportunity to import does not significantly affect any of the R&D outcomes, and product, process, and service innovation are negatively affected. The results suggest a positive causal link between firm-specific export opportunities and innovative activities.

Document title: The Social Lifecycle Impacts of Power Plant Siting in the Historical United States
Document description: This paper examines the relative contributions of siting decisions and post-siting demographic shifts to current disparities in exposure to polluting fossil-fuel plants in the United States. The authors combine newly digitized data on power plant siting and operations from 1900-2020 with spatially resolved demographic data from the U.S Census from 1870-2020. They find little evidence that fossil-fuel plants were disproportionately sited in counties with higher Black population shares on average. However, event study estimates indicate that Black population share grows in the decades after the first fossil-fuel plant is built in a county, with average increases in Black population share of 4 percentage points in the 50-70 years after first siting. These long-run demographic shifts are driven by counties that first hosted a fossil-fuel plant between 1900-1949. The authors close by exploring how these long-run demographic shifts were shaped by the Great Migration, differential sorting in response to pollution, and other factors. Their findings highlight that the equity implications of siting long-lived infrastructure can differ dramatically depending on the time span considered.

Document title: Potential Growth and Productivity in the Caribbean
Document description: The document discusses the economic growth and medium-term growth prospects of Caribbean countries, which have weakened in recent years. Document title: What Does Consulting Do
Document description: This working paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study of management and strategy consulting using administrative business-to-business transaction data from Belgium between 2002 and 2023. The authors analyze transactions with the ten largest consulting firms to understand engagement patterns and their effects on client firms. They find that consulting usage is concentrated among large firms with high labor productivity, following a U-shaped pattern where both top and bottom performers hire consultants. Clients typically spend about three percent of their payroll on short-term engagements lasting less than a year. The study employs difference-in-differences designs to measure the impact of consulting on firm performance over five years. Results show a significant increase in labor productivity of 3.6 percent, driven by modest employment reductions rather than revenue growth. Average wages rise by 2.7 percent without a decline in the labor share of value added, indicating gains are not extracted from workers. The analysis also reveals organizational changes such as higher dismissal rates and increased spending on external services. Heterogeneity analysis suggests larger productivity gains for initially less productive firms, supporting an efficiency-enhancing view. These findings align with predictions from consulting practitioners but differ from the divided opinions of academic experts regarding productivity benefits.

Document title: Violent conflict and cross-border lending
Document description: This document examines the relationship between private finance and armed conflict through the lens of cross-border lending during violent conflicts. The authors analyze data on syndicated loans by 14,021 creditors to firms in 179 countries from 1989 to 2020 and find that foreign banks reduce overall lending to conflict countries relative to domestic banks, while simultaneously increasing lending to military-related sectors. The authors also find that foreign banks preferentially direct military financing toward non-aligned or politically distant countries while avoiding geopolitically similar nations. The study reveals that cross-border lenders with military expertise but limited country-specific relationships are relatively well positioned to capitalize on conflict-induced credit demand without having to compromise established country-specific client relationships. The results suggest that foreign banks strategically redirect credit toward military sectors during armed conflicts, despite reducing overall country exposure. The study provides a first glimpse into how global banks respond to violent conflicts and the implications for cross-border lending and financial stability.

Document title: Hand-to-mouth banks: deposit inflows and the marginal propensity to lend
Document description: This paper explores the concept of the marginal propensity to lend out of unsolicited deposit inflows (MPLD) in the context of banking. The authors propose a novel instrumental variable approach based on county-level dividend payouts to estimate the MPLD for U.S. banks. The study analyzes the behavior of over 13,000 U.S. banks from 1995 to 2021 and finds that before the start of Quantitative Easing (QE) in 2008, the average MPLD was around 1.1, indicating that most banks operated 'hand-to-mouth,' rapidly converting new funding into loans. However, after 2008, the MPLD fell sharply to about 0.35, suggesting that the abundant reserves created by QE relaxed liquidity constraints for many banks. The MPLD is found to be decreasing in banks' cash-to-asset ratios and deposit market power, and increasing in banks' deposit beta. The results have important implications for monetary policy transmission and the design of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs).

Document title: Hard to Learn for the Future? Field Evidence from a Digital– Green Classroom Pilot Shows No Gains and Lower Enjoyment
Document description: This document evaluates the effectiveness of a pilot program called Raise-Up, which aimed to improve vocational maturity and reduce dropout risk in Vocational Education and Training (VET). The program integrated project-based learning on digitization and the green transition into the regular curriculum for students aged 14-16. Despite its ambition, the program produced no quantitatively measurable gains. The evaluation found that treated students reported a decline in school enjoyment and a marginally significant drop in self-reported use of computer skills. The negative consequences of the program were driven entirely by its impact on female students, who experienced a reduction in perceived knowledge of green and digital jobs, self-confidence, and overall satisfaction. The results are sobering because early school leaving imposes large and lasting costs on both individuals and society. The policy imperative remains clear: to make VET more attractive, more connected to labor markets, and more effective at keeping students on track.

Document description: The document discusses the digital divide among marginalized households, particularly in low-income families with school-aged children. Document title: Measuring the Unmeasurable? Systematic Evidence on Scale Transformations in Subjective Survey Data
Document description: Economists use survey measures to study latent constructs like wellbeing, risk attitudes, and political preferences. However, the literature assumes that numerical response categories represent equal psychological intervals, which may not be true. This paper provides the first systematic test of this assumption, using original experimental data to show that respondents interpret survey scales in ways that deviate from linearity, but only mildly so. The authors then replicate 30,000+ coefficient estimates across more than 80 papers published in top economics journals, finding that coefficient signs are remarkably robust to mild departures from linear scale-use. However, estimates of relative effect magnitudes become unreliable, even under modest departures from linearity. This is especially problematic for policy applications. The authors also examine the risks of sign reversals and relative magnitude changes under plausible transformations, finding that the potential for non-linear scale use makes reliable statistical inference considerably more challenging.

Document title: Financial Shocks, Productivity, and Prices
Document description: This research paper investigates the relationship between financial shocks, productivity, and pricing behavior using administrative data from Belgian manufacturing firms. The authors distinguish between physical productivity, which measures input-to-output efficiency, and revenue-based productivity, which conflates price changes with efficiency. They find that tightening credit conditions cause a delayed but persistent decline in physical productivity growth. In the short run, firms respond to credit shortages by lowering prices to raise cash, which helps them maintain spending on innovation and training. However, standard revenue-based productivity metrics misinterpret this price drop as a decline in efficiency, leading to biased estimates. Over the medium to long term, as firms struggle to fund productivity-enhancing activities, physical productivity declines further and prices eventually rise. The study incorporates these findings into a quantitative model to show that accounting for pricing flexibility is crucial for understanding the long-term scarring effects of financial crises on aggregate welfare. The research highlights that firms utilizing low prices as internal financing suffer less productivity damage than those unable to adjust prices.

Document title: Industrial Policies and Firm Performance: A Nuanced Relationship
Document description: This paper studies the relationship between industrial policies and firm performance, showing it varies by instrument, firm and industry characteristics, value chain position, and time horizon. The authors find that protectionist domestic subsidies and export incentives have short-term positive effects on firm performance, but these effects decline over the medium term. In contrast, liberalizing trade barriers have a robust positive association with value added and total factor productivity. The authors also find that the relationship between industrial policies and firm performance varies across different firms within targeted industries, with younger and more credit-constrained firms experiencing larger increases in value added and capital. Industry-level characteristics, such as external financial dependence and markups, also matter, with the positive relationship between industrial policies and firm-level value added being stronger in industries with higher levels of distortions.

Document title: The Asymmetric Incidence of Business Taxes: Survey Evidence from German Firms
Document description: The document discusses the incidence of business taxes on German firms using survey evidence. It presents a novel approach to studying the effects of profit taxes on firms and their stakeholders, including employees, owners, and customers. The authors use a large-scale survey of German firms to examine the short-run direct effects of profit taxes on decision margins, such as wages, prices, and shareholder distributions. Document title: Clean Production, Dirty Sourcing: How Embodied Emissions Alter the Environmental Footprint of Exporters
Document description: This paper examines the relationship between international trade and firm-level environmental outcomes, focusing on how differences in production and sourcing decisions shape emissions. The authors revisit the exporter's environmental premium by incorporating emissions embodied in domestically and internationally sourced intermediate inputs. They document three stylized facts: embodied emissions account for over half of firms' total emissions, exporters' production involves disproportionately more embodied emissions, and once embodied emissions are considered, the exporter's environmental premium reverses. The authors develop a theoretical sourcing model that rationalizes the observed patterns and test its predictions using a shift-share IV strategy based on foreign demand shocks. The analysis reveals that exporters systematically rely on more material inputs and source inputs with higher embodied emissions, leading to a higher total emission intensity. The authors conclude that ignoring embodied emissions may systematically underestimate the true carbon footprint of exporting firms.

Document description: This paper investigates how multinational enterprises adapted their global operations in the post COVID-19 period. Document title: Politicized scientists: Credibility cost of political expression on Twitter
Document description: This study examines the reputational costs for academics when they express political opinions on social media platforms like Twitter. The authors analyze data from nearly 100,000 scientists to show that a significant portion of academics engage in political discourse on these platforms. Using an online experiment with thousands of participants, the researchers found that scientists who express political views are perceived as less credible than those who remain politically neutral. The penalty for political expression is monotonic, meaning that the stronger the political stance, the lower the perceived credibility and the less willing people are to engage with their work. This effect is particularly pronounced among audience members who hold opposing political views. The findings suggest that political engagement creates a credibility gap that extends beyond personal reputation to the credibility of their research. Surveys with scientists indicate that they are aware of these penalties and generally agree to limit political expression outside their professional expertise. The study highlights that political affiliation is the most influential factor affecting public perception of scientists, outweighing other attributes like institutional rank or gender.

Document title: Three Theories of Natural Rate Dynamics
Document description: The natural interest rate is a key concept in macroeconomics, defined as the risk-free real interest rate that would prevail in the absence of nominal rigidities and business cycle fluctuations. The traditional view is that the natural rate primarily depends on structural factors, such as demographics and productivity growth. However, this paper challenges this view by discussing three alternative theories of natural-rate determination, which link the natural rate to fiscal policy, monetary policy, and persistent supply shocks. The first theory considers a standard heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model with a fiscal block and an occasionally-binding zero lower bound, where the natural rate depends on the stock of public debt. The second theory builds a HANK model with a ZLB and aggregate demand shocks, where the natural rate is affected by precautionary savings motives. The third theory analyzes a representative-agent New Keynesian model with persistent supply shocks, where the natural rate is influenced by precautionary savings motives and shifts in the output gap. These theories share a common theme of precautionary savings motives, which have significant implications for monetary policy design, including the need for central banks to track the future path of the natural rate and avoid assuming it is a slow-moving variable.

Document title: The Untold Story of Internal Migration in Germany: Life-Cycle Patterns, Developments, and the Role of Education
Document description: This paper examines internal migration in Germany from a lifetime perspective using unique data on detailed residential biographies of individuals born in Germany between 1944 and 1986. The authors find substantial differences across the life course, with major location changes occurring around important educational decisions and striking differences across groups, especially by educational attainment. The paper investigates causality in the substantial education-mobility gradient and finds no effect of policy-induced sources of variation in education on internal mobility. The results are remarkably stable over the life cycle and robust to alternative model specifications, sample restrictions, and estimation procedures. The authors provide suggestive evidence that the lack of significant mobility effects is most likely due to insufficient effects on academic qualifications, which play a crucial role in certifying an individual's knowledge and skills acquired through education. The paper contributes to the literature on internal mobility patterns in the United States and other countries, providing a comprehensive analysis across the entire life cycle.

Document title: Violent Conflict and Cross-Border Lending
Document description: The document examines the relationship between private finance and armed conflict through the lens of cross-border lending during violent conflicts. It uses data on syndicated loans by 14,021 creditors to firms in 179 countries from 1989 to 2020 and finds that foreign banks reduce overall lending to conflict countries relative to domestic banks, but increase lending to military-related sectors. The reallocation is stronger among lenders less specialized in the conflict country, more specialized in military lending, and domiciled in politically non-aligned nations. The effects are geographically contained and temporally limited, dissipating post-conflict. The study reveals how global banks strategically redirect credit toward military sectors during armed conflicts, despite reducing overall country exposure.

Document title: The Debt Burden of Job Loss in a Nordic Welfare State
Document description: The document discusses the impact of job loss on debt problems in Finland, a Nordic welfare state. It uses linked employer-employee data combined with administrative data on debt enforcement to analyze the effect of job loss on debt-related issues. The results show that job loss increases the likelihood of entering debt enforcement by approximately 10%, with a persistent effect lasting at least ten years. The effect is particularly large for unpaid taxes and various private debts. The study also finds no statistically significant impact on personal bankruptcies within the nine-year follow-up period. Additionally, it provides novel evidence of spillover effects within families, showing that job loss slightly increases the probability that a spouse or child will enter debt enforcement proceedings by approximately 4%. The findings contribute to the broader literature on the economic consequences of job loss, particularly its long-term and intergenerational effects.

Document description: This document studies how public pensions impact lifecycle labor supply decisions in Ecuador. The authors analyze pension eligibility rules and their effects on retirement and earlier-in-life decisions about when to work formally versus informally. They find that workers tend to contribute the minimum number of years required to unlock pension benefits and then claim those benefits and retire when they are first eligible to do so. Document title: Labor Market Consequences of Homicides: Evidence from Mexico
Document description: This paper examines the labor market effects of escalating homicide rates in Mexico, revealing distinct gender dynamics in response to rising homicide rates. Men are more likely to exit the labor market due to reduced demand for their labor, while women increasingly join the workforce, mainly in the informal sector, to offset this decline. The presence of drug trafficking organizations, which primarily employ men in their operations, drives these outcomes. Escalating violence also increases labor mobility, leading to higher job separations, particularly among women seeking safer employment. The findings highlight that while increasing crime in the form of homicides may not induce large changes in the aggregate level of employment, there is evidence of labor reallocation across and within sectors, suggesting an increase in labor market misallocation. The study contributes to the literature on the economic effects of crime at the local level, expanding on the body of research examining the impact of crime on labor force participation and offering new insights into the gendered effects of crime on labor market dynamics.

Document description: The document expresses concerns regarding legislation that has historically been taken up during Police Week. Document description: This paper examines the relationship between monetary policy, mortgage underwriting standards, and rental market equilibria. Document title: Parental Leave from the Firm’s Perspective
Document description: This discussion paper investigates the firm's response to parental leave induced worker absence. The study uses a 20-week maternal leave expansion in Norway and detailed matched employer-employee data between 1983 and 2013 to identify the causal impact of absence on outcomes using a shift-share design. The results show that employers with greater exposure to absence hire more women aged 40 or less and face more employment turnover. These adjustments do not affect profits, but lead to greater investments and sales and to a lower value added and a lower wage bill. One important channel behind such changes is a significant growth of young female part-time employment. The study also highlights the importance of understanding how firms adjust to worker absence due to parental leave, as it can be costly for employers and may have a longer-term strategic impact on firms' human capital composition.

Document title: Participation in Pension Programs in Low and Middle Income Countries
Document description: Low- and middle-income countries are aging rapidly, but the stagnation of growth in participation in pension programs due to widespread informal employment presents a major fiscal challenge. The design and implementation of pension systems could be crucial for promoting or hindering participation. The willingness to contribute to formal pension programs depends on the other means of support available to households. Alternative strategies have evolved with economic development and in response to the introduction of formal pension programs. Pensions are imperfect substitutes for other strategies to cover longevity risk, including support through the family, which will remain crucial for many older people in fiscally constrained environments. Policy makers should integrate the design of contributory pensions, social pensions, and policies that facilitate other forms of elderly support. Participation in pension programs in LMICs responds to program rules, including the payroll tax rate, the retirement age, and the link between contributions and benefits. Financial incentives embedded in pension rules significantly affect participation, at least among salaried workers. The propensity to contribute tends to decline if non-contributory pensions are too generous, the benefits of participation too low, or if payroll contribution rates are too high.

Document title: The Impact of Refugees on Crime: Evidence from Syrian Influx in Türkiye by Nativity of Perpetrators and Victims
Document description: This paper studies the causal effect of immigration on crime in the context of the massive influx of Syrians to Turkey. The authors use comprehensive data that spans all stages of the judicial process and includes information on the nativity status of both perpetrators and victims. They employ a two-stage least squares estimation technique to isolate causal effects and exploit substantial exogenous variation in the migrant-to-native ratio. The findings reveal a slight increase in total crime at the prosecution stage, while no significant effects are detected for criminal court cases or convictions. Natives experience increased victimization at the prosecution stage, while their involvement in criminal activities remains unchanged. In contrast, both the likelihood of committing a crime and being a victim of crime increase among immigrants. The analysis further suggests that immigrants may be crowding out natives in specific crime categories, such as smuggling.

Document description: This document discusses the effectiveness of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) in preventing gender-based violence (GBV) among high school students in Mexico. The study suggests that CBT group-based interventions can be effective in addressing violence and crime among young people at-risk. The authors conclude that further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms through which CBT contributes to GBV prevention.

Document title: The Political Consequences of Controversial Education Reform: Lessons from Wisconsin’s Act 10
Document description: The document discusses the political effects of a controversial education reform in Wisconsin, known as Act 10, which was championed by a Republican governor in 2011. The reform weakened the collective bargaining power of public sector unions, prohibited collective bargaining over teachers' salary schedules, and cut teachers' health care and pension benefits. The authors examine the political effects of the reform, including its impact on voter support for the governor, campaign contributions, and union finances. Document title: Taming cycles
Document description: China's economy blends state planning with market mechanisms, using annual economic targets to guide development and macroeconomic management to ensure their achievement. Local governments set ambitious growth targets to align with central mandates and incentivize subordinates, leading to asymmetric adjustments. When a region falls short of its growth target, it increases infrastructure investment, land sales, and local government debt to close the gap. This has contributed to a 14.0% increase in local government debt relative to GDP. While these interventions stabilized GDP growth, they came at a steep price, and the disconnect between GDP growth and broader economic indicators may stem from mechanisms such as infrastructure investment facing diminishing returns and local government debt crowding out capital. The central government sets national growth targets to anchor local targets, and local governments use macroeconomic management to meet their targets. This has led to a ratchet effect in how local governments adjust their growth targets, raising them aggressively during economic booms but lowering them more cautiously during slowdowns.

Document description: This document explores the economic impact of climate-related physical risks on supply chains in Brazil. Document title: Inequality, urbanization, and the Kuznets process
Document description: This document discusses the relationship between inequality, urbanization, and the Kuznets process in India. It uses data from India's annual Periodic Labour Force Surveys to estimate inequality in monthly per capita household earnings over the period 2017/18 to 2022/23. The authors find that a 1 percentage point increase in the level of urbanization may increase the Mean Log Deviation by 0.5 to 0.7 per cent. They also estimate that inequality will start declining only when India's urbanization rate is in the region of 63 to 74 per cent. The study suggests that the development of the inequality-urbanization relationship at the sub-national level conforms to the Kuznets process. The authors focus on the impact of urbanization on inequality, which is closely related to the work of Kanbur and Zhuang in the context of China, India, Indonesia, and Philippines, and more recently that of Ravallion and Chen in the context of China. The study uses six rounds of India's annual Periodic Labour Force Survey to analyse the relationship between inequality and urbanization. The authors find that the between-group component accounts for between 14 and 16 per cent of inequality, suggesting that India's inequality is largely a story of within-sub-national-unit inequality. The study also finds that the empirical relationship between inequality and urbanization across India's major sub-national units conforms with the Kuznets process.

Document title: Rules versus Discretion in Capital Regulation
Document description: This paper investigates the time inconsistency problem inherent in capital regulation within a dynamic banking model. The authors demonstrate that when deposits are subject to default risk and have long maturities, regulators face a dilemma regarding their ability to commit to future capital requirements. While capital regulations aim to curb excessive leverage that dilutes depositors, optimal policies require balancing this dilution to prevent bank defaults. The study analyzes two scenarios: a baseline model with fixed deposit maturity and an extended model featuring non-maturing deposits where withdrawal decisions are endogenous. Theoretical results show that the ability to commit to future leverage levels significantly affects the optimal steady-state equity ratio and the dynamics of bank default risk. In models with non-maturing deposits, the value of commitment is amplified because commitments regarding future leverage influence current withdrawal behaviors. Furthermore, the research finds that regulatory commitment leads to stronger countercyclical adjustments, where regulators can better manage defaults during negative productivity shocks by maintaining lenient policies for extended periods. The authors also explore partial commitment mechanisms, finding that committing to either equity values or deposit prices can achieve similar incentive alignment as full commitment. Finally, empirical evidence supports the theoretical findings by linking deposit maturity characteristics to the persistence of leverage dynamics among smaller banks.

Document title: Improving Childhood Immunization through Maternal Support: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in Pakistan
Document description: This study evaluates the effectiveness of randomized interventions designed to improve childhood immunization rates in Pakistan by addressing maternal psychological barriers and information frictions. The researchers conducted a trial with 2,145 mothers in rural areas, comparing a psychological support intervention that used visualization techniques against an intervention involving audio messages from community influencers. Results show that the psychological support intervention significantly increased the number of vaccines received by children, with the effect being stronger for lower-income households who face greater stress and resource constraints. In contrast, the influencer intervention did not produce additional benefits and actually reduced the positive impact of the psychological support on vaccination uptake. The study also found that mothers who received psychological support demonstrated improved knowledge and higher expectations regarding the benefits of vaccination, suggesting that alleviating internal psychological barriers fosters better engagement with healthcare systems. While the intervention did not measurably improve overall maternal mental health scores, it appears to have helped mothers overcome specific psychological constraints that hindered their ability to make long-term health decisions. These findings highlight the importance of addressing internal motivators and psychological constraints rather than relying solely on external information or incentives in low-income settings where trust in authorities is low.

Document title: Competition and Consumer Discrimination
Document description: This paper studies consumer discrimination by modeling how firms respond to the preferences of majority and minority consumers in a competitive market. The authors argue that even without discriminatory preferences among business owners, firms will treat groups unequally if they anticipate that non-discriminatory customers will leave for competitors. They find that the ratio of non-discriminatory firms increases as the proportion of minority consumers rises, with the strongest effects observed in less competitive markets where the threat of losing customers is lowest. Using historical data from the mid-20th century, the study analyzes how changes in the Black-to-White consumer ratio influenced business behavior in hotels, restaurants, and gas stations. The researchers utilize exogenous variation in consumer composition derived from World War II casualty rates and migration patterns to isolate causal relationships. Results show that non-discriminatory firms charged higher prices than discriminatory firms, indicating that monopoly power amplified the costs of discrimination for minority consumers. The study highlights that market competition can sustain discriminatory outcomes and that access to non-discriminatory services was heavily dependent on local demographic composition.

Document title: How accurately do consumers report their debts in household surveys?
Document description: This document discusses the accuracy of consumer debt reporting in household surveys. It uses a unique match of a representative sample of individual borrowers from the Chilean Household Finance Survey and their banking loan records to analyze the discrepancies between survey reports and administrative records. The study finds that surveys differ from the credit registry in both the number and amount of loans reported, with a substantial degree of heterogeneity. However, borrowers report delinquency status accurately, and discrepancies in loan amounts can be explained by rounding error in survey answers. The study also finds that discrepancies are larger when respondents are not the highest-income member of the family. The analysis has implications for the measurement of aggregate debt and debt risk, and the study suggests that matched survey-registry datasets can improve this aspect of policy analysis.

Document title: Banks and the State-Dependent Effects of Monetary Policy
Document description: This paper presents empirical evidence that contractionary monetary policy is less effective when interest rates are high compared to when they are low. The authors argue that this state dependence results from the interaction between bank net interest margins and households' high propensity to consume liquid wealth. They construct a banking model where social dynamics influence household attentiveness to deposit rates and embed it within a nonlinear heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model. The analysis shows that after a period of low interest rates, a contractionary shock increases banks' net interest margins, whereas the same shock decreases margins after a period of high rates. This difference occurs because the pass-through of policy rate changes to deposit rates is greater in high-interest-rate environments, which increases household income from savings and dampens the decline in aggregate demand. The study develops both partial equilibrium and general equilibrium models to explain these mechanisms and demonstrates that they accurately capture the observed state-dependent patterns in the data. The research highlights that half of consumers do not know their deposit interest rates, which supports the model's focus on inattentive depositors. By accounting for these behavioral factors, the models explain why macroeconomic responses to monetary policy vary depending on the current interest rate environment.

Document description: The document discusses the relationship between social gaps, perceived inequality, and protests. Document title: Too much of a good thing? The macro implications of massive firm entry
Document description: This document evaluates a unique size-dependent policy in Belgium that subsidises the first employee of new employers. The policy, which exempted firms from paying payroll taxes for a single employee, led to a 7.2% increase in the number of firms with one employee three years after the reform, with little evidence of an increase in firms with more than one employee. A simple frictionless model of occupational choice is developed and calibrated using pre-reform data, which accurately predicts the observed increase in firms with one employee. The model suggests that the policy led to a slight wage increase and a negligible reduction in overall output. The primary beneficiaries of the policy are managers of firms with a single employee, who see their income rise by up to 6.5%. The main loser is the government, as the long-term budgetary cost is substantial. The analysis does not provide an economic justification for this policy, but it may still be supported for other reasons, such as a societal preference for small businesses.

Document title: Wage Fixing
Document description: This paper models and analyzes employer cartels that fix wages by committing to a wage ceiling within a frictional labor market featuring large employers competing via posted wages. The authors demonstrate that wage fixing reduces competition both inside and outside the cartel, leading to market-wide wage depression, with outside employers disciplining the cartel through their labor demand response. The study establishes a sharp characterization of the equilibrium pay distribution, showing that without wage fixing, wages are dispersed, but with a tight ceiling, all cartel employers offer the ceiling while outside employers offer wages just above it. The analysis reveals that wage-fixing cartels are more likely to emerge and remain stable when the labor market has slack, concentration is high, and firms also collude in the product market. The authors extend the model to include capital and inelastic product demand to assess how these factors influence the harm caused by wage fixing, noting that cartels are particularly damaging when outside competition is low or unresponsive. Using a benchmark US calibration, the study finds that removing a cartel results in modest wage gains, but variations in parameters show that wage losses can rise significantly when outside firms do not discipline the cartel effectively. Finally, the paper concludes by proposing a simple sufficient statistic to gauge the harm caused by a wage-fixing cartel without requiring complex production-function based approaches.

Document title: The Importance of Existing Social Protection Programs for Mental Health in Pandemic Times
Document description: The document discusses the importance of existing social protection programs for mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors use panel data from the Philippines to compare depression rates among beneficiaries of a conditional cash transfer program (4Ps) and non-beneficiaries of similar socioeconomic status. They find that depression rates were low and almost identical for both groups in late 2019, but increased dramatically for both groups during the pandemic. However, the increase was significantly lower for 4Ps beneficiaries, suggesting that the 4Ps program mattered more for mental health during the crisis. The authors attribute this to the regular cash support provided by the 4Ps program, which became more valuable during times of economic hardship and uncertainty. They also suggest that the existing program infrastructure enhanced the effectiveness of the government's emergency response to the pandemic, allowing for more timely distribution of emergency cash to existing 4Ps beneficiaries.

Document title: The effects of open banking on fintech providers: evidence using microdata from Spain
Document description: This document investigates the impact of open banking on the development of the fintech sector, focusing particularly on payment-related financial services. The authors use the implementation of the Second Payment Services Directive in Europe as a natural experiment and employ a difference-in-differences methodology to analyze a unique microdata set of 406 Spanish fintech firms from 2014 to 2022. The findings reveal that following the directive, fintech firms specializing in payment services improved their performance compared to non-payment fintechs, with this improvement driven primarily by revenue growth rather than cost reduction. Document title: Income Equality in the Nordic Countries: Myths, Facts, and Lessons
Document description: The document discusses the Nordic countries' social and economic model, which combines low income inequality with prosperity and growth. The authors argue that this model is built on four principal pillars: significant public investment in family policies, education, and health services; coordinated wage-setting within and across industries; substantial expenditure on social insurance to safeguard against income losses due to unemployment, disability, and illness; and high and progressive taxation of labor income. The authors present key facts and debunk some myths and misconceptions about income equality in the Nordic countries, finding that a more equal predistribution of earnings, rather than income redistribution, is the main reason for the lower income inequality in the Nordic countries compared to the U.S. and the U.K. They also argue that equality in hourly pay, not work hours, is the primary explanation for why the Nordic countries have much lower inequality in labor earnings than the U.S. and the U.K. The authors critically examine the evidence base for three popular economic explanations for income equality in the Nordic countries, including the role of daycare, education, and health policies, and the method of wage setting.

Document title: The Parenthood Gap: Firms and Earnings Inequality after Kids
Document description: This document discusses the dynamics of career paths around parenthood, specifically the role of employers in the emergence of the earnings gap between mothers and fathers. The authors use a new linkage between administrative data on U.S. workers' fertility and labor market histories to show that mothers transition to lower-paying firms after parenthood, diverging sharply from the career progressions of fathers. The study reveals four new facts about the emergence of the earnings gap among American mothers and fathers, including the substantial share of the decline in mothers' relative earnings that can be accounted for by transitions to lower-paying firms. The authors also quantify the contribution of gender differences in sorting across firms to the overall parental earnings gap, finding that the share of this gap that can be explained by differences in firm wage policy grows from 23 percent in the year of birth to 34 percent after a decade.

Document title: Institutions, Technology and Prosperity
Document description: This document is a review of the author's research on comparative development, colonialism, and institutional change, which was often conducted in collaboration with James Robinson and Simon Johnson. The author outlines a simple framework centered on a utility-technology possibilities frontier to organize these ideas and connect them with research on innovation and technology. This framework highlights how various types of institutions, market structures, norms, and ideologies influence moves along the frontier and shifts of the frontier. It provides a formalization of the social forces that lead to institutional persistence and those that can trigger institutional change. The framework also enables the conceptualization of how, during periods of disruption, existing and sometimes quite small differences can have amplified effects on prosperity and institutional trajectories. The author suggests some parallels between different disruptive periods, including the onset of European colonialism, the spread of industrial technologies in the 19th century, and decisions related to the use, adoption, and development of AI today. The text begins with the author's personal journey into social science, motivated by observing huge economic and political differences across countries. He describes how his interest in institutions developed after meeting James Robinson and discussing the work of Douglass North. The author details the formation of a research agenda focusing on how institutions emerged and why they remained in place for long periods of time. He explains how they met Simon Johnson to discuss the origins of democracy and the huge differences in economic prosperity around the world. The document concludes by describing the development of their 'Colonial Origins' paper, which used the local disease environment as a source of variation for an instrumental-variables strategy to test hypotheses about colonialism's impact on institutions.

Document title: Market Competition and Shock Propagation: Implications for Margins and Distress
Document description: This research paper investigates how adverse shocks to a firm's cash flows propagate through market competition to affect its industry competitors' profit margins and distress risks. Using local natural disasters as a quasi-experimental setting, the authors demonstrate that when a firm is directly hit by a shock, both it and its unaffected competitors reduce profit margins by approximately 0.8 percentage points due to intensified competition driven by predatory pricing, inventory liquidation, and weakened tacit collusion. The study finds that these margin reductions translate into significantly higher financial distress for competitors, even though they were not directly shocked by the initial event. The spillover effects are most pronounced in tradable industries and those with high entry barriers, large inventories, greater price flexibility, or tight financial constraints. To establish causal evidence, the authors employ a difference-in-differences approach while matching treated firms with non-treated competitors within the same industry to control for endogeneity and treatment externalities. The analysis also rules out alternative channels such as input-output linkages or shared creditors as primary drivers of these spillover effects. Ultimately, the paper highlights the complex nature of strategic market competition and its role in aggregating firm-specific shocks into broader macroeconomic fluctuations.

Document title: Student Loan Forgiveness
Document description: This research paper analyzes the economic impacts of the largest student loan forgiveness event in history, which occurred in March 2021 when the federal government cancelled approximately $132 billion in student debt. The authors utilize administrative credit bureau data to examine how this policy affected borrowers' consumption, borrowing behavior, earnings, and employment. They find that forgiven borrowers had higher predicted monthly earnings compared to those who did not receive relief, though the effect diminishes when accounting for lifecycle factors. The study estimates that for every dollar of student loan debt forgiven, other forms of debt such as mortgages, auto loans, and credit card debt increased by about nine cents. While the policy had little effect on non-student loan delinquencies, borrowers experienced a decline in earnings and employment levels over the months following the cancellation. The researchers attribute these findings to a dynamic difference-in-difference model and an instrumental variables approach to isolate causal effects. The results suggest a marginal propensity for consumption of 0.27 and a negative marginal propensity for earnings of 0.49, indicating that the wealth shock from debt relief was partially offset by reduced labor supply and increased debt in other categories.

Document title: Income Equality in The Nordic Countries: Myths, Facts, and Lessons
Document description: This article critically examines the claim that Nordic countries successfully combine low income inequality with prosperity and growth by analyzing the factors driving their economic model. The authors argue that income equality in these nations is primarily caused by the compression of hourly wages, which reduces the returns to labor market skills and education. This wage compression is achieved through a coordinated wage-bargaining system that operates both within and across industries, contrasting with explanations that rely on tax redistribution or public spending. The study finds that while public investments in family policies, education, and health are substantial, they play a minor role in explaining the observed wage equality compared to the wage premium differences seen in the U.S. and U.K. Additionally, the analysis highlights that equality in hourly pay, rather than work hours, is the main driver of lower earnings inequality. The paper further explores two opposing views regarding the impact of the Nordic model on productivity and growth, noting that empirical evidence to date remains largely correlational. Ultimately, the authors conclude that future progress requires advances in both theory and measurement to better understand labor markets and wage-setting institutions.

Document description: The document discusses government support in times of crisis, specifically the resilience of incumbents during economic downturns. Document title: Environmental Migration and Race during the Great American Drought, 1935-1940
Document description: This study examines racial disparities in internal migration responses to the severe drought of the 1930s using 1940 census data on 65 million adults. The authors find that individuals exposed to more severe drought were more likely to move between counties, with this response being significantly stronger for Black individuals than for White individuals. This difference was particularly pronounced among the rural population, where Black individuals showed a much higher migration premium despite facing systematic economic disadvantages. The analysis incorporates data on federal spending under the Agricultural Adjustment Act, which provided relief to agricultural communities but was limited to landowners. Results indicate that greater federal spending reduced migration responses for White individuals while simultaneously increasing it for Black individuals, thereby widening the racial gap in migration behavior. These findings suggest that government policy and economic constraints influenced how different racial groups adapted to the climatic shock. The study contributes to understanding how migration responses aggregate to determine the magnitude of disaster impacts and highlights the role of policy in disadvantaged groups' ability to adapt.

Document title: Capital Structure & Firm Outcomes: Evidence from Dividend Recapitalizations in Private Equity
Document description: This study examines the impact of large increases in firm leverage using data from private equity-sponsored dividend recapitalizations. The authors find that these transactions significantly increase the likelihood of financial distress over the following decade, bringing firms closer to failure levels. Despite the increased risk, dividend recapitalizations appear to improve returns for individual deals by accelerating cash flows, even though they reduce overall fund returns. The research also reveals negative consequences for employees, including a substantial decline in average wages and higher risks of firm exit. By isolating the causal effect of debt through specific credit supply channels, the paper provides evidence that higher leverage correlates with increased distress and wage suppression while potentially offering short-term financial gains to investors.

Document title: The Long-Run Effects of America's Largest Residential Racial Desegregation Program: Gautreaux
Document description: This paper examines the long-term consequences of the Gautreaux Assisted Housing Program, which was the largest residential racial desegregation initiative in U.S. history. Between 1976 and 1998, the program relocated thousands of Black families from urban Chicago neighborhoods to predominantly white areas to promote racial and economic integration. The authors link historical program records with administrative data to analyze how these specific moves affected children decades later. Results indicate that children placed in predominantly white neighborhoods experienced significant gains in future lifetime earnings and accumulated wealth compared to those placed in revitalizing Black areas. These children were also more likely to marry and were twice as likely to marry a white spouse, though this increased the distance from their families. Furthermore, adults who were desegregated through the program tend to live in more racially diverse neighborhoods with higher rates of upward mobility nearly forty years after the intervention. The study concludes that the distinct impacts of racial composition versus poverty rates highlight the importance of racial integration for social outcomes.

Document description: This paper investigates how family and firm investments interact to create gender gaps in career achievement using Danish administrative data. The authors document a spousal effect where family labor supply choices shape worker characteristics, which subsequently influence firms' training and promotion decisions. They develop a quantitative life cycle model that captures these interactions through household formation, joint career and fertility choices, and firm managerial training. Specifically, parental leave involves costly skill depreciation while the quota raises aggregate welfare by encouraging marital sorting toward families that invest in women. The analysis demonstrates that considering the joint reactions of families and firms is essential for designing effective policies to reduce gender gaps in access to leadership opportunities.

Document title: Market Macrostructure: Institutions and Asset Prices
Document description: This article reviews the emerging field of market macrostructure, which examines how the broad organization of financial markets into key players and institutional features influences asset prices and their dynamics. The authors present a simple theoretical model to analyze how active financial institutions interact with inactive end investors to determine equilibrium prices, highlighting that the strategies of large institutions significantly affect market outcomes. The paper identifies three complementary approaches used in the literature: quasi-natural experiments that provide empirical evidence of macrostructure effects, equilibrium models that focus on economic mechanisms and dynamics, and bottom-up approaches utilizing detailed asset position data. The review specifically highlights three major examples of shifting market structures, including the rise of passive investing in stock markets, the increasing dominance of central banks in bond markets through asset purchase programs, and the impact of levered financial intermediaries during financial crises. By synthesizing these perspectives, the authors aim to clarify the mechanisms through which institutional changes drive price levels and volatility across different asset classes. The discussion emphasizes the importance of quantity data and equilibrium modeling to better understand these structural shifts and their implications for financial stability.

Document description: This document is a discussion paper titled Public Pensions, Retirement, and Earlier-in-Life Labor Supply: Preliminary Evidence from Ecuador. Document title: Guns and Growth: The Economic Consequences of Defense Buildups
Document description: The document investigates the economic consequences of defense buildups, particularly in the context of rising geopolitical tensions. It draws on a large literature in macroeconomics, public finance, defense and peace studies, economic history, and the study of productivity. The main conclusions are that an increase in military expenditures can lead to economic expansion, with the economy accommodating at least part of the increased defense spending. However, the magnitude of this expansion and whether military spending crowds out or stimulates the private sector is still debated. The evidence suggests that military spending may have a positive impact on economic growth, particularly in the short run. Additionally, the document highlights the potential long-run productivity gains from military spending, particularly through learning-by-doing and R&D. It also emphasizes the need for European defense procurement to be more coordinated and for a more efficient use of resources. The document concludes that setting percent-of-GDP targets for military spending is counterproductive and that a long-run cost-benefit analysis of the materiel and personnel requirements is necessary.
