Document title: Workers' Job Prospects and Young Firm Dynamics
Document description: This discussion paper investigates how worker beliefs and job prospects impact the wages and growth of young firms, as well as the aggregate economy. The paper builds a heterogeneous-firm directed search model where workers gradually learn about firm types, finding that learning generates endogenous wage differentials for young firms. High-performing young firms must pay higher wages than equally high-performing old firms, while low-performing young firms offer lower wages than equally low-performing old firms. Reduced uncertainty or labor market frictions lower the wage differentials, thereby enhancing young firm dynamics and aggregate productivity. The results are consistent with U.S. administrative employee-employer matched data. The paper also uses the Census datasets to confirm these model predictions, finding that young firms with high past-average productivity pay more than their observationally similar mature counterparts, while those with low past-average productivity pay less compared to their otherwise similar mature counterparts. The earnings differentials are negatively associated with firm hiring and employment growth. Moreover, the paper estimates the impact of uncertainty on the earnings differentials of young firms, finding that earnings differentials are more pronounced in industries with higher uncertainty.

Document title: Intergenerational Mobility in Depression and Anxiety in India
Document description: This paper examines intergenerational mobility in mental health in India, a low- and middle-income country. Using data from over 4,000 parent-child pairs, the authors find that there is a strong intergenerational association in depression and anxiety scores, with children of parents with mental health issues experiencing similar problems. However, the authors also find that children of parents with mild to severe symptoms experience significant improvements in mental health, particularly in high-socioeconomic-status households. The study suggests that programs that improve mental health in one generation can also facilitate intergenerational mobility in mental health and related outcomes. The authors also find that even minimal symptoms of depression and anxiety can have significant economic implications for both children and adults. The study contributes to the literature on intergenerational mobility in mental health and provides new insights into the transmission of mental health across generations.

Document title: Passing as White: Racial Identity and Old-Age Longevity
Document description: This study examines the long-term effects of African Americans changing their racial identity to pass as white on old-age longevity. The authors analyze historical census data from 1880 to 1940 and link it with Social Security death records from 1975 to 2005 to create a longitudinal dataset of black families. Using family fixed effects, the research demonstrates that individuals who passed for white lived approximately 9.4 months longer than their non-passing siblings. The analysis suggests that improvements in education and occupational standing, along with differential parental investments, are likely pathways for these longevity gains. The study finds that the benefits of passing are particularly substantial for migrants and those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. While previous research has focused on short-term economic outcomes, this paper extends the literature by investigating the cumulative impact of racial passing on mortality. The findings contribute to a broader understanding of how life-cycle conditions and racial identity shape health outcomes over time.

Document description: This research paper analyzes the impact of World War II Army service on income and mobility among male veterans from various ethnoracial groups, including Non-Hispanic Whites, Blacks, Hispanics, Asians, and Native Americans. Document title: New approaches to labour market integration of migrants and refugees
Translated title: New approaches to labour market integration of migrants and refugees - Publications Office of the EU
Document description: The integration of migrants and refugees into the labour market remains a critical challenge for European countries. Labour market integration is hindered by various factors, including language barriers, skill downgrading, and legal obstacles. Migrants often experience higher unemployment rates, over-representation in lower-skilled jobs, and under-utilisation of their qualifications. Refugees, in particular, face compounded disadvantages due to their traumatic displacement experiences and legal uncertainties. This study provides a comprehensive review of existing research, challenges, and policy responses aimed at improving the labour market integration of migrants and refugees within the European Union. The study focuses on one specific element of migrant integration: labour market integration (or, economic integration). Labour market integration is defined as the extent to which migrants will achieve the same range of labour market participation as nationals of EU Member States by using their skills and realising their economic potential. A comprehensive evaluation of labour market integration requires consideration of multiple indicators. Employment status is often seen as the primary indicator of labour market integration, yet labour market participation and job quality are also crucial. Job quality spans various factors, such as wages, working conditions, contract type, working hours, and the match between jobs and workers' skills and qualifications—all contributing to migrants' ability to realise their potential in host countries. Successful labour market integration is vital for reducing reliance on welfare, increasing economic contributions, and addressing labour shortages, particularly in the context of ageing populations in Europe, thereby boosting overall income per capita and productivity. The role of policymakers is critical in this process; they should implement strategies that effectively utilise migrants' skills while safeguarding against exploitation, which aligns with key Sustainable Development Goals aimed at ensuring decent work and reducing inequalities, ultimately fostering responsible and effective migration policies for the future.

Document title: Credit rating agencies, developing countries and bias
Document description: This policy review explores the differences in sovereign credit ratings between developed and developing countries, investigating whether these differences are due to higher probabilities of default or biases against developing countries. The review finds that subjective indicators and sentiment play a significant role in determining rating opinions, creating scope for bias. Studies have identified various types of ratings bias that have historically favoured developed countries over developing ones. However, the review concludes that focusing on addressing perceived ratings biases may not be the most constructive way forward. Instead, it proposes several initiatives to improve the sovereign ratings process and limit negative impacts on developing countries, including developing a more effective global financial safety net and providing technical assistance to developing countries. The review also suggests that market movements sometimes lead and sometimes follow ratings decisions, and that reliance on ratings is reduced where the rated country acts to reduce information asymmetries. The analysis finds that financial markets tend to price the risks associated with countries' debt instruments independently, even when rating agencies assess their risks of default to be similar. The review also notes that acquiring a credit rating is usually a prerequisite for a debt issuer to participate fully in global capital markets, and that countries require a rating of BBB- or higher to access international capital at lower rates.

Document title: Artificial Intelligence Asset Pricing Models
Document description: This paper introduces a new asset pricing model that integrates a large-scale transformer architecture into the stochastic discount factor to improve prediction accuracy. The authors argue that traditional models focusing on individual assets fail to capture the full context provided by the broader market, a limitation that modern artificial intelligence techniques address through cross-asset information sharing. By embedding a transformer network, the proposed model leverages nonlinearities and massive parameterization to generate context-aware forecasts for asset prices. The researchers first develop a simplified linear version of this model to analyze the theoretical impact of attention mechanisms on portfolio weights, showing how cross-asset relationships can be modeled as additional parameters. Empirical tests on US stock data reveal that this approach significantly reduces pricing errors and increases Sharpe ratios compared to existing machine learning models. The study further demonstrates that performance improves as the model's complexity and depth increase, confirming the benefits of extensive parameterization. Finally, the authors compare their model's learned information patterns with observable economic linkages between firms, finding that both methods provide complementary insights into cross-asset relationships.

Document title: Voluntary Accreditation and Healthcare Quality: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial in U.S. Jails
Document description: This document presents findings from a randomized controlled trial conducted in U.S. jails to evaluate the impact of voluntary healthcare accreditation on care quality and mortality rates. The study, led by researchers from Stanford and Harvard universities, assigned 46 jails to either receive an offer of accreditation from the National Commission on Correctional Health Care or serve as a control group. Results indicate that accreditation significantly improved compliance with quality standards, particularly in areas such as personnel training and patient care, without requiring additional capital or labor inputs. The intervention led to a substantial reduction in the twelve-month mortality rate among incarcerated individuals, with the largest decreases observed in facilities that achieved the greatest improvements in quality metrics. The authors attribute these positive outcomes to mechanisms such as improved coordination between staff, better screening procedures, and enhanced oversight rather than changes in resource levels. Despite the widespread use of accreditation in other sectors like hospitals, its effectiveness in correctional settings has been understudied, and this research provides the first causal evidence of its benefits in this context. The study highlights the critical need for quality assurance mechanisms given the high rates of preventable deaths and the constitutional obligation to provide adequate healthcare to inmates. Document title: Externalities and the Taxation of Top Earners
Document description: This paper addresses the optimal taxation of top earners by incorporating externalities, which are effects top earners have on the broader economy. The author develops a reduced-form model that allows for both positive externalities like innovation and negative ones like rent-extraction without relying on specific theoretical assumptions. The analysis highlights that externalities running from top earners to bottom earners have significantly stronger tax implications than those occurring within the top group. The study derives simple formulas for optimal taxation that link directly to estimable statistics and recent empirical evidence regarding the externalities of entrepreneurs. Using quasi-experimental data, the author estimates that top earners generate positive externalities on the bottom population, leading to a higher optimal tax rate than currently applied. A calibration of these findings to the United States economy suggests that the optimal top tax rate should be approximately 50 percent, which is higher than the existing rate of 44.4 percent. The results demonstrate that while the optimal rate is lower than the standard Mirrleesian optimum, it remains substantial and necessary to account for the economic impact of high earners. The paper concludes by emphasizing the need for further empirical research to reduce uncertainty around the key externality parameters identified in the analysis.

Document title: Conspicuous Consumption and Visible Inequality
Document description: This document discusses the effect of visible inequality on household spending in the United States from 2010 to 2018. The authors propose a definition of visible inequality as differences in expenditures on highly noticeable consumption categories, including clothing, personal care, food away from home, and vehicles. They use data from the Consumer Expenditure Survey and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics to document a significant effect of visible inequality on household spending. The authors argue that their findings are driven by consumption externalities and not by confounding correlated effects or a failure to account for permanent income. They also discuss the challenges of distinguishing between the impact of group behavior on individual choices and the aggregation of similar individual behaviors. The authors' empirical strategy relies on a simple model of intertemporal choice that incorporates relative consumption and uses a measure of visible spending, a definition of reference groups, and a proxy for the distribution of visible spending within each reference group. They find that consumption externalities significantly distort household spending, which could have been up to 25 percent lower without these distortions. The authors also discuss the potential endogeneity concerns and address them by using a battery of fixed effects and controlling for individual permanent incomes. They conclude that their analysis contributes to the literature on consumption inequality by calling attention to the effect of visible inequality on spending behavior in the U.S. over the period 2010–2018.

Document title: Are Big Cities Important for Economic Growth?
Document description: This paper quantitatively evaluates the claim that large cities are engines of economic growth by analyzing their impact on output and technological progress in the United States between 1900 and 2010. The authors examine three specific mechanisms: static agglomeration effects that improve production efficiency, dynamic effects where urban scale increases the productivity of invention, and the role of improved sorting of people into high-productivity locations. Using data on population, output, and patents from Metropolitan Statistical Areas, the study compares actual growth to counterfactual scenarios where city sizes were artificially limited to one million or one hundred thousand people. The results indicate that the contribution of large cities to aggregate income growth is relatively small, with limiting city sizes to one million people reducing output by only eight percent by 2010. The authors attribute this finding to modest estimates of urban scale effects on output and human capital, as well as a negative feedback loop where lower technological progress in smaller cities reduces the efficacy of future research and development. While the study finds that larger cities foster more innovation from a given research workforce, the overall impact on long-term total factor productivity growth is limited by the diminishing returns associated with lower levels of technology.

Document description: This document examines the electoral repercussions of denialist campaigns during a global pandemic, focusing on the impact of COVID-19 on the electoral performance of Brazil's former president Jair Bolsonaro. Document description: This document analyzes the impact of geopolitical rivalry between major trading economies on the stability and purpose of the global trading system. The research utilizes a neoclassical trade model to show that geopolitical tensions generally lead to higher non-cooperative tariffs but do not eliminate the potential for mutually beneficial policy adjustments. The authors conclude that the World Trade Organization can continue to thrive if it adapts its rules and norms to address geopolitical imperatives rather than adhering rigidly to existing frameworks. Ultimately, the paper asserts that enlightened self-interest remains a driver for cooperation even in an era of geopolitical conflict, provided countries still value their own underlying objectives.

Document title: Tax evasion and the contribution-benefit link: the case of maternity benefits
Document description: This paper studies tax evasion and the contribution-benefit link in the context of maternity benefits in Hungary. The authors analyze reported earnings and employment before and after childbirth in an environment where the amount of maternity benefits received depends on earnings over a narrow time window before childbirth. The results show that in response to changing reporting incentives, reported earnings and formal employment increase during pregnancy, and this response is stronger after 2015. The authors also document an extensive-margin formalization response to maternity benefit incentives and find that tax evasion is responsive to the incentives created by the contribution-benefit link. The results highlight that contribution-dependent benefits can help formalize the employment and earnings of some workers.

Document title: Recidivism and Barriers to Reintegration: A Field Experiment Encouraging Use of Reentry Support
Document description: This document presents a field experiment that aims to reduce recidivism among previously incarcerated individuals by encouraging the use of reentry support services. The study found that participants who received a monetary incentive to complete a certain number of visits to a support service provider were more likely to complete visits and experience a reduction in rearrest rates. The results suggest that heterogeneity in treatment take-up might translate into heterogeneity in treatment effects, with Black participants being more likely to take up the treatment and experiencing a larger reduction in rearrest rates. The study also found that visits that included counseling, mentoring, or peer or job-related support were associated with the largest decline in arrests. The findings suggest that improving treatment assignment and increasing the use of effective services could help reduce recidivism.

Document title: The use and disuse of FinTech credit: When buy-now-pay-later meets credit reporting
Document description: This document explores the impact of credit reporting on the use of buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) credit. The authors analyze a unique dataset of 200,000 BNPL users from a large digital platform in China and find that credit reporting significantly reduces BNPL usage. The reduction in BNPL usage is particularly pronounced among borrowers with default histories, who also show improved repayment behaviors. The authors also find that the reduction in BNPL usage leads to a decrease in online consumption, supporting the financial constraint hypothesis. Furthermore, the authors highlight the synergies between BNPL lending and Big Tech platforms' ecosystems, which imperfectly substitute for formal enforcement institutions. The study contributes to the literature on FinTech, information sharing, and consumer credit by providing new insights into the benefits of credit reporting in containing BNPL usage and online consumption.

Document title: Residual Mortgage Debt, Insurance, and Defaults in the Netherlands
Document description: The document discusses residual mortgage debt, insurance, and defaults in the Netherlands. It examines how mortgage insurance affects decisions to default and combines a quasi-natural experiment with the estimation of a structural model. The findings reveal that the utility from future home equity negatively influences the likelihood of default. The study also investigates the effect of residual mortgage debt insurance on defaults and finds that it does not cause defaults in general, but it does lead to more defaults for borrowers who separate from their partners, possibly indicating moral hazard. The insurance becomes active when someone divorces or gets unemployed or disabled, but it does not condition the reimbursement of residual debt on defaulting. The study uses data from the Dutch mortgage market and focuses on the National Hypotheek Garantie, a residual mortgage debt insurance that is available for houses with values below a certain threshold. The threshold is set yearly and varies over time, providing a unique quasi-natural setting to identify the relevance of debt insurance in mortgage defaults. The study also discusses the institutional context of the Dutch mortgage market, including the mortgage market structure, the role of the National Hypotheek Garantie, and the characteristics of the mortgage contracts.

Document title: Vaccines on the Move and the War on Polio
Document description: The document investigates the impact of internally displaced people (IDPs) on the incidence of polio in host communities. The authors examine the mass displacement of the population from the conflict-affected Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) in Pakistan from 2008 onward. Using a difference-in-differences approach, they compare new polio cases in districts closer and further away from the FATA border before and after 2008. The authors find that an increase in predicted IDP inflow leads to a rise in new polio cases per 100,000 inhabitants, and that poorer vaccination levels among IDP children compared to native children in host communities are a main mechanism. They also evaluate an innovative program launched in 2012 that vaccinates IDP children during their migration journey, and find that it effectively targets IDP children, raising their vaccination likelihood and bringing broader health benefits. The authors suggest that the program mitigates the polio incidence in host districts, and that the vaccination gap between IDP and native children is a major channel. The study adds to the literature on the consequences of forcibly displaced populations in host communities' health outcomes, and has implications for designing interventions in transit zones and host communities.

Document title: New Approaches to Labour Market Integration of Migrants and Refugees
Document description: The integration of migrants and refugees into the labour market remains a critical challenge for European countries. Labour market integration is hindered by various factors, including language barriers, skill downgrading, and legal obstacles. Migrants often experience higher unemployment rates, over-representation in lower-skilled jobs, and under-utilisation of their qualifications. Refugees, in particular, face compounded disadvantages due to their traumatic displacement experiences and legal uncertainties. This study provides a comprehensive review of existing research, challenges, and policy responses aimed at improving the labour market integration of migrants and refugees within the European Union. The study identifies nine key integration challenges and discusses existing evidence and policy implications. The study concludes by drawing some policy recommendations, including early interventions soon after arrival, careful consideration of policy trade-offs, and the removal of unnecessary integration barriers. By addressing these challenges and implementing targeted policies, the EU and its Member States can better harness the potential of migrants and refugees, leading to more inclusive labour markets and stronger economic growth.

Document title: The firm-wage gender gap and formal sector churn over the life cycle
Document description: This study examines the firm-wage gender gap in South Africa, focusing on the role of firm sorting and worker transitions. The authors find that women sorting into lower-wage firms explains nearly half of the gender wage gap, with the gap growing steeply for 25-35-year-olds and narrowing for older workers. The increase in the gap is driven by continuously employed women being less likely to move to better-paying firms, while men are more likely to switch to better-paying firms. The study also finds that firm-wage gender gaps diverge at the period when women are likely to co-reside with their young children, and that women enter formal employment at worse-paying firms than men. The authors suggest that firm sorting plays a significant role in shaping gender wage inequality in developing countries, and that employment segregation across firms is an important factor.

Document title: Trade and Intergenerational Income Mobility: Theory and Evidence
Document description: This paper studies the impact of globalization on intergenerational income mobility. Exploiting U.S. data, it finds that stronger trade exposure at the commuting zone level lowers the intergenerational income mobility of residents. A general equilibrium theory is presented, which predicts that rising import competition reduces intergenerational income mobility, consistent with the empirical findings. The theory features path dependence in sector choice of individuals over generations and mobility frictions determining the dynamics of industrial compositions across locations in a country. The paper also presents numerical solutions to the theory, which show the reduction of intergenerational income mobility of workers from locations with relatively high exposure to a trade shock. The analysis points to globalization, by means of growing trade exposure, as a significant determinant of reduced intergenerational income mobility.

Document title: Robotizácia na Slovensku 2004-2022
Translated title: Robotization in Slovakia 2004-2022
Document description: This research paper examines the impact of robotic technologies on the labor market in Slovakia between 2004 and 2022, focusing on wages and employment levels. The authors utilize an instrumental variable approach to identify positive effects of robot adoption on wages, which aligns with findings from other studies. Regarding employment, the analysis reveals very small and statistically insignificant effects, suggesting that robots do not significantly displace human labor in Slovakia. These results support similar findings from companies in the Czech Republic and the Netherlands, as well as international data sources. The study highlights that robotized firms show increased productivity, which creates new job opportunities rather than displacing human workers. Additionally, the results indicate that the adoption of robotic technologies is primarily driven by industry-specific demand rather than local labor market conditions. The paper uses a panel dataset of employer-employee relationships to analyze individual outcomes and avoids relying solely on aggregate data. The study also defines robots according to the ISO 8373 standard, distinguishing them from other automation technologies based on their programmability and autonomy.

Document title: Determinants of Recidivism: How Criminal Justice Interactions and the Post-Release Environment Affect Repeat Offending
Document description: This research report by Randi Hjalmarsson examines the determinants of recidivism, focusing on four key factors: the probability of getting caught, alternatives to prison, prison conditions, and the post-release environment. The author reviews extensive research using quasi-experimental designs to distinguish between correlation and causation, with a specific focus on the Swedish context. The report analyzes evidence regarding police presence, DNA databases, and sexual offender registers, noting that while DNA registration reduces recidivism in some countries, similar evaluations are lacking in Sweden. It also evaluates alternatives to imprisonment, such as diversion and electronic monitoring, finding strong evidence that electronic monitoring reduces recidivism without increasing it. The study further explores the impact of prison time and conditions, highlighting mixed results on juvenile and adult incarceration while confirming that longer sentences and better prison conditions generally reduce reoffending rates. Additionally, the report discusses how exposure to other inmates and specific prison programs can influence behavioral outcomes. Finally, the text concludes that evidence-based policies are crucial for reducing crime, emphasizing the need to understand causal links rather than relying solely on observed correlations.

Document title: Spillovers in criminal networks: Evidence from co-offender deaths
Document description: This document studies the impact of co-offender deaths on criminal behavior within networks. The authors use administrative data from Sweden and leverage co-offender deaths as a natural experiment to investigate the spillover effects of permanently removing a co-offender from their co-offending network. They find that the death of a co-offender significantly reduces the criminal activities of other network members, with the effect decreasing as the network distance from the deceased co-offender increases. The authors also show that the death of a more central co-offender leads to a larger reduction in aggregate crime. Additionally, they provide evidence suggesting that the loss of a co-offender shrinks the future information set of offenders, which can influence their perceived probability of being convicted and consequently their criminal behavior. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for spillover effects in designing more effective strategies for crime prevention.

Document title: Financial Conditions Targeting
Document description: This paper presents evidence that noisy financial flows influence financial conditions and macroeconomic activity, prompting a reevaluation of how monetary policy should respond. The authors develop a model where it is optimal for a central bank to target and partially stabilize financial conditions beyond their direct impact on output and inflation gaps. In this framework, noise affects asset prices because arbitrageurs are reluctant to trade against them due to aggregate return volatility, creating a feedback loop that amplifies price fluctuations. The authors argue that announcing a soft Financial Conditions Index target and adjusting the policy rate to maintain it close to that target is a superior strategy compared to traditional interest rate forward guidance. This approach recruits arbitrageurs to absorb noise shocks in real time, thereby reducing volatility and stabilizing the output gap and inflation. Empirical analysis using U.S. data suggests that implementing such a policy could significantly reduce the variance of the output gap, inflation, and interest rates while decreasing the volatility of financial conditions. The study extends existing policy counterfactual methods to account for the endogenous risk reduction mechanism inherent in this theoretical model.

Document title: The Impact of Racial Segregation on College Attainment in Spatial Equilibrium
Document description: This paper explores the mechanisms behind racial segregation and the Black-White gap in college attainment in the St. Louis metro area. The authors build an overlapping-generations spatial-equilibrium model to study the forces that maintain racial segregation and the Black-White gap in college attainment. They find that the Black-White wage gap, amenity externalities, and additional barriers to moving faced by Black households account for 71% of the racial segregation and 64% of the college gap. The model also suggests that there exists a more integrated equilibrium with a lower college gap, and that place-based policy interventions can destabilize the segregated equilibrium. The authors compare various place-based policy interventions, including Moving to Opportunity and Opportunity Zones, to evaluate their effectiveness in reducing segregation and destabilizing the segregated equilibrium.

Document description: The document discusses the role of asymmetric public consumption rigidities in emerging markets. It highlights how emerging markets exhibit 'downward rigidity' by boosting spending during upswings but not effectively cutting back during downturns. This creates fiscal gaps and leads to sustained growth in the size of the state. The document also notes that public consumption expenditures play a crucial role in facilitating the provision of essential public goods, and that emerging markets tend to experience significant overspending during expansions and near-zero growth rates during contractions. In contrast, advanced economies exhibit more consistent spending behavior throughout the economic cycle.

Document title: Racial Screening on the Big Screen? Evidence from the Motion Picture Industry
Document description: This paper develops a theoretical model of discrimination to analyze racial underrepresentation in the US motion picture industry. The authors leverage a novel dataset containing racial identifiers for the casts of over 7,000 films released between 1997 and 2017 to test their theoretical predictions. They find that non-white movies, defined as those with two or more non-white top-billed performers, generate significantly higher average box office revenues compared to white movies. The study argues that these results are consistent with taste-based discrimination rather than customer or statistical discrimination. Specifically, the authors suggest that non-white movies are held to higher production standards, meaning they are only produced if their expected revenue exceeds a higher threshold than white movies. The research concludes that this pattern likely stems from either pure producer bias or a systematic underestimation of the commercial potential of non-white films.

Document title: r-g before and after the Great Wars 1507-2023
Document description: This paper presents new long-run data on the difference between real interest rates and economic growth rates for major advanced economies spanning over three centuries. The authors analyze these series using various econometric methods to determine their stability and trends over time. Their findings indicate that while the series are trend stationary, a significant structural break occurred around the first third of the 20th century. Prior to this break, there was a consistent downward trend in the interest rate minus growth rate differential, which leveled off in the early 1930s. Since then, the data shows high volatility combined with upward pressure on the differential, challenging the notion of permanently low rates. The authors attribute this historical shift to the establishment of welfare states and changes in government expenditures. These results suggest caution regarding the assumption that public debt sustainability has improved structurally in recent decades. The study also incorporates riskier components of capital returns to assess dynamic efficiency and highlights the role of financial repression in maintaining low interest rates. Overall, the research provides a critical long-term perspective on macroeconomic dynamics and debt sustainability that contrasts with recent literature focusing on shorter time horizons.

Document description: This research paper evaluates the impact of Step Up, a cognitive behavioral therapy program designed to reduce violence and improve safety in jails. The study focuses on the Lubbock County Detention Center in Texas, where participants with violent backgrounds engage in a structured curriculum involving group classes, counseling, and workbooks to manage emotions and change behavior patterns. Document title: The Signaling Value of Government Action: The Effect of Istanbul Convention on Female Murders
Document description: This paper analyzes the signaling value of government action by examining the impact of Turkey's ratification and subsequent withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention, an international treaty aimed at protecting women from violence. The authors argue that while the withdrawal did not change formal laws, it sent a signal of increased tolerance for violence, leading to a measurable rise in female murders. Using data on domestic violence and homicides, the study employs a difference-in-difference model to compare the effects of the convention's entry in 2011 and its exit in 2021. Results indicate that the withdrawal resulted in approximately 65 additional female murders per year, with most victims being intimate partners. Conversely, the initial entry into the convention led to a decrease in female murders, suggesting that the act of signing served as a powerful normative signal against violence. This effect was particularly pronounced in provinces with lower education levels and stronger support for religious-conservative parties. The findings support the broader premise that government actions function as signals that shape societal norms and influence behavior, even when they do not alter the specific legal penalties for crimes.

Document title: The Economics of “Buy Now, Pay Later”: A Merchant’s Perspective
Document description: This paper analyzes the economics of Buy Now Pay Later services from the perspective of merchants, arguing that bundling a product with a subsidized loan allows sellers to price-discriminate based on customer willingness to pay. The authors present a theoretical model showing that offering delayed payment options increases sales, particularly among customers with lower creditworthiness, while also noting that such services are more common in online than physical retail settings. Using microdata from a German furniture retailer, the study confirms that making BNPL available increases sales by approximately 20 percent, with a significant portion of this growth driven by new customers rather than existing ones. The analysis reveals that customers with higher credit scores and those interested in high-margin products are more likely to receive approval for these loans. Despite the costs associated with providing zero-interest loans and potential defaults, the authors find that BNPL significantly increases merchant profitability, following an inverse U-shape where the service is most profitable for customers with average creditworthiness. The study concludes that the merchant's role in subsidizing the loan is crucial for this mechanism to work, distinguishing it from other forms of consumer credit like credit cards.

Document title: r-g before and after the Great Wars 1507–2023
Document description: This document explores the econometric properties of advanced economy interest rate-output growth spreads (r-g) over the very long-run, based on new data. The authors reconstruct annual-level r-g series for key advanced economies over centuries, including the U.K., the U.S., Germany, and France, exploiting recent data advancements. They find strong evidence of trend stationarity in these series, although they confirm a major structural break in the first third of the 20th century. The authors associate this break with the establishment and growth of welfare states in advanced economies and the surge in non-defense, non-interest expenditures. They also discuss the implications of their findings for debates on debt sustainability and dynamic efficiency. The authors suggest that existing notions of secularly improving debt sustainability in advanced economies should be treated much more cautiously, taking into account the possibility of adverse dynamics since the interwar era. They conclude that their results challenge the prevailing consensus that r-g differentials in advanced economies will likely continue to be historically low and regularly be negative.

Document title: Tax Policy, Investment and Profit Shifting
Document description: This paper investigates the relationship between tax policy, investment decisions, and profit shifting by multinational enterprises using UK administrative data. The authors develop a model that accounts for both intensive and extensive margin profit-shifting decisions, where some firms shift all profits to tax havens due to high fixed and variable costs. By estimating structural parameters, the study finds that micro-level elasticities significantly underestimate aggregate elasticities by approximately 50% when ignoring extensive margin responses. The research quantifies the costs of profit shifting, estimating fixed costs at 1.5% and variable costs at 3.1% of the true tax base. The authors validate their model using a quasi-natural experiment based on an Italian tax reform that restricted profit shifting by foreign-owned subsidiaries. The findings suggest that curbing profit shifting reduces investment in productive assets and provides insights into the welfare impacts of potential tax reforms such as global minimum tax rates.

Document title: Forced Displacement, the Perpetuation of Autocratic Leaders, and Development in Origin Countries
Document description: This paper investigates the economic and political consequences of forced migration in Venezuela between 1992 and 2021, focusing on how mass exodus affects origin countries with weak institutions. The authors analyze data from oil price shocks after 2013 and historical foreign settlement shares to determine the impact of migration on local development. They find that municipalities with higher migration rates experienced significant GDP contraction, reduced income per capita, increased inequality, and lower employment levels. Document title: Liquidity Shocks and Firm Exports: Evidence from Cash Shortages During India’s Demonetization
Document description: This paper investigates how liquidity shocks caused by currency shortages impact firm-level exports, specifically analyzing the effects of India's 2016 demonetization policy. The authors utilize novel high-frequency customs transaction data matched with firm balance sheets and domestic trade records to isolate the influence of cash shortages on export performance. While the study finds that currency shortages do not directly affect exporters who likely rely on electronic payments, it identifies a significant decline in exports for firms whose domestic customers experienced liquidity constraints. The results suggest that exporters are indirectly harmed because their domestic buyers cannot pay for goods due to the lack of cash, which disrupts the supply chain and reduces the exporters' ability to cover input costs. The analysis further indicates that this negative impact was short-lived, dissipating by late 2017, and was driven by supply chain linkages rather than the exporters' own reliance on physical currency notes. Overall, the study provides evidence that liquidity constraints within the domestic economy can significantly reduce international trade flows through domestic supply chain channels.

Document title: Self-reinforcing Glass Ceilings
Document description: The document discusses the persistence of the gender pay gap in the labor market, despite convergence in education and work experience. The authors argue that the labor market can respond in ways that counteract reductions in the gender pay gap and contribute to the persistence of gender inequality. They show that when the gender pay gap narrows in a particular sector, women are more likely to seek jobs there, while men readjust their search toward less equitable sectors. This compositional effect reduces female participation in less equitable sectors, which typically pay higher wages, reinforcing gender stereotypes and social norms that contribute to the glass ceiling. The authors also find that the sectoral gender gap widens following bank deregulation, perpetuating gender imbalances across industries along the pay distribution. They conclude that the self-reinforcing channel they present complements existing mechanisms and highlights the challenges in closing the gender pay gap.

Document description: The document discusses the increase in violence in the Brazilian Amazon, particularly in the western portion of the region. Document title: Why are cement prices high but falling in Africa?
Document description: Africa has the highest price of cement of any continent, but its price and markup have fallen dramatically since 2011. The prices of intermediate goods, including cement, are higher on average in the world's poorest countries, including many in Africa. This is important because higher prices for intermediate goods can slow economic growth. The authors investigate why markups on cement remain high in Africa and find that limited demand, determined by the small average market size of many African countries, can account for high markups in prices in African markets. They also observe rapid entry and a decline in marginal costs in Africa at the time of fast economic growth, explaining the price drop observed in the data. The authors' findings have important policy implications, suggesting that governments need to focus on increasing the size of the market to lower prices of key intermediated goods rather than only changes in regulation.

Document title: Caring Dads? Universal Childcare, Paternity Leave and Fathers' Involvement
Document description: The document discusses the impact of universal childcare and paternity leave on fathers' involvement in childcare. The authors examine the effect of publicly subsidised childcare on fathers' involvement in childcare, starting from their early engagement through parental leave-taking, to their subsequent responsibility for childcare and labour supply decisions. The study uses a quasi-experimental approach, leveraging the varying pace of childcare expansion across counties in Germany. The results show that a higher regional childcare availability increases actual childcare attendance after children's first birthdays. Subsidised childcare availability increases fathers' parental leave take-up, but has no significant effect on fathers' continued involvement in caregiving on weekdays for children aged 12-35 months. The main impact of subsidised childcare is on maternal employment, with significant increases in mothers' labour market participation and working hours. Overall, the results suggest that publicly subsidised childcare mainly substitutes for maternal caregiving, with little effect on fathers' involvement in childcare beyond their parental leave.

Document title: Rethinking Short-Term Real Interest Rates and Term Spreads Using Very Long-Run Data
Document description: This paper analyzes the long-run properties of short-maturity real interest rates and term spreads using multi-century data from the United Kingdom and the United States. The authors argue that utilizing very long-run data reveals strong evidence of trend stationarity and relatively fast adjustment speeds, challenging the view that short-term rates are non-stationary. They find that term spreads have been rising secularly while inflation volatility has decreased, a pattern that contradicts many existing term structure models. The study suggests that the neutral interest rate should be modeled as a stationary process and that recent structural breaks in interest rate behavior may not be as permanent as previously believed. By combining historical data with modern statistical techniques, the researchers aim to provide a more accurate foundation for ongoing monetary policy debates regarding the neutral rate. The findings indicate that crucial stylized facts about interest rates may need reconsideration when applied over much longer time horizons.

Document title: Dual labor markets and the equilibrium distribution of firms
Document description: Many labor markets are characterized by a two-tier system, with the co-existence of open-ended contracts and fixed-term contracts. The use of fixed-term contracts is very heterogeneous across firms within narrowly defined sectors. A directed search model of multi-worker firms is used to understand these facts and the macroeconomic consequences of dual labor markets. The model delivers two key results: high-skilled workers are more productive in high-type firms, and recruiting costs are higher for open-ended contracts. These results explain the main empirical facts that are documented in the data. The calibrated economy exhibits a significant degree of misallocation of workers between firms, with output losses equal to 3.9% relative to an economy where the marginal product of each type of worker is equalized across all existing firms. The share of highly productive firms is 26% among entrants and 40% among incumbents. The model is used for counterfactual analysis to assess the effects of dual labor markets on the aggregate economy.

Document description: The document discusses the relationship between government-guaranteed credit and populist politics in France. The results are robust to several alternative specifications and also for legislative elections in France.

Document description: This report examines discrimination and racism within the Norwegian school system through a study commissioned by the Directorate for Integration and Diversity. The researchers analyzed data from a survey involving 203 teachers and conducted qualitative interviews with 10 teachers and 53 middle school students. The study found no evidence that teachers use names to discriminate when grading students, suggesting that observed disparities in grades stem from other factors rather than grading practices. However, the research reveals that students frequently experience racist and discriminatory comments in school, which they perceive as normalized behavior used to test boundaries among peers. These students tend to define racism individually based on specific instances rather than understanding it as a broader ideological structure, making it difficult to distinguish between racism and other forms of bullying. The findings highlight the need for schools to develop better tools for handling such comments and to foster critical thinking among students regarding social issues. The report concludes that the current normalization of racist language creates a challenging environment that negatively affects student mental health and educational aspirations.

Document description: The document examines the relationship between bank funding costs and the financial sophistication of bank customers. It uses a natural experiment to identify banks that price deposits in a way that can result in financially unsophisticated customers being shortchanged. The results show that these banks have significantly lower deposit funding costs, providing evidence that having financially unsophisticated customers may provide banks with substantial market power and be an important component of the value of a bank's deposit franchise. The study also explores how banks interact with customers who may lack financial sophistication, revealing a rich amount of cross-sectional variation in how banks price CDs of different tenors. The findings have implications for current banking theory and research, suggesting that financial sophistication may play a central role in determining the value of a bank's deposit franchise.

Document title: Fear and Dreams: Understanding the Non-Institutional sources of Leader Strategy
Document description: This document explores the non-institutional sources of variation in leader strategy, specifically in the context of Colombian paramilitarism. The authors develop a theory that predicts a co-variation in public good provision and massacres as a consequence of the social preferences of paramilitary front commanders. They argue that commanders with reciprocal preferences, typically from rural backgrounds, find it optimal to offer public goods in exchange for contributions and punish those who do not reciprocate with violence. The authors test these predictions using unique datasets compiled from transitional justice documents and exploit detailed information on the geographical location of front boundaries. They use a Spatial Regression Discontinuity Design to compare neighboring pairs of fronts, one with a peasant commander and the other without, to estimate the causal effect of having a peasant commander on the strategy of the front. Document title: Capital-Skill Complementarity in Firms and in the Aggregate Economy
Document description: The document discusses capital-skill complementarity, a concept where technological advances embodied in capital equipment are more complementary with high-skilled than low-skilled labor. The authors propose a theory that characterizes the aggregate elasticity of the skill premium with respect to the price of capital equipment in terms of firm-level factor intensities and elasticities of production and demand. They use French data to estimate the key micro-level elasticities and perform a main aggregation exercise to compute the aggregate degree of capital-skill complementarity. The results show that a 1% decline in the price of equipment generates a 0.06% increase in the observed skill premium in France. The authors also find that skill-biased technical change not embodied in capital equipment is responsible for the gap between the observed small rise in the skill premium and the reduction in the skill premium caused by the evolutions of labor supply and the equipment price.

Document title: School-Based Mental Health Initiatives
Document description: The document discusses school-based mental health initiatives, their challenges, and considerations for policymakers. It highlights the lack of high-quality evidence supporting these initiatives, the incoherent delivery of mental health services in typical neighborhood public schools, and the potential harms of universal mental health programs. The document emphasizes the need for policymakers to be clear-eyed about these challenges and to prioritize serving youth with current cases of mental disorders across a full continuum of care. It also suggests rolling back universal mental health and wellness programming and instead pursuing structural solutions such as setting and following school-wide behavioral expectations and maintaining full in-person school days. The document provides a tiered framework of school-based mental health interventions and notes that most neighborhood public schools offer some form of mental health programming, primarily Tier 1 universal programs. It also discusses the recent expansion of school-based mental health initiatives driven by factors such as the 1970s disability laws, mental health policy prioritizing prevention and early intervention, and federal funding for these initiatives. The document concludes that federal policy should make clear that the core goal of the public education system is to provide academic learning in preparation for productive participation in society, while the core responsibility of the public mental health system is to address untreated serious mental illnesses and serious emotional disturbances in youth.

Document title: Self-employment within the firm
Document description: This paper explores the nature of firms in low-income countries, specifically in Uganda, and how they organize labor. The authors collect time-use data from a sample of 1,000 manufacturing firms and find that even the largest firms resemble a collection of self-employed individuals sharing a production space rather than modern firms with specialized labor. They interpret the evidence through an equilibrium model of occupational choice and task assignment within the firm and find that the gains from organizing labor into firms are limited. The authors suggest that the lack of labor specialization is due to the production technology and the nature of demand, with customized products making it difficult to specialize labor. They propose that policy interventions aimed at spurring firm growth should also lead to the adoption of more scalable organizations.

Document title: Responsible Digital Finance Ecosystem (RDFE): A Conceptual Framework
Document description: The rapid digitization of financial services presents both opportunities and challenges. While it has broadened access to and reduced the costs of financial services, it has also led to fragmentation in the provision of financial services, complicating financial consumer protection efforts. Technologies such as automation and extensive data sharing have heightened consumer risks, including fraud, data misuse, and inadequate recourse mechanisms. Regulators and supervisors are facing challenges in adapting their consumer protection frameworks to fast-evolving technologies, such as artificial intelligence and crypto assets. Despite advancements in global frameworks, there are increasing types of risks, and the rate at which digital finance risks grow often surpasses the rate at which digital financial services are adopted. Financial consumer protection efforts tend to be siloed and primarily carried out by a financial sector authority, and are often reactive rather than proactive. It is time to enhance financial consumer protection in the digital age to ensure consumers continue to derive value and positive results from digital financial services and the sector can realize its immense financial inclusion potential.

Document title: Skills and Human Capital in the Labor Market
Document description: This document discusses human capital and its relationship with earnings in the labor market. The authors argue that human capital theory, which explains why education leads to higher wages, has been influential but has limitations. They highlight two key limitations: the assumption that human capital is one-dimensional and can be measured by education or test scores alone, and the treatment of human capital as augmenting the marginal product of labor. The authors propose a new approach where workers are treated as agents who make choices and respond to incentives, and traditional cognitive skills augment the marginal product of labor in tasks, while higher-order skills govern the choice of tasks. They also discuss the economic returns to human capital and how they have changed over time, with a focus on the decline in returns to cognitive skills and the growth in returns to non-cognitive skills.

Document title: He Said, She Said: Who Gets Believed When Spreading (Mis)Information
Document description: This document discusses the gender gap in social media influence, where women receive fewer likes and attract fewer followers than men. The authors design an online experiment to test whether perceived poster gender influences users' propensity to doubt the veracity of a given post. They find that men are more likely to flag female-authored posts as the post's topic domain becomes more male-stereotyped, while female users do not exhibit the same bias. The findings are consistent with the explanation that biased beliefs (stereotypes) about differential abilities of men and women in certain tasks lead to discrimination and result in gender gaps in outcomes. The study contributes to a growing literature exploring the role of gender stereotypes in perpetuating disparities in wages and career progression within traditionally male-dominated fields. The authors also investigate the demand-side of spreading information (truthful and false) and test whether receivers of information respond to the identity of the person sharing it.

Document title: Risk, the Limits of Financial Risk Management, and Corporate Resilience
Document description: This document argues that existing corporate finance theory incorrectly suggests that idiosyncratic risk does not matter for widely held firms, whereas evidence shows that total risk significantly affects expected cash flows and firm value. The author explains that firms should actively manage all risks they face, even for diversified shareholders, because avoiding known risks increases shareholder wealth, similar to installing fire sprinklers to prevent fire damage. While financial risk management using derivatives is effective for mitigating near-term, well-defined risks, it is limited in scope because long-term risks are difficult to quantify and hedging them can create unwanted volatility in accounting performance and liquidity. The text emphasizes that optimal risk management for long-term or unknown risks requires building corporate resilience through operational and financial policies rather than relying solely on financial instruments. Consequently, the author calls for greater research into the costs and benefits of resilience strategies to complement traditional financial risk management practices.

Document title: Uncovering sources of heterogeneity in the child penalty
Document description: This research report explores sources of heterogeneity in the child penalty in Denmark, using both conventional and data-driven approaches. The study finds that the child penalty varies across labour market and individual characteristics, such as industry, employment level, and female representation. The data-driven approach, using a causal forest estimator, identifies the share of household wage income earned pre-childbirth as a key determinant of heterogeneity in the child penalty. The study also finds that a lower share of pre-childbirth household wage income earned by the mother is associated with a higher child penalty for mothers. Additionally, the analysis finds that a higher penalty is associated with firms with high revenue, and lower penalties are associated with being employed in certain industries.

Document title: Striking the Right Balance: Why Standard Balance Tests Over-Reject the Null, and How to Fix It
Document description: The document discusses the use of balance tests in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to demonstrate the comparability of treatment and control groups. They propose and compare three alternative methods to assess balance, including an omnibus F-test of joint orthogonality with randomization inference p-values, the minimum sharpened q-value to adjust p-values from pairwise t-tests, and a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test to assess whether p-values from pairwise t-tests are uniformly distributed. The authors conclude that omnibus F-tests of joint orthogonality with randomization inference p-values exhibit excellent performance in terms of both statistical power and size, for both individual and cluster RCTs.

Document title: Reciprocity and the China Shock
Document description: The document discusses the link between reciprocity and labor market adjustments in the context of China's accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001. The authors formalize the GATT/WTO principle of reciprocity in quantitative trade models and investigate its labor market impacts. They show that reciprocal tariff cuts that hold terms of trade fixed and leave each country's wage unchanged, and that a country's own tariff cuts are a sufficient statistic for the change in local relative price that it will experience as a result of the negotiations. The authors apply their theoretical results to China's WTO accession and find that China's tariff reductions exceeded reciprocity norms, increasing real incomes but amplifying the manufacturing employment dislocation in the United States and globally. They also derive closed-form expressions for the measure of labor market dislocation that partition the contributions of multilateral tariff changes to a country's labor market dislocation into two components: the country's own tariff changes and the deviation from reciprocity that the negotiated tariff changes imply.

Document title: Fair Trade Agreements
Document description: The legitimacy of the world trading system is under growing attack, as challenges to its conformity with norms of fairness and social justice are increasingly voiced by citizens and their governments around the world. The authors of this paper attempt to fill a lacuna in the literature by considering the purpose and design of trade agreements when governments are responsive to the fairness concerns of their constituents. They take a novel 'bottom up' approach to the analysis of fair trade agreements, building on four pillars: treating each citizen as their own moral philosopher, assuming that citizens suffer psychological harm from unfair trade, allowing governments to be concerned about the perceived unfairness of trade pressures, and evaluating the efficacy of a trade agreement's design by its ability to bring its member governments to the efficiency frontier as judged by their preferences. The authors demonstrate that the answers to the questions posed above hinge on how a country's citizens evaluate whether they have been treated fairly, and that two features are critical for determining the purpose and design of a fair trade agreement: whether the fairness of the trade pressures that a citizen faces is judged on the basis of the trade pressures alone or rather on the basis of those trade pressures in light of the particular foreign government policies that give rise to them, and whether fairness concerns extend to the proper use of tariffs by one's own government.

Document description: This document investigates the impact of wealth on political preferences and participation. Document title: The Lifecycle of Protests in the Digital Age
Document description: The document discusses the lifecycle of protests in the digital age, proposing a theory of protest dynamics with heterogeneous protest technology and intensity. They use various NLP techniques to analyze the radicalization process on a panel of discussants and their posts on Yellow Vest Facebook pages, confirming that the online mobilization followed the same trends as the street protests. Document title: IGC Evidence Paper - Firms, trade, and productivity
Document description: Productivity growth is the driving force behind economic development. The existing evidence on transformations and evolving priorities for research is reviewed. Climate change and a degraded environment decrease firm and worker productivity. Resilient firms are essential for adapting against shocks. Economic transformations can drive more productive and higher earning work. Innovations in firm capabilities, improving the functioning of markets, and integrating firms within global value chains and world markets are necessary. Low and middle-income countries are characterised by a large number of small, unproductive firms and a small number of very few large, highly efficient, and disruptive companies. Large technologically advanced firms may be better adapted to climate change. Management practices explain an important part of the overall dispersion in productivity across firms and countries. The adoption of technologies at the global innovation frontier is often limited in low- and middle-income countries. Barriers to innovation, including green innovation, are examined. Distortions that inhibit the optimal use of inputs and the broader market distortions that constrain the availability of inputs are discussed. The way inputs, when aggregated across all firms in an economy, may be significantly misallocated is examined. Competitive forces may be weaker in low- and middle-income countries. Industrial policy can raise aggregate productivity by targeting sectors with external economies of scale and which face distortions. Firms' interactions with world markets, including trade and connections with multinational enterprises, are explored.

Document title: The Micro and Macro Productivity of Nations
Document description: This document examines aggregate productivity differences across nations using cross-country firm-level data and a quantitative model of production heterogeneity with distortions. The authors find that differences in selection and technology driven by observed cross-country distortions explain the majority of the micro and macro productivity differences across nations. They also show that the cross-country facts can be reconciled by incorporating producer selection and technology investment into the standard model of misallocation. The model explains more than half of the cross-country labor productivity gap and highlights the important interaction between the firm-level productivity distribution and allocative efficiency. Document title: Monetary tightening, inflation drivers and financial stress
Document description: The document explores the effects of monetary policy tightening on financial stress, focusing on the role of inflation drivers. It finds that financial stress increases after a monetary tightening when inflation is supply-driven, but remains unchanged or decreases when inflation is demand-driven. The authors suggest that this finding points to a potential trade-off between price and financial stability when inflation is high and supply-driven. They also argue that policy rate hikes may not affect or may even reduce financial stress in the presence of demand-driven inflation, especially if it is strong. The paper uses local projections to estimate the effect of high-frequency identified monetary policy surprises on a variety of financial stress measures, differentiating the effects based on whether inflation is supply-driven or demand-driven. The findings are consistent with the dynamics of financial stress during the most recent monetary tightening episode in the US. The authors conclude that the effects of a policy rate hike on financial stability may depend on the nature and magnitude of shocks in the economy at the time of the hike.

Document title: The Shifting Finance of Electricity Generation
Document description: The document discusses the shift in finance of electricity generation in the US. Private equity, institutional investors, and foreign corporations own a significant portion of wind, solar, and natural gas electricity generation. These new entrants are more likely to create new power plants than incumbent domestic listed utilities, highlighting a new role for private equity in large-scale asset creation. The new owners create more efficient plants and improve acquired ones. Market deregulation drives the results, highlighting the dual importance of competition and new financing for both creation and acquisitions. The study uses a unique dataset on the ownership of US power plants and analyzes three questions: the extent to which ownership changes occur due to financing of new assets versus sales and decommissioning of existing assets, the extent to which deregulation versus other economic factors contribute to attracting finance from new modes, and the implications of the changing ownership structure for power plant operating performance. The results show that private equity and foreign corporations are disproportionately financing new greenfield solar, wind, and natural gas plants, while incumbent domestic listed utilities play a smaller role. Document description: The document examines whether banks price maturity-transformation risk into the rates they offer customers. Document title: Innovation Spillovers across U.S. Tech Clusters
Document description: This research paper investigates how innovation spillovers occur across different technology clusters in the United States by analyzing merged patent and census data. The authors find that larger tech clusters increase the productivity of inventors not only locally but also within other clusters connected to them through parent firm networks. These cross-cluster effects are driven by the diffusion of knowledge through internal channels like emails and video conferencing rather than physical proximity. The study develops a model to measure the difference between social and private returns to innovation, ranking clusters based on this wedge. Results indicate that while large clusters have a higher social-private wedge, this is primarily due to their strong connections to other clusters rather than local knowledge spillovers alone. The authors demonstrate that inventors act as antennas for knowledge, allowing firms to benefit from innovations in distant locations without needing physical presence there. Counterfactual analysis suggests that increasing the interconnectedness of tech clusters would raise the social-private innovation wedge across most locations. The findings highlight the importance of firm networks in facilitating innovation beyond traditional geographic boundaries.

Document title: Barriers to Entry and the Labor Market
Document description: This document studies the labor market effects of temporary barriers to entry. The authors use a mixed-frequency Bayesian vector autoregression model to estimate the effects of temporary barriers to entry on job creation, employment concentration, unemployment, and the size distribution of firms. The results show that temporary barriers to entry reduce job creation by new entrants but boost it for incumbent firms, increase employment concentration in large firms, temporarily reduce unemployment but are recessionary in the long run, and are mainly the result of federal regulation. The authors also develop a macroeconomic model that aligns with the empirical findings, featuring heterogeneous firms, endogenous entry and exit, and labor market frictions. The model shows that temporary barriers to entry temporarily boost short-run economic activity by favoring existing firms but are ultimately costly. The policy message of the paper is that while temporary barriers to entry may promote economic activity in the short run, they remain costly and entail welfare costs.

Document description: This paper analyzes the role of large firms in South Korea's economic growth between 1972 and 2011 by examining how rising firm concentration contributed to the country's performance. Document title: The Long and Variable Lags of Monetary Policy: Evidence from Disaggregated Price Indices
Document description: This document studies the effect of monetary policy on prices using local projections. The authors analyze the responses of subcomponents of the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index (PCEPI) to exogenous interest rate changes. They find that the aggregate response masks stark differences across individual price categories, with some prices responding negatively after a long delay or even with a positive initial response. The authors also develop a re-aggregation procedure for their cross-sectional impulse response function estimates and their standard errors, taking into account the dependence between different prices. They find that changes in expenditure shares have not accelerated the response of the PCEPI to monetary policy. The authors' results echo the famous insight of Friedman that monetary changes have their effect only after a considerable lag and over a long period, and that the lag is rather variable. They also discuss potential mechanisms through which a faster response than suggested by their estimates might have occurred, by inspecting state-dependence and asymmetries in their local projection setup.

Document title: The Role of Firms and Job Mobility in the Assimilation of Immigrants: Former Soviet Union Jews in Israel 1990-2019
Document description: The document studies the role of firms and job mobility in the assimilation of immigrants, specifically former Soviet Union Jews who migrated to Israel in the 1990s. The researchers use administrative data to track the immigrants' job mobility and firm ladder climbing over three decades. They find that immigrants are more mobile than natives and faster at climbing the firm ladder, and that firm-to-firm mobility is a key driver of their long-run prosperity. Document title: Negotiating agricultural trade in a new policy environment
Document description: Global agricultural trade has more than tripled between 2000 and 2014, driven by increased demand for red meat, dairy, and poultry products, particularly in developing countries, and by increases in non-food uses of cereals, especially for biofuels. Currently, as much as 25 percent of global wheat consumption and 45 percent of global soybean consumption are supplied by imports. Even in the case of rice, for which most consumption is supplied domestically, the import share has doubled to 10 percent of consumption since 2000. These trends are projected to continue over the next 35 years, with global food demand expected to increase by as much as 50 percent from 2012-2013 levels by 2050. Much of this increased demand is projected to be met by imports. The challenges to meeting the growing global food demand—population and income growth and supply uncertainties complicated by climate change, environmental pressures, and water scarcity—all point to the increasing importance of trade and the need for a more, not less, open trading system. The rules-based system established under the World Trade Organization (WTO), particularly the Uruguay Round Agreement on Agriculture (AoA), has facilitated growth in agricultural trade. However, progress since the Uruguay Round has been limited, and serious efforts are needed to renew the negotiations and achieve further progress in the liberalization of world trade.

Document title: Macroeconomic Expectations and Cognitive Noise
Document description: This document discusses the limitations of standard models of information frictions in explaining why forecasts sometimes respond excessively to news. The author argues that these models define information frictions too narrowly, emphasizing constraints on processing new information while assuming past information remains fully accessible. A unified framework is proposed that integrates both attention and memory frictions, which reflects constraints on processing new and past information, respectively. The model is shown to better match observed forecast biases, enable joint identification of the two frictions from survey data, and provide novel insights for optimal monetary policy responses to cost-push shocks. The author estimates attention and memory frictions using survey forecasts for nine macroeconomic variables and finds that the estimated friction parameters imply horizon-dependent forecast biases. The author proposes a unified framework that integrates attention frictions, which limit the processing of new data, and memory frictions, which limit the retention and retrieval of prior beliefs. This broader model explains observed forecast biases such as sluggish adjustments in consensus forecasts and over-sensitivity in individual forecasts by accounting for cognitive noise in both new and old information. The study demonstrates that at short horizons, attention frictions dominate leading to slow responses, whereas at longer horizons, memory frictions create a spike-and-fade dynamic in expectations. Using survey data from professional forecasters, the author jointly estimates these two frictions, finding that memory frictions are quantitatively significant and were previously misattributed to attention frictions in standard models. The paper concludes by analyzing optimal monetary policy, showing that cognitive frictions suggest a look-through approach to inflation stabilization rather than aggressive tightening. Ultimately, the research highlights the necessity of incorporating both attention and memory constraints to accurately model expectation formation and design effective monetary policy responses.
