Document title: Micro MPCs and Macro Counterfactuals: The Case of the 2008 Rebates
Document description: The document discusses the implications of high estimated marginal propensities to consume (MPCs) from household studies on macroeconomic counterfactuals. Using the 2008 tax rebate as a case study, the authors calibrate a standard medium-scale New Keynesian model with the estimated MPCs to construct counterfactual macroeconomic consumption paths in the absence of a rebate. The counterfactual paths imply that consumption expenditures would have plummeted in spring and summer 2008 and then recovered when Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008. The authors argue that these paths are implausible and that the actual stimulus effect of the rebates must have been modest. They then explore two possibilities to reconcile the high estimated micro MPCs with the implausible general equilibrium counterfactuals: an upward bias in the existing household MPC estimates and general equilibrium forces that dampen the micro MPCs. The authors find that both possibilities are key to explaining the implausible counterfactuals and that the aggregate effects of the rebate are small, less than 20 cents for each dollar.

Document title: Location, Location, Location
Document description: The document discusses the effects of location on earnings, using data from the Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program. It estimates the average earnings premiums associated with jobs in different commuting zones and different CZ-industry pairs. The study finds that about half of the variation in mean wages across CZs is attributable to differences in worker ability, while the other half is due to place effects. The place effects from a cross-sectional wage model overstate the causal effects of place, while those from a model with person fixed effects understate the causal effects. The study also finds that local industry agglomerations are associated with higher wages, but overall differences in industry composition and in CZ-specific returns to industries explain only a small fraction of average place effects. Additionally, the study explores locational differences in the pay gap between different education groups, finding that the skills of the college-educated workforce are higher in larger and higher-wage places, and that this differential sorting explains approximately two-thirds of the observed correlation between CZ size or CZ average earnings and the place-specific gap between college and high school wages.

Document title: A “Green Revolution” for Sub-Saharan Africa? Challenges and Opportunities
Document description: Sub-Saharan Africa is one of the world's poorest regions, with low land productivity exacerbating local households' uncertainty regarding livelihood and food security. Despite efforts to improve agricultural productivity, this has not occurred in the region. Farmers' adoption of modern technologies is constrained by poor access to credit and insurance, as well as behavioral barriers such as lack of information and present-bias. Long-term climatic shifts and increased weather shocks make implementing adaptation and mitigation policies for agriculture imperative in this region. Improving agricultural productivity can lead to lasting effects, but this requires improvements in security, political stability, and effective health systems. The development of improved seeds could play a central role in improving agricultural productivity in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly because little has been invested in research on the seeds used in the region compared to seeds commonly used elsewhere. The provision of finance in several areas, including credit to farmers and funding for research and development of improved seeds, is essential for increasing agricultural yields. However, focusing solely on increasing agricultural productivity will not suffice, and massive improvements in security, political stability, and education are also necessary for sustainable growth and development in the region.

Document title: The Role of Firms and Job Mobility in the Assimilation of Immigrants: Former Soviet Union Jews in Israel 1990–2019
Document description: The document discusses the role of firms and job mobility in the assimilation of immigrants, specifically former Soviet Union Jews in Israel between 1990 and 2019. It studies how job mobility, firms, and firm-ladder climbing can shape immigrants' labor market success. The authors use a unique dataset featuring administrative records of immigrants in Israel, which allows them to track immigrants' job mobility and firm-specific pay premiums. They find that immigrants are persistently more mobile than natives and faster at climbing the firm ladder. The authors also estimate immigrant- and native-specific firm pay premiums and quantify how within-firm, differential pay-setting policies shape immigrant-native gaps. The study provides a detailed view into immigrants' job mobility dynamics and climbing of the firm ladder over three decades.

Document title: Market Access and Migration: Evidence from the Panama Canal Opening during the First Great Migration
Document description: This paper examines the influence of transportation infrastructure on migration decisions in the context of the Great Migration in the United States. Focusing on the opening of the Panama Canal in 1920, the authors isolate the effect of improved economic opportunities from reduced migration costs. Using full-count Census data, they find that Southern African American migrants preferred areas with enhanced market access, leading to higher inflows after 1920. The study highlights the interplay between migrant networks and labor markets in shaping migration patterns. The authors' findings underscore the significance of local market conditions induced by improvements in local market access in influencing migration decisions during the Great Migration. They also demonstrate that the changes in Market Access due to the Panama Canal resulted in increased African American migration beyond what would have been predicted based solely on initial migrant networks. The existing migrant networks played a crucial role in facilitating the transformation of the Canal-induced benefits into higher migration flows. The study contributes to the literature on location decisions during the Great Migration by demonstrating the complementarity between migrant networks and improved labor markets.

Document title: When It Hurts the Most: Timing of Parental Job Loss and a Child's Education
Document description: The document investigates the stages of childhood at which parental job loss is most consequential for a child's education. It uses Danish administrative data to track children whose parents experienced a plant closure when children were of different ages. The study finds that parental job loss disproportionately reduces test-taking, scores, and high school enrollment among children exposed during infancy (age 0-1). Effects are largest for low-income families and low-achieving children. The causal chain from job loss to education likely works through reduced family income. Maternal time investment partially offsets the effect of reduced income. The study also finds that negative impacts of parental job loss on achievement are stronger for children with relatively weak potential outcomes. A distributional analysis shows largest impacts on the probability of scoring in the bottom half of the achievement distribution. The study concludes that infancy represents a crucial stage for human capital development, and that interventions targeted at children exposed early in life may substantially benefit human capital development.

Document title: Activating Change: The Role of Information and Beliefs in Social Activism
Document description: This discussion paper investigates the factors that lead individuals to engage in social activism, focusing on three common forms of activism: signing a petition, making a donation to an NGO fighting for the cause, and watching an informational video on the cause and on how to take actions. The authors conduct an online experiment with nearly 2000 Indian men, providing information about the social problem and correcting downward biased beliefs about others' willingness to take action. The results show that providing information and correcting downward biased beliefs increases petition signing, but has no impact on donations and video viewing. The study aims to provide insights on the motivations behind participation in collective efforts for social change.

Document title: Accelerating Innovation Ecosystems: The Promise and Challenges of Regional Innovation Engines
Document description: The document discusses the importance of location in research and innovation, highlighting how the location of research enterprises impacts productivity and impact. It explains how research investment and innovation outputs are highly skewed across different geographic areas, with some regions, such as the San Francisco Bay Area, accounting for a disproportionate share of patented inventions and venture capital investment. The document introduces the concept of innovation ecosystems, which refers to the interconnected set of institutions within a geographic region that allow each organization and researcher to leverage the knowledge, resources, and specialized capabilities of others. It argues that place-based innovation policy interventions, such as the Regional Innovation Engines program, can enhance innovative productivity and impact by addressing the specific needs and challenges of each region. The document emphasizes the importance of stakeholder engagement, holistic ecosystem assessment, and implementable strategic choice in designing effective place-based innovation policy interventions.

Document title: Estimating the Impact of the Age of Criminal Majority: Decomposing Multiple Treatments in a Regression Discontinuity Framework
Document description: This paper studies the impact of adult prosecution on recidivism and employment trajectories for adolescent, first-time felony defendants. The authors use linked Criminal Justice Administrative Record System and socio-economic data from Wayne County, Michigan, to examine changes to future criminal activities, employment, and earnings. They find that a felony case in the adult system results in about a 20% reduction in subsequent felony cases, but also generates worse labor market outcomes, lowering annual earnings over the next 5-years by almost 30% and increasing poverty rates by about 33%. The authors develop a novel econometric framework that combines standard regression discontinuity methods with predictive machine learning models to identify mechanism-specific treatment effects that underpin the overall impact of adult prosecution. They consider four policy counterfactuals, including raising the age of majority, increasing adult dismissals to match the juvenile disposition rates, eliminating adult incarceration, and expanding juvenile record sealing opportunities to teenage adult defendants. All four scenarios generate positive returns for government budgets, but the net impact on society after accounting for potential victim costs becomes more ambiguous.

Document title: Soap operas and pro-savings attitudes in poor rural areas of Peru
Document description: The document discusses a field experiment in Peru where a five-episode soap opera was shown to women living in poor rural areas to promote positive attitudes and behaviors related to trust in banking institutions and pro-savings messages. The study found that women who watched the soap opera improved their attitudes towards savings, especially as a precautionary motive. The soap opera was designed to provide positive embedded messages related to the importance of keeping savings in a safe, secure place, such as a bank. The study targeted beneficiaries of the Peruvian Conditional Cash Transfer program, 'Juntos', and found that the intervention had a significant impact on women's attitudes towards savings. The study suggests that edutainment, the idea that media can be entertaining while conveying useful educational and informational messages, may have the potential to help target difficult development-related objectives, including those related to financial inclusion. The study's findings have implications for policy and practice in promoting financial inclusion and savings in developing countries.

Document title: Gender-Biased Technological Change: Milking Machines and the Exodus of Women from Farming
Document description: This paper studies the link between gender-biased technological change in the agricultural sector and structural transformation in Norway. After WWII, Norwegian farms began widely adopting milking machines to replace the hand milking of cows, a task typically performed by women. The adoption of milking machines triggered a process of structural transformation by displacing young rural women from their traditional jobs on farms in dairy-intensive municipalities. The displaced women moved to urban areas where they acquired a higher level of education and found better-paid employment. The paper analyzes the relationship between gender-biased technological change, structural transformation, and the long-term earning opportunities of displaced workers. The study focuses on Norway, which provides an ideal setting in which to evaluate the economic consequences of the introduction of milking machines. The paper develops a simple theoretical model to better understand who was affected by the adoption of milking machines and who complied to leave farming, move into cities, and invest in human capital. The findings show that the large-scale adoption of milking machines after WWII triggered a process of structural change in Norway that increased the return to education and long-term earning opportunities for young women who grew up in dairy-intensive municipalities.

Document title: Educational Mobility Across Three Generations in Latin American Countries
Document description: This paper presents new evidence on educational mobility across three generations in six Latin American countries. The authors combine survey information with national census data to create a dataset of 50,000 triads of grandparents-parent-children born between 1890 and 1990. They estimate five different intergenerational mobility measures, showing that the empirical multi-generational persistence is high in Latin America, much larger than what Becker and Tomes' theoretical model predicts. The authors also find that while relative measures suggest stagnant mobility across generations, there are significant improvements according to non-linear measures. They test competing theories of multigenerational persistence, namely Becker and Tomes' theory and Clark's theory of high and sticky persistence, and find that Clark's theory provides a better approximation for describing mobility across multiple generations in developing countries. The authors also explore the role of compulsory schooling laws in explaining educational mobility patterns and find that their implementation significantly reduces the dispersion in educational attainment among cohorts.

Document description: This consensus study report assesses federal policies that contribute to racial, ethnic, and tribal health inequities in the United States. The committee of experts examined how historical and current structural racism, combined with economic instability and lack of access to education and healthcare, creates significant health disparities among minoritized populations. The study provides a comprehensive review of the current landscape of health inequities and outlines data gaps that hinder effective policy making. Ultimately, the report aims to inform public policy decisions by presenting evidence-based findings and recommendations to advance health equity. The authors conclude with a roadmap of specific recommendations and a call to action for federal agencies to address these systemic issues.

Document title: Exporting, Global Sourcing, and Multinational Activity: Theory and Evidence from the United States
Document description: The document studies the relationship between firms' foreign production locations and their international trade patterns. It uses newly merged data on US firms' trade and multinational activity by country to show that multinational firms are more likely to trade with countries in which they have affiliates, and also with other countries within their affiliates' region. The authors rationalize these patterns with a new source of firm-level scale economies that arises when country-specific fixed costs to source from or sell in a market are shared across all the firm's plants. The document also finds that US MNEs' exports are oriented towards their foreign manufacturing locations, and that they are more likely to trade with countries that are physically close to their affiliates. The authors extend this analysis to all countries and control for firm and country characteristics, and find that US MNEs are more likely to import from countries in which they do not have affiliates, but that are in the same region as one of their manufacturing plants.

Document title: Housing, Household Debt, and the Business Cycle: An Application to China and Korea
Document description: This document discusses the relationship between housing, household debt, and the business cycle in China and Korea. The authors note that both countries have experienced substantial increases in household debt and are now facing a weakening economy. They explore the 'credit-driven household demand channel' and its implications for the two economies. The authors use regression analysis to predict the impact of household debt on GDP growth in China and Korea. They find that a rise in household debt is associated with a decline in subsequent real GDP growth. The authors also compare the household debt booms in China and Korea to previous episodes in history, including the US and UK before the Great Recession. They note that the current booms are comparable in magnitude to these previous episodes. The authors conclude that the credit-driven household demand channel is operative in China and Korea and that the two economies face a significant economic slowdown in the years ahead.

Document title: The Impact of Racial Segregation on College Attainment in Spatial Equilibrium
Document description: This paper investigates the impact of racial segregation on college attainment in the St. Louis metro area. The authors build an overlapping-generations spatial-equilibrium model to study the mechanisms behind racial segregation and the racial gap in college attainment. The model incorporates three channels through which race impacts household outcomes and neighborhood choices: the Black-White wage gap, amenity externalities, and additional barriers to moving faced by Black households. The authors find that these channels account for 71% of the racial segregation and 64% of the college gap in the data. They also show that the presence of spillovers and externalities generates multiple equilibria, and that St. Louis is in a segregated equilibrium, but there also exists a more integrated equilibrium with a lower college gap. The authors use the model to compare two place-based government interventions: Moving to Opportunity and Opportunity Zones. They find that these interventions can destabilize the segregated equilibrium and reduce segregation and the college gap.

Document title: Vacancy posting, firm balance sheets, and pandemic policy
Document description: This document assesses how balance sheets propagated labour demand shocks during the Covid-19 pandemic using novel matched data on firms and online job postings. It finds that financially healthy firms increased vacancies more in response to positive shocks, while less-leveraged firms and firms with higher credit scores increased postings more in response to certain policy interventions. The study complements existing analysis on the labour market effects of the pandemic and provides insights into the role of firm balance sheets in propagating shocks to labour demand. It also adds to the literature on the link between firm balance sheets and labour decisions, highlighting the importance of credit constraints in labour market outcomes. The findings suggest that policy interventions can effectively mitigate the link between credit constraints and employment.

Document title: Exposure to the One-Child Policy and Fertility among Chinese Immigrants to the US
Document description: The document discusses the impact of China's one-child policy on the fertility decisions of Chinese immigrants to the US. The authors examine whether women exposed to the policy change their fertility decisions when they migrate to a country without fertility restrictions. They use American Community Survey data from 2010 to 2020 to compare the childbearing decisions of Chinese-born women with varying degrees of exposure to the policy before migrating to the US. The results show that Chinese women aged 35-45 exposed to the policy for a longer duration have significantly fewer children than women who were not exposed to the policy. The authors suggest that exposure to the fines and propaganda associated with the policy altered social norms surrounding the appropriate family size and dampened the fertility preferences of women growing up in China during this period. The study contributes to the understanding of the long-lasting influence of the one-child policy on fertility decisions and its impact on the social norms surrounding family size.

Document title: Accident-Induced Absence from Work and Wage Ladders
Document description: The document discusses how temporary absence from work due to accidents affects individuals' labor trajectory and wage growth. The authors use a wage ladder model to analyze the impact of accidents on wage offers and reallocation to employers. They find that even short periods of absence due to accidents decrease workers' wages relative to their counterfactual self, with an estimated wage loss of 2.5-5 percent. The authors argue that this is due to forgone opportunities to climb the wage ladder while being absent, rather than human capital depreciation or productivity losses. They also find that workers reallocate to lower-paying employers and occupations after returning to work. The results are robust to different identification strategies and are driven by young and white-collar workers.

Document title: Financial Crises and the Global Supply Network: Evidence from Multinational Enterprises
Document description: This paper examines the effect of financial crises on the organization of production and performance of multinational enterprises (MNEs). The authors use a long panel dataset covering the network structure of MNEs from 2006 to 2015 to study the impact of the financial crisis on MNEs in Europe. They find that MNEs with a more financially-hit others network perform worse in both revenues and employment growth over the 2006-2015 period. The effects are substantial, with an MNE with a financial shock to its network equal to one standard deviation of the financial shock displaying a 7.6 and 10.7 percent lower growth rate in revenues and employment, respectively. The authors also show that MNEs whose network experiences a more significant financial shock react by reducing the growth in their number of affiliates in the following years relative to less affected MNEs. The effect of a shock of magnitude equal to one standard deviation of their MNE-specific network shock is to reduce by 4.1 percent the growth rate in the number of affiliates. The authors also provide evidence consistent with financial frictions playing a prominent role in driving these results.

Document title: Preferences over the Racial Composition of Neighborhoods: Estimates and Implications
Document description: The document discusses the racial composition of neighborhoods and how it influences where people choose to live. The authors estimate a dynamic, forward-looking model of neighborhood choice using data from 197 metropolitan divisions in the United States. They find that households have strong preferences for living in neighborhoods with a similar racial composition, with some households exhibiting homophily, where utility increases if the share of same-race households in the neighborhood increases. The authors use a new shift-share instrument to estimate the impact of racial composition on location choice, which involves comparing households' preferences for neighborhoods from different metropolitan areas with different racial compositions. The study suggests that the current demographic composition of neighborhoods is not stable due to these strong preferences. The authors argue that their estimates capture preferences for the bundle of race and the endogenous amenities that tend to come with race, rather than just skin color. They also discuss the implications of their findings for understanding how neighborhoods change over time in response to small shocks or changes to government policy.

Document title: Privacy Regulation and Quality-Enhancing Innovation
Document description: This document studies the potential trade-off between privacy and quality-enhancing innovation. A monopolist offers a free service to users and derives revenues by disclosing user data to third parties. Users decide whether to use the service and how much information to provide, trading off higher privacy for higher utility from the firm's service. A cap on data disclosure affects the monopolist's incentives to invest in innovation, altering its disclosure revenues and gains from innovation. The cap's impact on innovation depends on the size of the share of privacy-concerned users in the market. If the share is small, the cap leads to lower innovation, but if it is large, the cap increases the firm's incentives to invest in innovation. The regulator faces a trade-off between privacy and innovation, and the cap is desirable for users only if the number of privacy-concerned users is not too small. The study provides insights into the factors that a regulator should consider when deciding whether to set restrictions on a dominant firm's data disclosure policy.

Document title: Elections and Policies: Evidence from the Covid Pandemic
Document description: This paper examines the evolution of public policies before the scheduled political elections based on the government responses to the Covid pandemic. The results of an event study in a sample of countries that experienced political elections during the first year of the pandemic suggest that 'lockdown style' policies were more stringent the further away countries were from election dates. The gradual relaxation of 'lockdown style' restrictions ahead of the elections was driven by policies in low-income, less democratic countries, and countries with relatively low social trust. Covid-related 'economic support' policies were not significantly affected by the scheduled political elections. The findings are robust to removing elections that were postponed due to the pandemic. The results indicate that the restrictions were relaxed before the elections in the less democratic countries and in countries with lower social trust. The relationship between Covid-related policies and social trust can be reciprocal, and the results suggest that politicians in low-income, less democratic countries, and countries with relatively low social trust relaxed restrictions before elections to attract voters.

Document title: Does Anger Drive Populism?
Document description: The document studies the relationship between anger and the rise of populism in the United States. The authors use a unique dataset tracking emotions for a large sample of respondents from 2008 to 2017 to explore the relationship between anger and the populist vote share across U.S. counties. They find that more angry counties displayed stronger preferences for populist candidates during the 2016 presidential primaries and elections. However, once they control for other negative emotions and life satisfaction, anger no longer operates as a separate channel in driving the populist vote share. Instead, their results indicate that a more complex sense of malaise and gloom, rather than anger per se, drives the rise in populism. The authors also discuss the characteristics of anger and its potential impact on voting behavior, citing literature on the psychology of anger and its effects on judgment and decision-making.

Document title: The Impact of Fear on Police Behavior and Public Safety
Document description: This document examines the impact of police officer deaths on police behavior and public safety. The authors investigate how changes in the salience of workplace risk affect police behavior, specifically looking at cases of police officer deaths while on duty. They find that officers respond to a peer death by decreasing arrest activity for one to two months, consistent with heightened fear. Reductions are largest for low-level arrests and are more pronounced in smaller cities. Despite the decline in arrests, crime does not increase on average during this period, nor do they observe crime spikes in cities with larger or longer arrest declines. The authors conclude that officer fear does not ultimately contribute to higher rates of crime. They also provide evidence that the observed arrest reductions are due to behavioral changes in enforcement decisions rather than changes to police manpower.

Document description: The document discusses the importance of global public goods, specifically vaccines, in preventing pandemics and improving health in both regions. Document title: Maternity Benefits and Marital Stability after Birth: Evidence from the Soviet Baltic Republics
Document description: This discussion paper examines the impact of maternity benefits on marital stability after birth using a large expansion in maternity benefits in the Baltic countries of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania in 1982. Document title: New Evidence on the Underrepresentation of Asian Americans in Leadership Positions
Document description: The document discusses the underrepresentation of Asian Americans in leadership positions, presenting new evidence on the extent of this phenomenon. It examines differences in leadership representation between US-born Asian and White men, finding that Asian men are significantly less likely to work in management and executive positions compared to White men with similar qualifications. The study also assesses various mechanisms that may explain racial differences in representation, including racial differences in preferences for leadership positions, selection into self-employment, intergenerational transmission effects, immigration recency, and ethnic attrition. Document title: The Confederate Diaspora
Document description: The document explores the role of white migration from the postbellum South in diffusing Confederate culture throughout the United States. Document title: De-skilling: Evidence from Late Nineteenth Century American Manufacturing
Document description: This document discusses the long-standing view in US economic history that the shift from artisan shops to mechanized factories led to 'labor deskilling'. The authors investigate the Department of Labor's 1899 Hand and Machine Labor Study using causal inference statistical techniques and find that the adoption of inanimate power did indeed induce deskilling, but the effects were statistically significant and accounted for only 7-15 percent of the deskilling observed in the sample. They also find that the increased division of labor, as captured by the increase in scale of operations and the ratio of workers to tasks, accounts for a larger fraction of deskilling. Document description: The document discusses the impact of the Voting Rights Act on the political behavior of whites in the US South. The authors analyze county-level voter registration rates by race between 1956 and 1980 and find that the VRA increased both black and white political participation. The authors use a unique dataset on county-level voter registration rates by race and exploit pre-determined variation in exposure to the federal intervention to identify the effects of the VRA.

Document title: Fertility, Son-Preference, and the Reversal of the Gender Gap in Literacy/Numeracy Tests
Document description: This study examines the relationship between fertility decline and the reversal of the gender gap in literacy/numeracy test scores in China. The authors propose that in a society with son-preference, the Quantity-Quality trade-off would be larger for daughters than for sons. They test this hypothesis using data from China Family Project Survey and find that a reduction in one sibling narrows the gender gap in numeracy and literacy test scores. The pattern is more pronounced in regions with a higher proportion of people who prefer a son over a daughter. The authors also provide evidence that the channel of the effect is indeed largely through the increased probability of girls living in single-sex families. They argue that the reduction in sibling size causes a narrowing/reversal of the gender gap in adult test scores by using a novel instrument capturing the unique county-level time-varying intensity of the Family Planning Policy.

Document title: Pay-for-Performance Contracts in the Lab and the Real World: Evidence from Nigeria
Document description: The document discusses pay-for-performance contracts in health care, specifically in Nigeria. The authors conduct a two-stage experiment to examine the effect of adding varying sizes of incentives to the prime, spillovers on actions that are unprimed and primed-only, and whether PFP effects persist in real-world tasks after the contract has ended. The first stage is a lab-in-the-field experiment that randomizes 1,359 maternity health workers in 690 health facilities to one of three study arms: information, rewards, and penalties. The results show that adding incentives to the prime improves worker performance, regardless of whether they are framed as rewards or penalties. A small incentive generates most of the performance gains, and there is evidence for positive spillovers of incentives on unincentivized actions. The effects of adding incentives may persist into real-world tasks, whereas the effect of priming does not. The findings have important implications for the design of PFP contracts in health care, supporting the adoption of at least small incentives in lieu of information-only interventions.

Document title: Jim Crow and Black Economic Progress After Slavery
Document description: This paper studies the long-run effects of slavery and Jim Crow on Black Americans' economic outcomes. The authors use linked census and administrative records to measure how long Black families were enslaved and where they lived during Jim Crow. They show that Black families who were enslaved until the Civil War have considerably lower education, income, and wealth today than Black families who were free before the Civil War. The disparities between the two groups have persisted because most families enslaved until the Civil War lived in states with strict Jim Crow regimes after slavery. The authors also find that state-specific factors, such as Jim Crow regimes, drive the long-run persistence of the socioeconomic gap between Black families who were enslaved until the Civil War and those who were free before the Civil War. They use a regression discontinuity design to isolate the effect of Jim Crow regimes on Black economic progress and find that Black families freed in states with more oppressive regimes experienced sharply lower rates of economic progress starting in the Jim Crow era.

Document title: Externalities and the Erosion of Trust
Document description: This document presents a theory linking political and social trust to explain trust erosion in modern societies. The authors argue that individuals disagree on the seriousness of an externality problem, leading to diverging policy opinions and subsequent disappointment with government policies. This disappointment breeds institutional distrust, while the rules enacted by the government also shape individuals' notions of civic behavior, driving a wedge between expected and actual behavior. The authors conduct a survey experiment in four European countries, showing that trust dynamics come to the surface when policy issues are highly salient and mired in coordination failures. The results suggest that the most concerned individuals develop interpersonal distrust, while the less concerned develop feelings of distrust mainly towards institutions. The authors also find that support for the welfare state erodes alongside sliding trust levels.

Document title: Hukou Status and Children's Education in China
Document description: This discussion paper investigates the causal effect of hukou status on children's education in China by exploiting an exogenous change in hukou status induced by the hukou reform in 1998. The reform allowed children to inherit either their father's or mother's hukou status, providing a unique opportunity to identify the causality between hukou status and education. The paper uses China's 2010 population census data and a difference-in-differences strategy to examine the impact of hukou status on children's education. The results show that the younger cohorts exposed to the reform are more likely to have urban hukou and be at the grade level appropriate for their age. The effect is more pronounced amongst girls, and children from educated families or from large cities. The paper contributes to existing literature by identifying the causal impact of hukou status on educational attainment and exploring the stage at which hukou transformation plays a more critical role in promoting educational equity.

Document title: Crisis Risk and Risk Management
Document description: This paper assesses the current state of knowledge about crisis risk and its implications for risk management. It discusses the predictability of financial crises, the impact of interactions between risks, and the concept of polycrises. The paper also explores the role of resilience in risk management and the limitations of statistical tools in assessing crisis risk. It highlights the importance of considering the frequency of crises and the potential for unknown or unknowable risks. The paper concludes that a better understanding of crisis risk is essential for determining the type of events a firm needs to be prepared for. Strategies that increase firm operational and financial flexibility appear successful at reducing the adverse impact of crises on firms.

Document title: A Theory of Non-Coasean Labor Markets
Document description: This document discusses a theory of labor markets in a monetary economy with four realistic features: search frictions, worker productivity shocks, wage rigidity, and two-sided lack of commitment. The authors develop a model that bridges the Keynesian and search-theoretic traditions by explicitly modeling the equilibrium distribution of wages and employment in a frictional labor market subject to wage rigidity. The model predicts that inefficient job separations occur in the form of endogenous quits and layoffs, and that wages are allocative in the sense that they matter over and above match surplus for job creation and destruction. The authors also analyze the effects of a monetary shock on aggregate employment and real wages, and provide a novel characterization of competitively determined entry wages in their non-Coasean setting. They show that the share of inefficient job separations indirectly measures a firm's expected returns from posting an additional vacancy, and that the anticipation of inefficient job separations in the future also has consequences at the time of match formation.

Document title: The Economic Approach to Personality, Character and Virtue
Document description: This document discusses an economic approach to personality, character, and virtue. It presents a framework for examining the study of personality and character that underlies concepts of virtue. The authors interpret Aristotle's ideas on virtue through the lens of an economic model, which provides a useful framework for giving precision and empirical content to the study of virtue ethics. The study of virtue ethics introduces important distinctions that inform economic research, such as the distinction between intrinsic rewards associated with Aristotelian virtue and extrinsic rewards. The authors also discuss how economists view the act of being virtuous as a consequence of underlying preferences and external rewards and constraints, and how philosophers are less inclined to accept this notion of virtue. The document aims to conceptually unify notions of character and virtue across diverse fields and give these ideas empirical content.

Document title: Miracle seeds: Biased expectations, complementary input use, and the dynamics of smallholder technology adoption
Document description: This document discusses the adoption of new agricultural technologies by smallholder farmers in developing countries. It highlights the importance of complementary inputs and practices, such as fertilizers, pesticides, and irrigation, in achieving desired yields and outputs. The authors present a simple model of technology adoption that incorporates the ideas of biased expectations and complementary input use. They test the model's predictions using a field experiment conducted with over 3,500 maize farmers in eastern Uganda. The results show that farmers who were shown a short video highlighting the importance of complementary investments were more likely to dis-adopt the improved maize variety. The authors attribute this behavior change to increased knowledge and expectations that are more in line with realized outcomes. The document suggests that farmers may hold inflated expectations of new technologies due to a lack of awareness about the need for substantial complementary investments. This can lead to disappointing outcomes and subsequent dis-adoption of the technology.

Document title: Financial Crises and the Global Supply Network: Evidence from Multinational Enterprises
Document description: This paper examines the effect of financial crises on the organization of production and performance of multinational enterprises (MNEs). The authors use a rich long panel dataset covering the network structure of MNEs from 2003 to 2015 to study the impact of the 2007-2012 financial crisis on European MNEs. They find that MNEs with a more financially-hit network of affiliates perform worse in both revenues and employment growth over the 2006-2015 period. The effects are substantial, with an MNE with a financial shock to its network equal to one standard deviation of the financial shock displaying a 7.6 and 10.7 percent lower growth rate in revenues and employment, respectively. The authors also investigate how the MNE network is reshaped due to the financial shock, finding that MNEs whose network experiences a more significant financial shock react by reducing the growth in their number of affiliates in the following years relative to less affected MNEs. The effect of the financial shock builds up slowly over time, and the authors document other margins of MNE network adjustment that can help to illuminate different theories.

Document description: This paper examines how austerity measures in the United Kingdom between 2011 and 2019 influenced political participation and the public's desire for redistribution. The authors analyze data from local government districts to assess welfare losses caused by cuts to public spending and services. They find that exposure to these welfare losses leads to increased voting, greater appeals for political reform, and stronger preferences for government redistribution, though it does not significantly increase peaceful protesting. To establish causal evidence, the researchers conducted a large-scale online experiment where participants were shown videos about austerity policies versus unrelated topics. The experimental results confirm that learning about austerity mobilizes citizens to demand change through voting and appeals but fails to drive protest behavior. The study highlights the importance of redistributive preferences in shaping how individuals respond to economic hardship and policy cuts. Ultimately, the research provides new insights into the relationship between fiscal consolidation and democratic engagement in the UK context.

Document title: Financial Literacy, Experimental Preference Measures and Field Behavior – A Randomized Educational Intervention
Document description: This document presents the results of a randomized educational intervention to study the effects of teaching financial literacy to 16-year-old high-school students. The intervention consisted of eight hours of teaching and was conducted over four weeks. The study found that teaching financial literacy made subjects behave more patiently, more time-consistent, and more risk-averse in incentivized experiments on risk and time preferences. The effects of the intervention persisted for up to almost five years after the intervention. The study also found that behavior in the risk and time preference experiments was related to financial behavior in the field, including spending decisions and financial independence as young adults. The study contributes to the literature on randomized intervention studies with respect to financial literacy and the formation of economic preferences.

Document title: The Right Tool for the Job? Mortgage Distress and Personal Insolvency during the European Debt Crisis
Document description: The European debt crisis led to widespread household debt distress, with mortgage debt being the primary source of distress. The crisis posed challenges in designing and implementing legal reforms to address household debt distress. Effective debt resolution regimes can play a critical role in maintaining credit discipline and fostering growth through consumption and financial stability. The paper examines the challenges in designing and implementing legal reforms in this area and draws lessons from the European crisis. It highlights the need for a consumer insolvency regime and discusses the problem of distressed mortgage debt. The analysis uses examples from selected European countries, including Cyprus, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Latvia, Portugal, Romania, and Spain. The paper concludes that addressing household debt distress requires a comprehensive strategy, including reviewing supervisory oversight of banks, prudential norms, legal and institutional frameworks for debt enforcement and insolvency, and other supporting measures. The role of the government can vary greatly, and interim measures may be required to complement the systems for debt resolution and address special needs and circumstances in a crisis.

Document title: 2023 Cost-Effective Approaches to Improve Global Learning
Document description: The Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel (GEEAP) report provides a guide for governments and other stakeholders in low- and middle-income countries about what works in improving learning and education outcomes. The report updates a previous version of the Smart Buys and summarizes the best, most up-to-date evidence on cost-effectiveness at scale in a user-friendly way for policymakers. It groups many different types of education policies and programs into categories from Great Buys to Bad Buys, along with categories where more knowledge is needed. The report aims to support policymakers' decision-making on education investments in low- and middle-income countries. The GEEAP panel consists of leading education experts from around the world, convened by the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, the World Bank, UNICEF, and USAID. The report highlights effective but relatively expensive interventions, such as providing information on the benefits, costs, and quality of education, and targeting teaching instruction by learning level, not grade. It also identifies promising but limited evidence interventions, such as using software that allows personalized learning and adapts to the learning level of the child, and leveraging mobile phones to support learning. The report emphasizes the importance of context, political economy, and implementation details in the effectiveness of each intervention. It encourages policymakers to review both the contextual factors and the evidence on cost-effectiveness when contemplating scaling these interventions.

Document title: Estimating the distribution of wealth in New Zealand
Document description: This paper discusses alternative methods to estimate the distribution of wealth in New Zealand. It develops a taxable income capitalisation method for estimating the distribution of wealth in New Zealand that is based on the approach of Saez and Zucman. The New Zealand capitalisation method combines Inland Revenue taxable income administration data with Stats NZ's Household Balance Sheet to give new estimates of the distribution of New Zealand individuals' wealth. The method uses an individual taxpayer unit of analysis, which differs from the household measures typically used for distributional analysis. The paper presents results for 2010, 2015, and 2018, and compares these distributions with those recorded by the Household Economic Survey (HES) 2018. The New Zealand capitalisation method suggests more wealth at the top of the distribution than estimated by HES, which is consistent with similar work internationally. The method also allows for wealth estimates of smaller groups than can be reliably obtained through HES, including estimates of the wealth held by the top 0.1% of the wealth distribution.

Document title: Non-college Occupations, Workplace Routinization, and the Gender Gap in College Enrollment
Document description: The document discusses the college gender gap in the US, where women now exceed men in college enrollment. The authors argue that men have a comparative advantage in non-college work and that the widening disparity in non-college job prospects contributed to the widening of the reverse college gender gap. They use routinization - the displacement of routine tasks by automation - as a shifter of non-college job prospects and find that it increased college enrollment among young women. The authors develop a Roy model that examines educational and occupational choices and simulate the average treatment effect for all individuals in the sample, predicting a larger gender gap in college enrollment due to routinization. Document description: This paper discusses alternative methods to estimate the distribution of wealth in New Zealand. Document title: Improving Enrollment and Learning through Videos and Mobiles: Experimental Evidence from Northern Nigeria
Document description: This paper presents experimental evidence on two complementary interventions that use entertainment education and adaptive educational technologies to address several constraints faced by rural communities in northern Nigeria. The study is a cluster randomized controlled trial designed to experimentally answer two questions: 1) Can aspirational videos change parental attitudes toward education and improve enrollment and learning outcomes in traditional societies? and 2) Can educational technologies boost their effectiveness? The interventions included community screenings of aspirational videos and the distribution of mobiles with engaging apps to teach 6-9-year-old children to read. The results show that aspirational videos can be an effective tool to increase school enrollment for girls and boys, and the mobile learning add-on increased both literacy and numeracy skills for the target child and older siblings. The combined intervention also increased parental self-efficacious beliefs about their own capability to help their children learn at home, increased parents' aspirations for seeing their children continue studying in the future, and for delaying early transitions into the labor market. The study contributes to the literature on educational interventions in communities governed by traditional social norms, and it provides evidence from a middle-income country using mobile-based technologies to offer a TaRL approach to low-literate populations.

Document title: Derisking Real Estate in China’s Hybrid Economy
Document description: The document discusses the risks faced by China's real estate sector within its hybrid economy, which combines market mechanisms with state planning and government intervention. The real estate sector is crucial for China's economic growth, with real estate investment contributing to approximately 10% of GDP and the real estate and construction sector accounting for over 15% of urban employment. However, the sector is facing challenges, including a debt problem plaguing many real estate firms, drops in real estate prices, an increase in unsold housing inventory, and a slowdown of the urbanization process. The hybrid structure of the real estate sector allows the government to control the supply of land and use revenue from land sales to fund infrastructure and urban development projects. This structure also creates an environment where the real estate sector is seen as 'too important to fail', leading to implicit and explicit guarantees from the government. These guarantees create moral hazard and distortions in both state intervention and the market, exacerbating overinvestment and overleverage in the real estate sector. Document title: The Unintended Consequences of Curfews on Road Safety
Document description: The document discusses the unintended consequences of curfews on road safety. During the COVID-19 pandemic, curfews were implemented in over 100 countries to manage the spread of the virus. However, their justification lacked empirical or theoretical underpinning. The authors investigate the impact of curfews on road safety in an urban setting, specifically in Nairobi, Kenya. They find that curfews lead to large reductions in crashes during the curfew hours when cars are off the road, but these reductions are fully offset by an increase in crashes during the hours before the curfew when people rush to get home. The authors conclude that the use of curfews in future crises and pandemics should be carefully scrutinized and designed to minimize unintended negative effects. They also demonstrate that curfews create large negative spillovers on road safety, increasing the probability of a crash during non-curfew hours. The study sheds light on the question of whether curfews affect road safety and provides evidence on the effects of curfews on mobility and other economic outcomes.

Document title: Children and the gender earnings gap: evidence for Australia
Document description: This document examines the impact of children on the gender earnings gap in Australia. The authors use an event study approach to estimate the effect of children on the earnings of women and men in Australia. The results show that the arrival of children has a large and persistent impact on the earnings of women, reducing their earnings by 55% in the first 5 years after parenthood, while men's earnings remain unchanged. The authors attribute the gap in earnings to lower participation rates and reduced working hours amongst mothers. They also investigate several potential drivers of the motherhood penalty, including health issues, employer discrimination, and choices within households based on each parent's comparative advantage in the labour market. The authors suggest that the motherhood penalty is not driven by differences in preferences between men and women, but rather by constraints driven by workplace and social norms or institutions. They propose that policy can play a role in reducing these constraints to allow new parents to share work and care responsibilities more evenly.

The authors conducted a large-scale information provision experiment involving a representative population of European scholars who were randomly assigned to view either a publisher's promotional video or a copyright activist's counter-narrative. Document description: The document discusses a study abroad programme in Brazil, named Science without Borders, which was launched in 2011 to promote student and professional exchange in STEM fields. The results indicate that approved applicants are less likely to pursue a postgraduate degree in a Brazilian university and have a formal job in the first three years after the call. Document title: The Decline of Routine Tasks, Education Investments, And Intergenerational Mobility
Document description: This document presents a research paper titled 'The Decline of Routine Tasks, Education Investments, And Intergenerational Mobility' by Patrick Bennett, Kai Liu, and Kjell Salvanes. The authors investigate how a large structural change to the labor market affects education investments made at young ages. They exploit differential exposure to the national decline in routine-task intensity across local labor markets and find that the secular decline in routine tasks causes major shifts in education investments of high school students. Students invest less in vocational-trades education and increasingly invest in college education. The results highlight that labor demand changes impact inequality in the next generation, with low-ability and low-SES students being most responsive to task-biased demand changes. Intergenerational mobility in college education increases as a result. The authors also leverage parent-child linkages at the individual level to estimate the impact of shifting education investments on intergenerational mobility.

Document title: Hard and Soft Skills in Vocational Training
Document description: This paper studies the effects of an oversubscribed job-training program on skills and labor-market outcomes using both survey and administrative data. The program improves labor-market outcomes, particularly by increasing formal employment. A second round of randomization evaluates how applicants to otherwise similar job-training programs are affected by the extent that hard versus soft skills are emphasized in the curriculum. The results show that admission to a vocational program that emphasizes technical relative to social skills generates greater short-term benefits, but these relative benefits quickly disappear. The program fails to improve the soft skills or broader labor-market outcomes of women. The study advances the ongoing debate in the literature on vocational training by experimentally testing the extent that technical and soft skills produce different labor-market dynamics in the field.

Document title: Gender-targeted transfers by default? Evidence from a child allowance reform in Sweden
Document description: This document presents a study on the impact of a child allowance reform in Sweden, which changed the default disbursement option for child benefits from a 50/50 split between parents to 100% to the mother. The researchers exploit a sharp birthday discontinuity in the data to estimate the causal effect of the default transfer recipient on the long-term division of child transfers and other outcomes related to gender equality. The study finds that the 100%-to-the-mother default had a huge and persistent impact on child allowance disbursements, with a 55 percentage point increase in the share of parental couples allocating 100 percent of the transfer to the mother one year after childbirth. The researchers also find that the default option had a significant effect on divorced parents at all income levels, including low-income parents, and that the 100%-to-the-mother default shifted resources from separated fathers to separated mothers. However, the study finds no significant causal effects on the division of earnings, temporary paid parental leave, and regular paid parental leave.

Document description: This paper studies the impact of paid family leave policies in California, New Jersey, and New York on the labor market and mental health outcomes of individuals whose spouses or children experience health shocks. Document description: The document discusses collective action problems, where a group of individuals must work together to achieve a common goal, but each individual has an incentive to free-ride on the efforts of others. The authors propose a simple mechanism, called the Voluntary-Based Organization (VBO), which can be used to achieve collective goals in large groups. The VBO mechanism involves agents reporting whether they are willing to contribute to the group's goal, and if the number of willing agents meets a certain threshold, the group's goal is achieved. The authors show that the VBO mechanism is asymptotically optimal and can achieve a high probability of success even in large groups. They also discuss the implications of their findings for the study of collective action problems and the design of optimal mechanisms.

Document title: Does War Foster Cooperation or Parochialism? Evidence from a Natural Experiment among Turkish Conscripts
Document description: This study examines the social and political legacies of armed conflict exposure among Turkish conscripts. The authors exploit a natural experiment and an innovative survey design to identify the causal impact of conflict exposure on cooperative behaviors, such as social and political participation, altruism, attitudes towards conflict resolution and minorities, and general political inclination. Document description: The document studies the volume dynamics around Federal Open Committee (FOMC) announcements in the stock market. It finds that the stock market volume decreases in anticipation of FOMC announcements and increases afterward. The study attributes the volume dynamics to discretionary liquidity trading resulting from the presence of private information. The research also examines the FOMC volume dynamics for individual stocks and links it to firm characteristics. The cross-sectional analysis suggests that stocks that are perceived to be more exposed to discretionary liquidity trading exhibit more pronounced volume changes when private information presents. The study shows that the turnover volume of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) on average decreased by around 24% in the 24 hours before FOMC announcements and increased by a similar amount in the 24 hours after announcements. The FOMC volume dynamics in the stock market is consistent with a model with discretionary liquidity trading when private information presents.

Document title: Surrogate Data Models: Interpreting Large-scale Machine Learning Crisis Prediction Models
Document description: Economic crises are costly and can have long-lasting effects on a country's growth and productivity. To reduce the costs associated with economic crises, central banks and policymaking institutions have developed early warning systems and crisis prediction models. Machine learning models have been used to predict economic crises, but they often include many features and can be difficult to interpret. This paper proposes using surrogate data models to reduce the dimensionality of machine learning models and enhance their interpretability. Surrogate data models can translate model results into the economic domain familiar to senior policymakers and facilitate scenario analysis. The paper provides a concrete illustration of the surrogate data model approach as applied to a suite of machine learning models developed at the International Monetary Fund to predict sectoral economic crises. The results show that surrogate data models can provide useful insights for policymakers and can be used to perform scenario analysis of economic projections.

Document title: Policies to strengthen the resilience of global value chains
Document description: This document discusses the resilience of global value chains in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. It uses new indicators of global value chain dependencies and econometrically estimates the effects of supply disruptions abroad on domestic output. The results suggest that the adverse effects of supply disruptions are particularly large when concentration of supplying countries and supplying firms is high. Counterfactual simulations of the econometric model suggest that diversification of suppliers would have sizeable benefits in terms of shielding domestic production against country-specific supply shocks. Technological innovation that reduces foreign dependencies can have similar benefits as diversification. Public policies can enhance global value chain resilience by facilitating a quick rebound after a shock occurs or by mitigating the risk of shocks from abroad. A rapid rebound can be promoted by agility policies before a shock occurs or by adaptation policies after it materialises. Risk mitigation includes measures to diversify or partially onshore global value chains and to reduce technological dependencies.

Document title: Optimal Monetary Policy with Heterogeneous Agents: Discretion, Commitment, and Timeless Policy
Document description: This paper analyzes optimal monetary policy in a canonical heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model with wage rigidity. The authors study policy under discretion and commitment, characterizing the optimal long-run policy, time consistency, and stabilization policy. They find that a utilitarian planner faces an incentive to redistribute towards indebted, high marginal utility households, leading to inflationary bias under discretion. With commitment, zero inflation is the optimal long-run policy, and the planner trades off aggregate stabilization against distributional considerations. The authors also explore the implications of household heterogeneity for optimal monetary policy, using sequence-space methods to compute optimal stabilization policy in response to productivity, demand, and cost-push shocks.

Document title: Parental Education and Invention: The Finnish Enigma
Document description: This paper investigates the relationship between parental education and invention in Finland, a country known for its low income inequality and high social mobility. The authors use data on 1.45 million Finnish individuals and their parents to examine the causal effect of parental education on the probability of offspring becoming inventors. They find that parental income is positively associated with the probability of becoming an inventor, but this effect is greatly diminished once parental education is controlled for. The authors also find that the education reform implemented in the late 1960s has reduced the causal impact of parental education and income on the probability of inventing. They suggest that this reform has reduced the number of 'lost Einsteins and Marie Curies' in Finland. The paper contributes to the literature on innovation-based growth and the effects of parental education on offspring invention.

Document title: Discussion Topics (Working Papers) Should inequality factor into central banks' decisions?
Document description: The document discusses whether central banks should consider inequality when making monetary policy decisions. It presents a model that investigates how inequality affects desirable monetary policy in an economy subject to technology shocks. The authors find that a central bank that maximizes a welfare function that includes inflation and output gaps fares only slightly worse than the central bank that maximizes the full Ramsey problem. They also find that targeting the labor share through an augmented Taylor rule raises welfare, particularly in an economy with high inequality. This is because stabilizing inequality coincides with stabilizing the labor share, which benefits poor agents. The authors conclude that the role of inequality for monetary policy depends crucially on the interaction between steady-state inequality and a biased response in wages and profits to technology shocks.

Document title: Long COVID : The Evolution of Household Welfare in Developing Countries during the Pandemic
Document description: This paper examines the welfare impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, using harmonized data from 343 high-frequency phone surveys conducted in 80 economies during 2020 and 2021, representing more than 2.5 billion people. The analysis focuses on the scarring effects of the initial losses of employment and income by examining their evolution over time across and within countries, as restrictions on mobility and economic activity were introduced and then gradually relaxed. The employment and welfare outcomes of some groups that were impacted to a greater degree initially, including women, informal workers, and those with less education, have been improving at a slower pace. The social protection response in lower-income economies was largely insufficient to protect households from the pandemic shock. Unmitigated welfare losses are highly correlated with food insecurity, which likely led some households to sell physical assets and deplete their savings. The uneven welfare impacts associated with COVID-19 may be amplified over the medium to long term, leading to future increases in poverty and inequality.

Document title: How Do Corporate Tax Hikes Affect Investment Allocation within Multinationals?
Document description: This paper studies how corporate tax hikes transmit across countries through multinationals' internal networks of subsidiaries. The authors argue that a focus on tax competition is incomplete because it does not capture the full picture of multinationals' networks, which feature significant intra-firm production linkages. They develop a model that incorporates both tax competition between jurisdictions and production linkages between upstream and downstream subsidiaries within a multinational company. The model shows that production linkages can generate negative spillover effects, highlighting a surprising negative investment spillover due to within-multinational production linkages. The authors empirically test the implications of their model using subsidiary-level data of multinational companies from 20 European countries during 2004-2017. They find that treated subsidiaries reduce investment relative to other multinationals' subsidiaries without such exposure, suggesting that the negative effect of intra-firm production linkages outweighs positive spillovers from tax competition. The overall effect is economically sizable, with a 1% increase in the foreign corporate tax hike intensity associated with a drop in treated subsidiary investment of 0.4%.

Document title: Pushing Bonds Over the Edge: Monetary Policy and Municipal Bond Liquidity
Document description: This document examines the role of institutional investors in monetary policy transmission to asset markets, specifically in the $4 trillion municipal bond market. It finds that institutional investors, particularly mutual funds, dominate secondary market trading and are essential in price formation. The document shows that the exit of mutual funds from the secondary market leads to significantly lower liquidity, and that unexpected monetary policy tightening amplifies this effect. The study also finds that institutional investors dispose of bonds approaching the de minimis threshold, which is the point at which investors must pay ordinary income taxes on realized price appreciation. The document contributes to the literature on the role of taxes in municipal bond pricing and the impact of monetary policy on asset liquidity and pricing. It suggests that the interaction of fiscal and monetary policy may have large unintended consequences on asset liquidity and pricing. The study also finds that mutual funds exit makes large swaths of the municipal bond market illiquid during episodes of contractionary monetary policy.

Document title: Tools to Promote Productivity in Finland
Document description: The document discusses the recent productivity development in Finland, focusing on what distinguishes companies at the frontier of productivity from other companies. It presents an overview of the productivity growth potential of innovation policy measures that promote the creation of innovations that benefit society at large and the dissemination of knowledge in the economy. The measures include allocating public R&D subsidies to companies with high innovation capabilities, supporting R&D projects in centers of expertise, and promoting work-based immigration. The document also highlights the importance of ensuring that product and labor markets are well-functioning and provide an operating environment that encourages companies to make R&D investments and other intangible investments. Additionally, it notes that Finland's productivity growth has been weak, and the country has lost its competitive edge in many industries. The document suggests that the government should focus on supporting the development of high-productivity companies and promoting innovation and knowledge dissemination. It also emphasizes the need to address the issue of low productivity in the service sector, which is a major challenge for Finland's economic growth. The document concludes that innovation policy measures have a high potential for promoting productivity growth and suggests that the government should prioritize these measures.

Document title: Macroprudential Regulation: A Risk Management Approach
Document description: The document discusses macroprudential regulation and the management of systemic risk in the banking sector. Regulators use macroprudential capital requirements to manage ex-ante risks of a systemic crisis. However, there is currently little theoretical guidance on how to calibrate these capital add-ons. The authors propose a risk management approach to address this issue, using market-based estimates of systemic risk and a structural framework for credit risk assessment. They develop two approaches to map measures of systemic importance into add-on macroprudential buffers, including an equal expected impact approach and an optimization-based approach. The authors also discuss the use of credit default swap (CDS) contracts to estimate banks' default probability and default correlations. They argue that CDS prices of contracts written on subordinate debt are not contaminated by implicit put options provided by central banks' bailouts.

Document title: The Great Migration and Educational Opportunity
Document description: This paper studies the impact of the First Great Migration on children, using the 1940 Census to estimate selection-corrected place effects on education for children of Black migrants. The results show that moving to the North during the first wave of the Great Migration had substantial positive impacts on educational outcomes of children, with a 0.8 year increase in educational attainment. The study also finds that place effects varied within the North and South, with some Southern destinations being beneficial to children. The analysis reveals that factors such as school quality, labor market opportunities for Black adults, social capital, and crime rates were associated with place effects. The study concludes that many of the places with the largest positive place effects in 1940 offer relatively limited opportunities for Black children today.

Document title: Impacts of COVID-19-Era Economic Policies on Consumer Debt in the United Kingdom
Document description: The document examines the impacts of COVID-19-era economic policies on consumer debt in the United Kingdom. It uses anonymized individual-level consumer financial data on 2 million UK consumers to track the effects of the expanded Universal Credit and mortgage forbearance policies. The results show that average nonmortgage debt increased by 17 percent from October 2019 to December 2021. The expansion of Universal Credit was intended to help financially vulnerable families, but consumers who were more likely to benefit from the policy took on 1 percent more total nonmortgage debt after the policy expansion. Mortgage holders benefited from mortgage forbearance by accumulating less nonmortgage debt. The findings suggest that policies implemented in the UK to protect families might have exacerbated prepandemic inequalities.

Document title: What Drives Paternity Leave: Financial Incentives or Flexibility?
Document description: This discussion paper examines the factors that influence fathers' take-up of paternity leave in Austria. They find that the availability of shorter leave options increased leave-taking by 23 percent, while the introduction of income-dependent benefits raised take-up by another 13 percent. The authors also investigate the impact of the reforms on labor market outcomes, including employment rates and earnings, and find that the reforms did not affect these outcomes. Document title: Job Ladders by Firm Wage and Productivity
Document description: This discussion paper investigates whether workers reallocate up firm productivity and wage job ladders, and the cyclicality of this process. The authors document that productivity is a better measure of the job ladder than the average wage, since high productivity firms relative to low poach more workers than high wage firms relative to low. Employment cyclicality over the business cycle differs between the firm wage and productivity ladders. In recessions, employment decreases more in low than in high productivity firms, while employment decreases more in high than in low wage firms. The authors find that productivity is a better predictor of voluntary employment transitions than average firm wages, and that how productivity is measured matters. They also document that low productivity firms shed more employment in recessions than high productivity firms, and that the difference between high and low productivity firms in terms of net poaching rates becomes smaller in recessions.

Document title: Predicting and Preventing Gun Violence: An Experimental Evaluation of READI Chicago
Document description: The document discusses gun violence in American cities, specifically Chicago, and a community-researcher partnership called READI Chicago. The program aimed to identify men at high risk of shooting involvement and provide them with 18 months of subsidized work combined with group cognitive behavioral therapy.
