Document title: Blockbusting and the Challenges Faced by Black Families in Building Wealth through Housing in the Postwar United States
Document description: This document studies the impacts of blockbusting, a practice where real estate professionals used aggressive and discriminatory practices to orchestrate the rapid racial turnover of urban neighborhoods. The study finds that blockbusting caused substantially lower house values over the next few decades. The researchers analyze property-level data in one neighborhood in Baltimore, Maryland, and find that new residents who purchased their properties through blockbusters were charged higher prices and had higher foreclosure rates than new residents who purchased directly from existing property owners. The study suggests that blockbusting extracted wealth from Black families and left them with onerous financial obligations, hindering their ability to build wealth through housing. The researchers also find that blockbusting contributed to the racial tipping of neighborhoods, where the Black population increased significantly. The study's findings provide insight into the history of wealth building by Black families in the postwar period and highlight the need for policies to address housing market and finance discrimination.

Document title: The Geography of Business Dynamism and Skill Biased Technical Change
Document description: The document discusses the growing economic disparities across cities in the United States since 1980, known as the Great Divergence. It explores the underlying causes of this trend, focusing on the geographic distribution of relative wage inequality, firm dynamics, and technology adoption. The author develops a spatial model to analyze the diffusion of a new technology that favors skilled workers, showing that firms in big cities adopt more of this technology due to market size, ex-ante differences in technology, and amenities. The model also explains the changing relationship between business dynamism and city size, as well as the increasing investment in information and communication technology in big cities. The author finds that selection becomes tougher in big cities, leading to an increase in dynamism rates and a divergence in average total productivity between big and small cities. The document also analyzes policies aimed at increasing adoption, suggesting a tension between increasing aggregate technology adoption and decreasing geographic inequality.

Document description: The Latin American and Caribbean economies are facing complex conditions, with multiple concurrent crises threatening to exacerbate structural problems. The region has an opportunity to chart a new course towards sustainable development with gender equality at its centre. Document title: What Contributes to Rising Inequality in Large Cities?
Document description: This working paper analyzes trends in income inequality within large cities across a selected sample of OECD countries over the last two decades. The authors employ a combination of dynamic and static approaches to estimate the contributions of various determinants to changes in income distribution. Using reweighting techniques and recentered influence functions, the study identifies an upward trend in inequality within large cities and higher levels of inequality compared to other areas. The results indicate that these trends are primarily driven by changes in the returns to endowments rather than changes in their distribution. The magnitude of these findings varies significantly across the analyzed countries, with the skill premium contributing more to inequality in the United States than in European nations. Educational attainment is identified as one of the most important factors explaining these trends, alongside age, household composition, and household size in European contexts. The paper concludes that income inequality is generally higher in large cities than in other areas, supporting the thesis that urbanization correlates with increased disparity.

Document description: This discussion paper studies the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the livelihoods and mental health of urban informal-sector workers in India. The authors find that men's employment declined significantly during the pandemic, while women's employment remained unaffected. Men's monthly earnings also declined by 89 percent, while women reported higher levels of mental stress. The authors suggest that part of this gendered pattern in pandemic-induced mental stress may be explained by employment losses suffered by men, which affected wives more than husbands. They also find that social networks play a mitigating role for men's mental health, but an exacerbating role for women's mental health. The authors conclude that the pandemic has had a devastating impact on the mental well-being of urban informal-sector workers in India, particularly women.

Document description: The document discusses the impact of floods on European manufacturing firms during the period 2007-2018. Document title: Back to the future? Macroprudential policy and the rebirth of local authority mortgages in Ireland
Document description: The global financial crisis led to the introduction of macroprudential mortgage regulations in Ireland, which safeguard the financial system but can lead to credit access difficulties for first-time buyers. The Rebuilding Ireland Home Loan (RIHL) scheme was introduced to address this issue, providing direct public mortgages for low-to-middle-income first-time buyers through local authorities. The scheme has been popular, with €178 million lent out in the first 16 months, and has helped to bridge credit gaps while ensuring commercial banks are subject to strong macroprudential rules. The scheme's loan-to-income levels are higher than those available through commercial banks, and the loan product has been well-targeted at those facing credit access difficulties due to high house prices and macroprudential regulations. The scheme's lending conditions, including loan-to-value and debt-service-to-income ratios, are well-calibrated to limit risk ex ante. The paper demonstrates that the RIHL lending product correctly targets the group of households most affected by the stricter loan-to-income ratio, and that using a tailored measure such as this allows for a strong macroprudential framework for the commercial banking sector while ensuring that first-time buyers can access housing credit once they are creditworthy.

Document title: The Impact of Paid Family Leave on Families with Health Shocks
Document description: This paper analyzes the impact of paid family leave (PFL) policies in California, New Jersey, and New York on the labor market and mental health outcomes of individuals whose spouses or children experience health shocks. The authors use data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) to study hospitalizations and surgeries as measures of health shocks. They find that PFL access leads to a 7.0 percentage point decline in the likelihood that the healthy wives of individuals with medical conditions or limitations who experience a hospitalization or surgery report leaving a job to care for home or family. The authors also provide suggestive evidence that caregivers whose employers do not offer paid sick leave benefits and who work in firms with 50 or more employees experience larger reductions in self-reported poor mental health and in the use of mental health prescription drugs as a result of access to PFL.

Document description: The document discusses transition risk, a type of risk associated with climate change. Document title: How Substitutable Are Workers? Evidence from Worker Deaths
Document description: The document discusses the substitutability of workers in labor markets. It presents an empirical analysis of the effects of unexpected worker deaths on firms' demand for incumbent workers and new hires. The study uses administrative data from Germany and finds that worker deaths raise the remaining workers' wages and retention probabilities. However, the effects are heterogeneous across skill groups, occupational boundaries, and labor markets. The study also estimates the costs of replacing workers and finds that firms face substantial replacement costs, which are larger in thin markets and when skills are specialized. The findings are hard to reconcile with frictionless labor markets and perfect substitutability between incumbents and outsiders. The study contributes to the literature on labor demand and wages, rent-sharing, and labor pooling as an agglomeration force.

Document description: This document studies how salary history disclosures affect employer demand and how salary history bans shape hiring and wages. The authors conducted a novel, two-sided field experiment where hundreds of recruiters reviewed over 2,000 job applications. They found that employers make negative inferences about candidates who refuse to disclose their salary history, and that disclosures by men and other highly paid candidates yield higher salary offers. However, these disclosures also yield fewer callbacks. The authors also found that recruiters correctly anticipate that women are less likely to disclose their salary history at any level, and thus they punish women less than men for silence. The study highlights important trade-offs between disclosures and callback rates, and the authors use their results to evaluate salary history bans and their design choices.

Document description: The document discusses the effects of economic incentives on parental leave in Sweden, specifically the 'jämställdhetsbonusen' (gender equality bonus) introduced in 2008. The bonus was a financial incentive for parents to share parental leave more equally. The study examines the impact of the bonus on the distribution of parental leave between mothers and fathers, as well as its effects on labor market outcomes. The results show that the bonus reduced the gap in parental leave between parents with the highest and lowest leave, but did not affect the gap between mothers and fathers. The study also finds that the bonus had an interesting pattern of effects on labor market outcomes, with mothers who received a negative effect on parental leave also experiencing a decrease in their labor market income and an increase in their use of VAB (temporary parental leave for care of a sick child). The study concludes that economic incentives can be effective in promoting more equal parental leave, but that the design of such incentives is crucial to avoid unintended effects.

Document description: The document discusses the reduction of the gender gap in parental leave through economic incentives in Sweden. It presents evidence from a unique parental leave policy, the gender equality bonus, introduced in 2008. The bonus rewarded parents with a financial bonus as a function of their division of paid parental leave. The study finds that the policy significantly reduced the absolute difference in leave days between parents, particularly in the small group of parents where the father had the highest uptake. The results suggest that a bonus-system can be a potent policy instrument for affecting the division of paid parental leave. The study also examines the link between the division of early parental leave and long-term division of home and market production, finding that parents who changed their uptake of paid parental leave due to the bonus adjusted their more long-term childcare involvement. The findings have implications for policies aimed at achieving a more equal division of home and market production.

Document title: Internet Use and Fertility Behavior among Reproductive-Age Women in China
Document description: The document discusses the impact of internet use on fertility behavior among reproductive-age women in China. The authors use longitudinal data from the 2014-2018 China Family Panel Studies to investigate the effect of internet use on fertility. They find that internet use reduces the number of children born, with more pronounced effects among women with a moderate level of education, those aged 16-19, rural residents, and those who are married. The authors suggest that internet use may operate through multiple channels, including decreased marital satisfaction, changed attitudes toward traditional gender roles, and a reduction in the importance placed on ancestral lines. The study contributes to the literature on the internet-fertility nexus and provides insights into the linkage between internet use and fertility in China and other economies.

Document title: The European Green Deal - Perspectives for the EU-Asia Relationship
Document description: The European Green Deal is a plan by the European Union to make Europe the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. The deal aims to create a viable and internationally competitive economy that is also sustainable. The EU needs partners in all parts of the globe to achieve this goal, and the Asia-Pacific region is pivotal in efforts to accelerate the shift towards resource-efficient and environmentally friendly economic and growth models. The study explores the current situation, underlying conditions and developments in four Asian countries: Japan, China, India, and Singapore. The results reveal a variety of fields for cooperation, but also indicate that sustainability policy is closely intertwined with geopolitical conflicts and fundamentally different political concepts and values. The study provides a differentiated picture of parameters and processes for sustainable development, and elaborates cornerstones and recommendations for EU cooperation within the framework of the European Green Deal. The EU should take into account the diversity of the Asian continent and its different strategies for shaping change in its concepts and offers of cooperation. The study contributes to a better understanding of the conceptual foundations and the political consequences of the European Green Deal adopted in 2019 with a view to the European Union's relations with the rest of the world, especially in the Asia-Pacific region.

Document title: Keep Calm and Carry On: The Short- vs. Long-Run Effects of Mindfulness Meditation on (Academic) Performance
Document description: The document discusses the effects of mindfulness meditation on academic performance in higher education. Mindfulness meditation is becoming increasingly popular in Western societies, including in education and business. The authors conducted a field experiment in an educational setting to investigate the causal impact of mindfulness meditation on academic performance. They found that the intervention improved students' mental health and non-cognitive skills, but it marginally decreased short-term academic performance. However, the long-term effects of the intervention were positive, with a significant increase in academic performance by about 0.4 standard deviations six months after the intervention. The authors also found that the intervention led to an increase in daily healthy routine and self-care practices, which were the best predictors of changes in short-term grades. The study suggests that mindfulness meditation may have positive effects on academic performance in the long run, but its effects may be more complex and nuanced than previously thought.

Document title: Employee Evaluation and Skill Investments: Evidence from Public School Teachers
Document description: This document presents evidence on how employee evaluation affects the performance of teachers. It studies public school teachers in Tennessee who were subject to a new teacher evaluation strategy in 2012. The policy required new performance measures and performance incentives linked to those measures. The results show that teacher performance began improving before any rewards or consequences were linked to a teacher's measured performance. Anticipation of future incentives increased teacher value-added by 0.023σ or more. New performance measures boosted value-added as well, separate from incentives. The combined effect of the two treatments was 0.047σ for pre-tenure teachers. The effects of prior tenure incentives on value-added persisted after those incentives had ended. The gains accumulated before earning tenure persisted after earning tenure. The new performance incentives had little to no effect on teachers quitting or changing jobs. The document contributes empirical evidence of anticipation effects and persistent effects on job performance.

Document title: Does War Foster Cooperation or Parochialism? Evidence from a Natural Experiment among Turkish Conscripts
Document description: This study investigates the social and political legacies of armed conflict exposure among Turkish conscripts. The authors use a natural experiment and an innovative survey design to identify the causal impact of conflict exposure on cooperative behaviors. They find little evidence that exposure to war violence promotes prosociality, but instead, it fosters parochialism, measured by increased opposition to peaceful means of conflict resolution, animosity towards minorities, and the tendency to support right-wing political parties. The study design eliminates the need for social insurance, security concerns, and community-level paradigm shifts, and the analysis rules out labor market outcomes, human capital formation, and military socialization from the list of usual suspects. The authors conclude that violence exposure, in and of itself, is not sufficient to foster cooperative behaviors but promotes parochialism. Further analyses show war-driven grievances, the normalization of violence in everyday life, and changes in parochial norms and preferences as the transmitting pathways.

Document title: The Big Three and Board Gender Diversity: The Effectiveness of Shareholder Voice
Document description: The document discusses the effectiveness of shareholder voice in increasing gender diversity on corporate boards. In 2017, three major institutional investors launched campaigns to increase gender diversity, which led to a significant increase in the number of female directors on US boards. The campaigns were successful in increasing the number of female directors, with one standard deviation greater ownership stake associated with a 76% increase in the net flow of new female board members and an 11% increase in the overall proportion of female directors. The growth in female directors was not driven by firm characteristics other than Big Three ownership, and the campaigns spurred a push to develop a greater pipeline of female directors. Shareholders voted overwhelmingly in support of the new women, awarding them even more votes than newly appointed male directors. The results illustrate shareholder advocacy's potential to expand women's participation in corporate leadership more robustly than do government mandates.

Document title: How Substitutable Are Workers? Evidence from Worker Deaths
Document description: The document discusses how easily firms can replace workers who leave their jobs. It presents an empirical analysis of the effects of unexpected worker deaths on firms' demand for the labor of their remaining workers. The study uses administrative data from Germany and finds that worker deaths affect firms' demand for the labor of their remaining workers, leading to a statistically significant earnings increase of about 0.6% in the year after the death. The analysis also shows substantial heterogeneity in the effects across skill groups, occupational boundaries, and labor markets. The study contributes to the literature on labor economics by quantifying the frictions that firms face in replacing workers and providing direct evidence for a mechanism that gives rise to rent sharing.

Document title: Trust as state capacity
Document description: The document discusses the link between trust in government and state capacity, with a focus on how citizens' trust in their government can increase compliance with policies. The authors explore a specific channel whereby citizens who are convinced that a policy is worthwhile are more motivated to comply with it, reducing the government's cost of implementing a policy. The paper provides empirical evidence consistent with the model's findings using the Integrated Values Survey and voluntary compliance during COVID-19 in the UK. The authors suggest that trust in government can play a role in building and expanding state capacities. The document also discusses the role of trust in government in increasing compliance and building state capacity, with a focus on situations where state action has two key elements: the state's informational advantage and the need for supportive action by citizens. The authors consider a world where citizens are motivated to comply as long as they perceive their actions to be serving the common good. The paper relates the ideas in this paper to the large literature on political trust and state capacity, and discusses the underpinnings of prosociality which play a role in the modeling framework. The authors develop a core model along with a number of extensions, and link the model to the origins of trust in government. The paper also discusses the empirical implications of the ideas and contains some concluding comments.

Document title: Keep calm and carry on: The short- vs. long-run effects of mindfulness meditation on (academic) performance
Document description: This document presents a discussion paper from the WZB Berlin Social Science Center investigating the causal impact of an eight-week mindfulness meditation training on the academic performance of university students. The authors conducted a randomized controlled trial where students were assigned to either a treatment group receiving the course or a control group, with data collected on grades, mental health, and various skills before and after the intervention. The study finds that while the program significantly improved students' self-reported mental health and non-cognitive skills, the immediate effect on academic grades was actually negative, resulting in a marginal decrease in performance during the short term following the course. However, when examining the long-term effects approximately six months after the intervention ended, the researchers observed a significant increase in academic performance by about 0.4 standard deviations. These results suggest that while mindfulness meditation helps with mental well-being, its benefits on academic achievement are not immediate and may take several months to materialize. The paper discusses potential mechanisms such as the temporary diversion of cognitive resources during the learning phase versus the long-term gains in focus and stress management. The authors conclude that the timing of the effects is crucial, highlighting a delay between the intervention and its positive impact on grades. This research fills a gap in the literature regarding the spillover effects of mindfulness practices on specific life outcomes like academic performance.

Document title: How Substitutable Are Workers? Evidence from Worker Deaths
Document description: This document estimates how easily firms can replace workers after an unexpected worker death. The authors analyze 34,000 worker deaths in Germany and find that firms' demand for incumbent workers increases after a worker death, resulting in higher wages and retention rates. The effects are larger for workers with more specific human capital, such as longer tenure or specialized occupations. The findings suggest that firms face substantial replacement costs, which are larger in thin markets and when skills are specialized. The authors also estimate a simple wage posting model to quantify the deviation from a frictionless labor market and find that firms face replacement costs on the order of magnitude of two annual salaries of a deceased worker. The results are consistent with some internal labor market models but are harder to reconcile with models of slot constraints and vacancy chains.

Document title: The Effects of Combat Deployments on Veterans' Outcomes
Document description: The document discusses the effects of combat deployments on veterans' outcomes, including physical and mental disability, mortality and suicide, and antisocial behavior. It presents a study that estimates the causal effect of combat deployments on veterans' outcomes using a novel dataset that matches military and non-military administrative records. The study also finds that more dangerous deployments have limited effects on outcomes beyond death and injury directly resulting from combat. The results suggest that deployment cannot explain trends in outcomes not directly related to warfighting, such as noncombat deaths, and that changes in soldiers' observable characteristics, such as AFQT scores and moral conduct waivers, are closely connected to changes in these outcomes.

Document title: Empowerment, Aspirations, and Girls’ Education
Document description: The document discusses the relationship between education and girls' empowerment and aspirations. It highlights that simply sending girls to school does not guarantee empowerment and that learning boosts indicators of empowerment more than just going to school. It notes that education's initial role in the empowerment process was understood primarily as sending children to school with little attention paid to the schooling process or outcomes beyond enrollment and completion. The document concludes that empowerment is still sometimes inaccurately seen as a direct result of schooling and can often be conflated with the terms self-confidence and self-esteem.

Document description: This paper examines the relationship between labor costs, firm structure, and development. Document title: Learning Inequalities during COVID-19: Evidence from Longitudinal Surveys from Sub-Saharan Africa
Document description: The COVID-19 pandemic has had a significant impact on learning outcomes in low-income countries in Sub-Saharan Africa. The authors analyze data from 34 longitudinal surveys from seven countries to assess the effects of the pandemic on learning inequalities. They find that the pandemic resulted in lower school enrolment rates and reduced learning activities, with households with higher education levels or living standards being more likely to engage their children in learning activities. The authors also find that policies targeting individual household members are most effective for improving learning activities, followed by those targeting households, communities, and regions. A sharp education gradient exists, where household heads who completed primary education are more likely to engage their children in any learning activities, but the corresponding figures are two to three times higher for heads with some secondary education or post-secondary education. The authors conclude that the pandemic has exacerbated existing learning inequalities in low-income countries and that targeted policies are needed to address these inequalities.

Document title: Global Fund Flows and Emerging Market Tail Risk
Document description: This document explores the relationship between global risk and risk aversion shocks and their impact on emerging market capital flows and returns. The authors use a panel quantile regression approach to analyze the distributional implications of these shocks on cross-border flows and asset prices. They find that shocks to the quantity and price of risk have distinct implications for the median emerging market flow and return and the tails of the distributions. Document title: The Effects of Racial Segregation on Intergenerational Mobility: Evidence from Historical Railroad Placement
Document description: This paper provides new evidence on the causal impacts of city-wide racial segregation on intergenerational mobility. The authors use an instrumental variable approach that relies on plausibly exogenous variation in segregation due to the arrangement of railroad tracks in the nineteenth century. Their analysis finds that higher segregation reduces upward mobility for Black children from households across the income distribution and White children from low-income households. Segregation also lowers academic achievement while increasing incarceration and teenage birth rates. The authors investigate mechanisms and find that segregation reduces government spending, weakens support for anti-poverty policies, and increases racially conservative attitudes for White residents. They conclude that segregation lowers upward mobility by 46% for the poorest Black children and by 30% for the poorest White children, translating into decreases in children's long-run income of nearly $80 billion per year.

Document title: Gender diversity in bank boardrooms and green lending : evidence from euro area credit register data.
Document description: This document investigates the relationship between gender diversity in bank boardrooms and green lending. The authors use granular credit register data to analyze the influence of female directors on banks' lending decisions towards less polluting firms. They find that banks with more gender-diverse boards provide less credit to more polluting companies and that female directors' specific characteristics, such as education level, matter for lending behavior. The study also shows that the 'greening' effect of female members in banks' boardrooms is stronger in countries with more female climate-oriented politicians. The findings have important implications for regulators and policymakers, highlighting the crucial role played by banks in driving the transition towards a greener economy.

Document title: Intergenerational Mobility in the Land of Inequality
Document description: This document estimates intergenerational income mobility in Brazil, a developing country with extreme inequality in socioeconomic conditions. The authors use a combination of administrative registries and large-scale surveys to link incomes across generations and estimate the degree of persistence. They find that a 10 percentile increase in parental income is associated with a 5.5 percentile increase in child income, and that children born to parents in the bottom quintile face a 46% chance of remaining at the bottom when adults. The authors also document substantial heterogeneity in mobility across individual characteristics, such as gender and race, and across Brazilian regions. They find that upward mobility is lower in Brazil than in other countries, and that social mobility varies significantly across the Brazilian territory. The authors also explore the association of parental income with a broad array of long-term outcomes, including education, occupation, and mortality.

Document title: The Impact of the Spatial Population Distribution on Economic Growth: Evidence from the United States
Document description: The document discusses the impact of spatial population distribution on economic growth in the United States. The authors introduce a new measure called Spatial Population Concentration (SPC) to capture the weighted average population surrounding every person within a geographic area. They find that the SPC measure has the strongest relationship with subsequent economic growth for a 25km radius, and that regional policies that affect density as infrastructure projects should target this distance range to maximize growth. The authors also find that education plays a key role in growth and has the highest impact in densely populated areas. They suggest that policymakers should strive to increase population concentration and avoid city sprawling, and that transportation and communication infrastructure also contribute to growth.

Document title: Who Protests, What Do They Protest, and Why?
Document description: The document discusses protests and demonstrations in the United States during the summer of 2020, focusing on the Black Lives Matter movement and protests calling for less stringent public health measures to combat COVID-19. Document title: The Role of Firms in the Gender Wage Gap in Germany
Document description: This report provides a detailed analysis of the gender wage gap in Germany, focusing on the role of firms. The report uses administrative data to analyze the gap in pay between men and women with equivalent skills within and between firms at each age. The findings suggest that three-quarters of the gender wage gap is due to differences in pay within firms, mainly due to men and women having different tasks and responsibilities. The report recommends a comprehensive policy package to tackle the gender wage gap, including education and family policies, and policies directed at firms to promote better working conditions for all workers. The report also suggests that public paid parental leave policies should continue to promote equal use by fathers and mothers, and that public investment in Early Childhood Education and Care services needs to be sustained and expanded. Additionally, the report recommends strengthening labour market policies to promote women's access to better quality jobs, and introducing pay transparency measures to increase awareness of existing hiring and career development outcomes within firms.

Document title: "Workhorses of Opportunity": Regional Universities Increase Local Social Mobility
Document description: The document discusses the impact of regional public universities on local social mobility. It presents a study that uses data from Opportunity Insights to identify the effects of regional universities on the educational attainment and economic mobility of nearby children. The study finds that regional public universities increase the fraction of children in the county who obtain at least a four-year degree and at least some college, especially for children from lower-income families. The study also shows that these universities improve the fraction of children in the county who are employed in their mid-30s and their income percentiles, with effects concentrated among children from lower-income families. The study explores potential mechanisms that may explain the effect of regional public universities on social mobility and suggests that the mechanism is perhaps the most obvious one: regional public universities increase access to higher education for students in the local area and this increases mobility.

Document title: Cyclical Earnings, Career and Employment Transitions
Document description: This paper studies the cyclical behaviour of earnings risk and career changes. It documents that the procyclical skewness of the earnings growth distribution arises mostly from the earnings changes of employer and occupation switchers. The paper proposes a multi-sector business cycle model with on-the-job search and endogenous occupational mobility to investigate the relative importance of employer and occupational mobility in driving cyclical earnings changes. The model reveals that idiosyncratic occupational mobility is the main driver of cyclical earnings risk, mainly due to cyclical shifts in the returns to this mobility. The paper also finds that the sullying effects of recessions are long-lasting and manifest themselves through a collapse of the job ladder and forgone lifetime earnings gains, especially for low-paid workers, and through large lifetime earnings losses among high-paid workers who experience forced occupational mobility and poor re-employment outcomes.

Document title: All Clear for Takeoff: Evidence from Airports on the Effects of Infrastructure Privatization
Document description: This document examines the effects of infrastructure privatization on airport performance. The authors analyze a dataset of 2,444 unique airports in 217 countries and find that private equity ownership improves airport performance, including volume, efficiency, and quality. They also find that private equity owners invest in new physical capacity and negotiate more effectively with airlines. The authors suggest that the benefits of private equity ownership are concentrated in airports with competing airports nearby, under longer-term leases, and in less corrupt local governments. They also find that non-private equity private firms tend to target more corrupt locations and fail to outperform government ownership. The authors conclude that private equity ownership can be a effective way to improve airport performance, but that the benefits depend on the specific context.

Document title: Cyclical Earnings, Career and Employment Transitions
Document description: This paper studies the cyclical behaviour of earnings risk and career changes over the business cycle. It is well documented that during recessions those individuals who separate directly to another job face lower earnings gains, while those who lose their jobs suffer larger earnings losses relative to expansions. The distribution of earnings growth exhibits procyclical skewness, with the right tail compressing and the left tail expanding in recessions and vice versa in expansions. The paper shows that career changes, specifically occupational mobility, are the main driver behind the cyclical patterns of the earnings growth distribution. Occupational mobility due to workers' evolving idiosyncratic career prospects rather than occupation-wide productivity differences makes occupational mobility the more important component. The paper also finds that employer mobility on its own does not contribute as much as occupational mobility in shaping cyclical earnings risk. The sullying effects of recessions are long-lived, manifesting themselves through a collapse of the job ladder, particularly for occupation switchers, and forgone lifetime earnings gains especially for low-paid workers, and through large lifetime earnings losses faced by high-paid workers who experience forced occupational mobility and poor re-employment outcomes.

Document title: Filling the Gap: The Consequences of Collaborator Loss in Corporate R&D
Document description: This document examines the consequences of collaborator loss in corporate R&D. The authors argue that the loss of a collaborator affects not only the remaining collaborators but also the employer, who seeks to fill the gap left by the lost collaborator. This shift in bargaining power may lead to benefits for the remaining collaborators, such as additional resources or more attractive working conditions. The authors empirically investigate the consequences of collaborator loss by exploiting unexpected deaths of active inventors and find that the loss of a collaborator has a moderate negative effect on the productivity of the remaining collaborators. However, this negative effect disappears when the remaining collaborators work for the same employer as the deceased inventor. The authors also find that the remaining collaborators with the same employer are more likely to be promoted and less likely to leave their current employer. The study contributes to the literature on collaborations and the careers of knowledge workers by investigating the effects of collaborator loss on the career trajectories of knowledge workers.

Document title: Using Social Media to Change Gender Norms : An Experiment within Facebook Messenger in India
Document description: This paper experimentally tests the effectiveness of two short edutainment campaigns delivered through Facebook Messenger at reshaping gender norms and reducing social acceptability of violence against women in India. The campaigns consisted of video clips with implicit or explicit messaging formats. The study found that both edutainment formats worked, with effects varying for different outcomes. The implicit format was more effective at raising knowledge and reshaping attitudes related to gender norms and violence against women, while the explicit format was more impactful in increasing willingness to share video clips with friends and promoting online information-seeking behaviors. In the four-month survey, individuals assigned to the docuseries were 91% more likely to add the frame 'End Violence Against Women' to their Facebook profile picture. The study also found that the social channel is not a necessary condition for changing individuals' attitudes and behaviors through online campaigns. The results lend support to the possibility of achieving a self-sustained virtuous circle of social change.

Document title: The Usual Suspects: Offender Origin, Media Reporting and Natives’ Attitudes Towards Immigration
Document description: This document analyses the impact of media reporting on natives' attitudes towards immigration. It takes advantage of a change in reporting policy by the German newspaper Sächsische Zeitung in July 2016, which started systematically disclosing the origins of criminals. The study uses individual-level panel data from the German Socio-Economic Panel and crime-related articles in German newspapers to estimate how this policy change affects natives' concerns about immigration. The results show that systematically disclosing the origins of criminals reduces natives' concerns about immigration, driven by a disproportionate increase in the disclosure of the origins of native offenders. This effect is interpreted within a Bayesian model where individuals form beliefs on foreign and native crime rates based on media information. The study also finds that native respondents uncouple the issues of crime and immigration after the policy change, blaming immigrants less and becoming more likely to identify crime as a central issue in itself.

Document title: The Employment Consequences of Anti-Dumping Tariffs: Lessons from Brazil
Document description: The document discusses the employment consequences of anti-dumping tariffs in Brazil. The authors use data on all anti-dumping investigations in Brazil and match it to firm-level administrative employment information. They find that anti-dumping tariffs decrease imports and increase employment in the protected sector, but decrease employment and wages in downstream firms. The authors also build a small open economy model that features international trade, input-output linkages, and labor force participation to quantify the aggregate effect of these tariffs. They show that the Brazilian anti-dumping policy increased employment and GDP, but the effect of tariffs on employment depends on the position of the tariffed product along the value chain. The authors conclude that tariffs should be targeted at items produced by sectors at the end of the value chain that use inputs from a wide range of sectors to maximize employment.

Document title: NAFTA and Drug-Related Violence in Mexico
Document description: This document studies the impact of NAFTA on drug-related violence in Mexico. The authors propose a novel mechanism according to which positive trade shocks trigger the rapacity effect, increasing profits for Mexican cartels and incentivizing them to use violence to compete over smuggling routes. The introduction of NAFTA in 1994 increased the value of controlling the corridors for transporting illegal drugs into the U.S. for drug-trafficking organizations, leading to an increase in drug-related homicides by approximately 2.3 per 100,000 inhabitants in municipalities with a predicted drug-trafficking route. The results suggest that NAFTA had displacement effects, diverting violence from regions further away to those in close proximity of routes. The authors also find that municipalities traversed by routes still experienced higher levels of drug-related homicides in the 2000s, and that route location is significantly related to homicides resulting from inter-cartel conflict.

The document also notes that poorer households are more likely to be left with less money after taxes have been paid and transfers received, and that poorer economies rely more on indirect taxes, which are less progressive. Document description: The document discusses the relationship between gender diversity in bank boardrooms and green lending. It explores the potential influence of women in the boardroom on banks' lending strategies, specifically whether a greater female representation can shape banks' decisions to discriminate lending between more and less polluting firms. The study uses a unique sample of almost a million loans extracted from the European System of Central Banks' analytical credit register, matched with firm-level information on greenhouse gas emissions. The findings have important implications for regulators and policymakers, highlighting the crucial role played by banks in driving the transition toward a greener economy. Document title: United Arab Emirates (UAE) : Legal Reforms to Strengthen Women’s Economic Inclusion - Case Study
Document description: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) introduced a historic package of legal reforms in 2019-2020 to strengthen women's economic participation, aligning with its national policy commitment to gender balance. The reforms included paid parental leave in the private sector for the first time in the Middle East and North Africa, enabling women to choose where to live and travel, introducing equal pay for work of equal value, and lifting the obedience provision in the UAE's Personal Status Law. The UAE has set an important precedent for legal gender equality in the region, becoming the first economy to introduce paid parental leave for male and female employees in the private sector. The reforms have shown that strong leadership commitment can lead to significant progress towards gender equality within a short period of time. The UAE has also demonstrated how changes to the Personal Status Laws can be implemented to create greater gender equality while aligning with sharia principles. The country has made significant progress in increasing female labor force participation, with a labor force participation rate of 58 percent in 2019, compared to 20 percent in the MENA region and 47 percent globally. However, despite these gains, female labor force participation in the UAE remained lower than men's, which has been relatively stable at over 90 percent since the 1990s. The UAE has a highly educated female population, with 47.8 percent of women over the age of 25 having obtained at least a Bachelor's degree or equivalent, compared to 45.9 percent of men. The country has also made efforts to address barriers to women's entry into the labor force, including access to childcare and flexible work options.

Document title: Evolving Financial Stress in China's Property Development Sector
Document description: Financial stress in China's property development sector has been a significant concern due to its potential impact on the broader Chinese economy. The sector has been a major contributor to China's economic growth, driven by rapid urbanization and high demand for housing as a financial asset. However, this model has left developers vulnerable to short-term funding stress, which was realized in 2021 with the default of China Evergrande Group. The sector's financial fragility is attributed to high leverage, declining profitability, and a complex corporate structure. The 'three red lines' policy, introduced in 2020, aimed to improve financial stability by setting debt-to-asset and net debt-to-equity ratios. However, this policy made the financial position of riskiest developers even more precarious. Evergrande Group's financial stress was a major concern, with its bond and equity prices falling rapidly due to negative news. The sector's financial stress has led to a wave of defaults and restructurings, which are likely to permanently change the structure of China's property development sector and reduce its capacity for rapid, large-scale development.

Document description: The document studies the evolution of the gender gap in earnings in the US real estate sector during the housing boom of the early-to-mid 2000s. The author finds that the gender gap in total earnings in US real estate increased significantly between 2000 and 2007, especially in local markets where house prices appreciated by relatively more. Document title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940–2018
Document description: This document studies the emergence of new work in the United States between 1940 and 2018. The authors construct a novel database of new job titles linked to US Census microdata and patent-based measures of occupations' exposure to labor-augmenting and labor-automating innovations. They find that the majority of current employment is in new job specialties introduced after 1940, with the locus of new work creation shifting from middle-paid production and clerical occupations to high-paid professional and low-paid services. The authors also establish that technological innovations that complement the outputs of occupations and demand shocks raise occupational demand, while innovations that automate tasks or reduce occupational demand slow new work emergence. They conclude that the demand-eroding effects of automation innovations have intensified in the last four decades, while the demand-increasing effects of augmentation innovations have not.

Document title: Internal Migration in the United States: Rates, Selection, and Destination Choice, 1850-1940
Document description: The document studies internal migration in the United States from 1850 to 1940, using linked census data. The study also finds that the relationship between internal migration and urbanization changed over time, with urbanites initially more likely to migrate than ruralists, but by the twentieth century, they were either less likely or approximately as likely to migrate. The 1930s marked a change in these patterns, with a decline in internal migration rates and a retrenchment in the degree to which urbanization growth or labor demand growth experienced by internal migrants exceeded that of stayers. The study contributes to a clearer understanding of historic US internal migration and its interaction with the development of the US economy.

Document title: No. 415 Electoral Cycles in Macroeconomic Forecasts
Document description: This document discusses the existence of electoral cycles in macroeconomic forecasts released by governments. The authors propose a theoretical model of political selection, where governments release overly optimistic GDP growth forecasts ahead of elections to increase their reelection probability. The model predicts the existence of political forecast cycles and the bias in forecasts depends on the political strength in parliament of the incumbent government. The authors test the model's predictions using high-frequency forecaster-level data from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Sweden, and find evidence of electoral cycles in the forecast bias for short-term real GDP growth. The results suggest that governments overestimate economic performances by up to 13 percent ahead of elections. The authors also find that the election timing matters and that the bias is more pronounced when the president has contingent individual reelection incentives, the party of the president has the majority in both branches of Congress, and elections are expected to be close.

Document description: This document discusses the relationship between housing wealth and divorce rates. Document title: Economies of Density, Team Synergies and Unobserved Heterogeneity: A Study of Home Care Services
Document description: The document discusses economies of density in the home care services industry, where caregivers drive to visit patients scattered in a district and deliver various care services at the patient's home. The authors use a unique data set to study the technological properties of these services and estimate the intensity of economies of density. They find that the home-care sector is characterized by excess entry and that a form of franchise-bidding regulation could be appropriate. The authors also study the unobserved heterogeneity of employees and use a quadratic-in-logs, finite-mixture model with latent groups to uncover a finite number of employee types with different cost curves. They show that some types, but not all, have U-shaped average cost curves yielding an aggregate average transportation cost that is itself U-shaped. The economies of density are mainly due to team synergies operating at the district level. The authors conclude that their results have consequences for regulation policy and that the French government could save around a hundred million euros every year.

Document title: The Effects of Teacher Quality on Adult Criminal Justice Contact
Document description: This paper estimates the impact of teachers on their students' future criminal justice contact. Using a unique data set linking North Carolina public school data to administrative arrest records, the authors find that teachers have a significant impact on their students' future arrests, convictions, and incarceration. The standard deviation of teacher effects on future arrests is 2.7 percentage points, and teachers' effects on short-run outcomes such as test scores, homework, and reading time are also significant. However, the authors find that teachers who boost test scores do not decrease their students' future criminal justice contact, but rather, teachers who improve their students' behavioral outcomes, such as reducing suspensions and improving attendance, have a significant impact on reducing future arrests. The results suggest that the development of non-cognitive skills is central to the returns to education for crime and highlight an important dimension of teachers' social value missed by test score-based quality metrics.

Document title: How the Great Migration Changed Black Children’s Educational Attainment
Document description: The Great Migration, a landmark event in American history, saw over seven million African Americans leave the South between 1915 and 1970 in search of better economic and social opportunities. Research has found mixed impacts on adults, but less is known about how the Great Migration affected the outcomes of migrants' children. This policy brief provides new evidence on how moving north affected the educational attainment of Black children. The authors analyze 1940 census records and find that moving to the North substantially improved educational outcomes, with an average increase of 0.8 years of schooling. The benefits of migrating varied widely across places, with some Southern destinations offering poor prospects for children. The Great Migration played an important role in narrowing U.S. educational disparities by race, with the education gap between White and Black individuals shrinking from 4.0 to 0.9 years between the 1900 and 1970 birth cohorts. The authors also examine the mechanisms behind the benefits of moving north and find that higher school quality, better labor market opportunities, and greater social capital were key factors.

Document description: The document discusses student absenteeism in high school, specifically a policy in Norway that started in the 2016/17 academic year. Document title: Public Pension Reforms and Retirement Decisions: Narrative Evidence and Aggregate Implications
Document description: This document examines the impact of public pension reforms on retirement decisions and labor market participation. The authors construct a database of public pension policy changes for ten OECD countries between 1962 and 2017, focusing on the motivation behind policy changes and implementation lags. They find that structural pension reforms can have a different impact on labor decisions depending on whether they come with phase-in periods or not. Document title: Four Facts about Human Capital
Document description: This document discusses human capital, which is the idea that education, training, and other forms of learning are investments that pay off in the future. The author synthesizes what economists have learned about human capital since Becker's seminal work in 1962 into four stylized facts. The first fact is that human capital explains a substantial share of the variation in labor earnings within and across countries. The second fact is that human capital investments have high economic returns throughout childhood and young adulthood. The third fact is that the technology for producing foundational skills such as literacy and numeracy is well-understood, and resources are the main constraint. The fourth fact is that higher-order skills such as problem-solving and teamwork are increasingly economically valuable, and the technology for producing them is not well understood. The author also discusses the Mincer equation, which models log annual earnings as an additive function that is linear in years of schooling and quadratic in years of experience. The author estimates the economic return to education using various methods, including instrumental variables and regression discontinuity, and finds that the return to an additional year of education is around 10-12 percent. The author also discusses the importance of human capital in explaining variation in labor earnings and the need for further research on the human capital production function.

Document description: This document explores the effect of oil import price shocks on political outcomes using a worldwide dataset on elections of chief executives. The authors find that oil import price shocks cause a reduction in the odds of reelection of incumbents, an increase in media chatter about fuel prices, and an increase in non-violent protests. The authors also show that the pass-through from international to domestic fuel prices is limited in autocracies, leading to limited effects on output, inflation, and unemployment. In contrast, oil import price increases lead to exchange rate depreciation and have no significant effect on the levels of foreign reserves and external debt in democracies. The findings point to the interdependence of goods markets and politics.

Document title: The Crime Effect of Refugees

Document title: The Long-Run Effects of Psychotherapy on Depression, Beliefs, and Economic Outcomes
Document description: This document studies the long-run effects of psychotherapy on depression, beliefs, and economic outcomes. The authors revisit two clinical trials in India that randomized depressed adults to a brief course of psychotherapy or a control condition. Four to five years later, the treatment group was 11 percentage points less likely to be depressed than the control group. The therapy changed people's beliefs about themselves in three ways: reducing their likelihood of seeing themselves as a failure or feeling bad about themselves, reducing over-optimistic belief updating in response to feedback, and increasing self-assessed levels of patience and altruism. The authors also found that therapy did not increase levels of employment or consumption, possibly due to other constraints on employment in the largely female study sample. The study provides a behavioral-science view of the effects of psychotherapy and aims to fill three gaps in the literature: the long-run effects of psychotherapy on depression, the effects of psychotherapy on economic beliefs and preferences, and whether psychotherapy increases economic wellbeing in the long run.

Document title: Redistribution with Performance Pay
Document description: The document discusses the impact of performance-based pay on income inequality and the optimal tax policy for performance-based earnings. Performance-based pay is a common feature in many jobs, particularly among high earners, and contributes to growing income inequality. The authors set up a model of moral hazard in the labor market to study the incidence of tax policy on performance-based contracts. They find that taxes have little effect on the contract, but the endogeneity of private insurance can have large effects on welfare. The authors derive formulas for the optimal rate of tax progressivity and the optimal tax rate on top income earners, taking into account the fiscal and welfare effects of crowd-out and crowd-in. They also show that it is optimal to tax bonuses strictly less than base pay. The authors conclude that the optimal tax policy with performance-pay contracts is close to that prescribed by standard models that treat pre-tax earnings risk as exogenous.

Document title: The Demand For Protection and the Persistently High Rates of Gun Violence Among Young Black Males
Document description: The document discusses the high rates of gun violence among young black males in the United States, with a murder rate 17 times higher than the general population. The authors argue that the violence is driven by guns and that the primary interest is to build a theoretical model to explain the high level and persistence of gun violence among young black males. The model is based on strategic complementarities and emphasizes multidimensional preference heterogeneity, capturing distinct offensive and defensive rationales for being armed. The authors examine the comparative statics of the model and find that a temporary shock in the population's modal preference can lead to a persistent shift in equilibrium. The model also shows that inter-group interactions serve as a pathway for shock spillovers and that information interventions are unlikely to succeed in countering the dynamic of overestimation of gun carry rates among young black males.

Document title: Neighborhood Choice After COVID: The Role of Rents, Amenities, and Work-From-Home
Document description: The document investigates how neighborhood preferences and choices changed one year after the beginning of the COVID pandemic. The authors study a Neighborhood Choice Program that helped graduating students choose where to live by providing new information about rents and amenities. They find that changes in rankings favor neighborhoods where social and professional network shares are higher, rents are lower, and are farther from the city center. The authors also estimate a neighborhood choice model to recover MWTP for amenities both before and after the pandemic, revealing that MWTP for network shares post-COVID is markedly lower than prior to COVID. The study uses panel data on neighborhood rankings before and after information and focuses on university graduates, who constitute a large fraction of new household moves. The findings suggest that preferences for lower rent and larger units point towards the suburbs, while the importance of network amenities points towards the city center. The authors also estimate a discrete choice model that recovers preferences for rents and neighborhood amenities, allowing for heterogeneity in preferences since individuals have different commuting tolerances and different work-from-home arrangements.

Document description: This document studies the impact of the Social Explosion and the Covid-19 pandemic on household debt in Chile. The Social Explosion in October 2019 was a massive protest that had a large impact on the economy, with a 2.4% decrease in GDP in the fourth quarter of 2019. The pandemic in 2020 had a significant impact on the economy, with a 14% and 10.3% decrease in GDP in the second and third quarters of 2020, respectively. The document uses the Chilean Household Finance Survey to estimate the impact of these crises on household debt. The results show that the Social Explosion increased household debt risk from 2.7% to 4.5%, while the Covid-19 crisis and associated policies decreased household debt risk slightly. The support policies were particularly effective after August, with the delinquency risk dropping to 2.8% until the end of the year, a value similar to the ones before the crises. The document is relevant to policymakers and academics interested in understanding the impact of social and economic crises on household debt. It provides a detailed analysis of the impact of the Social Explosion and the Covid-19 pandemic on household debt in Chile, and highlights the importance of considering the heterogeneity of household debt and the impact of policy measures on debt risk.

Document title: A p Theory of Government Debt and Taxes
Document description: The document presents a model for government debt and taxes, which takes into account tax distortions, government borrowing, and default options. The model shows that the optimal debt-GDP ratio is determined by four forces: primary deficit, interest payments, GDP growth, and hedging costs. The government's marginal cost of servicing debt is a key factor in determining the optimal debt-GDP ratio. The model also assumes that the government is impatient, meaning it has a higher discount rate than the interest rate. This leads to a backloaded tax schedule, where the optimal tax rate on output increases over time. The debt-GDP ratio moves towards a steady state, where it attains its maximally sustainable level. The model generates three disjoint regions for optimal debt-GDP dynamics: a lumpy debt issuance and payout region, a default region, and an interior region. The government's marginal cost of servicing debt is a measure of how much its value decreases in the absolute value when the government debt-GDP ratio increases by one unit. The model uses a first-order nonlinear ordinary differential equation to describe the government's value, a first-order condition for the optimal smooth tax rate, and a zero-drift condition to characterize the steady state where debt is at the maximally sustainable level.

Document title: The Long Run Impacts of Court-Ordered Desegregation
Document description: This document examines the long-run impacts of court-ordered desegregation in the United States. The authors use large Census samples linked to Social Security records to estimate the effects of exposure to desegregation orders on human capital and labor market outcomes. They find that African Americans who were relatively young when a desegregation order was implemented in their county of birth experienced large improvements in adult human capital and labor market outcomes. These effects are concentrated in the South, with no comparable changes in outcomes among whites in counties undergoing an order or among Blacks who were beyond school ages when a local order was implemented. The authors conclude that court-ordered desegregation was highly effective at improving the long-run socioeconomic outcomes of many Black students.

Document title: Is There a Foster Care-To-Prison Pipeline? Evidence from Quasi-Randomly Assigned Investigators
Document description: This study examines the relationship between foster care placement and adult crime in the United States. The authors use quasi-random assignment of child welfare investigators and administrative data from Michigan to show that foster care placement substantially reduces the chances of adult arrests, convictions, and incarceration for children at the margin. The study also finds that foster care improves a range of children's safety, academic, and behavioral intermediate outcomes, such as reducing the likelihood of being held in a juvenile detention center and improving math test scores. The authors suggest that the gains in children's outcomes due to placement could contribute to the estimated reduction in adult crime through several channels, including improvements in academic outcomes and educational attainment, a decline in juvenile justice contact, and improved mental health. The study provides new evidence on the causal relationship between foster care and adult crime, contrasting with previous research that found detrimental effects of foster care placement.

Document description: The document discusses the relationship between the real estate sector and the stock market in Chinese provinces. It presents an analysis of the causality and correlation between the stock market and real estate sector's trading volumes in 31 provinces of China. Document description: This paper examines how the arrival of an invention affects wage returns and the probability of moving out of employment for white- and blue-collar coworkers of the inventor. The study also finds that human capital indeed affects invention returns within a firm, with the level of education and time since education being significant factors. The probability of coworker non-employment decreases due to within-firm invention, but increases steadily with the time since education.

Document title: Sometimes It Works! The Effect of a Reform of the Short Vocational Track on School-to-Work Transition
Document description: The document discusses the impact of a reform on the length of school-to-work transition in Italy. The reform extended the short vocational track from two to three years, introducing mandatory general subjects and regulating educational institutions. The analysis shows that the reform had a positive impact, reducing school-to-work transition by around 5 months. The new short vocational track proved to be more effective for migrants and females, with a reduction in school-to-work transition of 1.4 years and 0.9 years, respectively. The adoption of a quasi-market organizational model was more effective than the traditional model in shortening school-to-work transition, particularly for immigrants. The study contributes to the literature on the labor-market effect of vocational education, highlighting the importance of lengthening the short vocational track and changing the overall content of curricula to speed up school-to-work transition. The results suggest that vocational education can be an effective policy tool to increase youth employability and favor school-to-work transitions. The study also highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the labor-market effects of vocational education, taking into account the specific characteristics of the educational system and the population being studied.

Document title: Historical Patterns of Inequality and Productivity around Financial Crises
Document description: The document discusses the relationship between financial crises and macroeconomic trends. It argues that rising income inequality and low productivity growth are robust predictors of financial crises. The author assembles a novel dataset of long-run measures of income inequality, productivity, and other macrofinancial indicators for advanced economies. The results show that changes in the top income shares and productivity growth are strong predictors of financial crises, and that these predictive relations are largely explained by the trend component in each of the variables. The document also finds that trends in top income inequality and productivity affect not only the likelihood of crises but also the recovery period. Recessions that are preceded by unusually strong increases in top income shares or low productivity growth are characterized by stronger declines in output compared with recessions without such ex-ante trends.

Document title: Gender Quotas and Support for Women in Board Elections
Document description: The document studies the impact of a gender quota for corporate boards in California, introduced in 2018. The quota required publicly held firms to have at least one female director and mandated that boards with five or more members have two or three female board members. The stock market reacted negatively to the quota, which has been interpreted as shareholders opposing the mandated addition of new female directors. The authors consider two alternative perspectives to explain the negative stock price reaction, including the possibility that boards are unable to recruit shareholders' preferred female directors or that boards make mistakes in the replacement process. The authors find that shareholder support for new female nominees was high before and after the quota, but stock prices reacted negatively when companies retained the least-supported male directors and replaced them with new female directors. The authors conclude that the quota destroys value for firms, but not because of the women newly appointed to directorships.

Document title: Mental Health Therapy as a Core Strategy for Increasing Human Capital: Evidence from Ghana
Document description: This document presents the results of a study on the impact of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) on mental and physical health, socioemotional and cognitive skills, and downstream economic outcomes in rural Ghana. The study found that CBT had strong impacts on these areas, particularly for individuals who were vulnerable to deteriorating mental health. The authors argue that CBT can improve human capital for a general population of poor individuals through two pathways: reducing vulnerability to deteriorating mental health and directly improving cognitive and socioemotional skills. The study also found that the impacts of CBT were not limited to individuals with diagnosed mental health issues, but rather were relevant for a general population. The authors draw on the concept of 'bandwidth' to explain how CBT can improve decision making and reduce the negative effects of scarcity. The study contributes to the literature on the economic impacts of therapy and argues for a broader relevance of therapy beyond treating specific mental health conditions.

Document title: Black Americans’ Landholdings and Economic Mobility after Emancipation: New Evidence on the Significance of 40 Acres
Document description: This paper examines the economic mobility of Black Americans after emancipation, focusing on the significance of landholdings. The authors build a dataset to observe Black households' landholdings in 1880 and link their sons to the 1900 census records to observe economic and human capital outcomes. They show that Black landowners and skilled workers were able to transmit substantial intergenerational advantages to their sons, but these advantages were small relative to the overall racial gaps in economic status. The authors also investigate the significance of fathers' land ownership and farm size in 1880 for the fortunes of their sons in 1900, finding that the returns in terms of sons' home ownership and literacy were substantial. However, even for Black sons of landowning farmers, average rates of literacy and homeownership in 1900 were far lower than for White sons. The paper provides new insights into the freedmen and their children, with unprecedented detail on variation in economic status within the large population of farmer-headed households.

Document title: Public School Funding, School Quality, and Adult Crime
Document description: This paper examines the relationship between public school funding, school quality, and adult crime. The authors use quasi-experimental variation in school quality due to increases in public school funding in Michigan to estimate the effect of school quality improvements early in children's lives on the likelihood that they are arrested as adults. They find that students exposed to additional funding during elementary school were substantially less likely to be arrested in adulthood. The authors also explore the mechanisms through which additional funding reduces adult crime and find that improvements in school quality, such as reductions in class sizes and teacher turnover, increases in teacher salaries and experience, and the hiring of additional district and school leadership, are associated with reductions in adult crime. They also find that increases in educational attainment and reductions in absenteeism explain a significant portion of the effect. The authors conclude that improving the quality of public schools can be an effective long-run crime-prevention strategy.

Document description: This document studies the impact of civil service reforms on the performance of the U.S. Post Office during the Gilded Age. Document title: New Evidence on Sectoral Labor Productivity: Implications for Industrialization and Development
Document description: The document discusses the importance of industrialization for the development of poor countries. It presents new evidence on the channels through which industrialization can help close the productivity gap with rich countries. The authors construct a new dataset of comparable labor productivity levels in agriculture and manufacturing for 64 mostly poor countries during 1990-2018. They find that cross-country labor productivity gaps in manufacturing are larger than in the aggregate and that there is no tendency for manufacturing labor productivity to converge. The results challenge the notion that expanding manufacturing employment is essential for the development of today's poor countries. However, the authors also find that higher labor productivity growth in manufacturing is associated with higher labor productivity growth in the aggregate and in several key sectors.

Document title: Can Public Policy Increase Paternity Acknowledgment? Evidence from Earnings-Related Parental Leave
Document description: The document discusses the impact of public policies on family structures, specifically paternity acknowledgment among unmarried parents. The authors analyze a reform of the German parental leave system, which increased mothers' income and reduced fathers' financial support burden. They use detailed birth record data to demonstrate that the reform incentivized unmarried fathers to acknowledge paternity, reducing single motherhood by 6% but leaving the share of marriages at birth constant. The change in relationship contract choices was mostly driven by parents of boys. The authors introduce a conceptual framework to analyze the impact of the reform on relationship contract choices, considering parents' utility from private consumption, child quality, and match quality. They find that the reform primarily led to an increase in paternity establishment for boys rather than girls, and that the effects appear to be driven by districts with relatively high male earnings. Document description: The document discusses the Puerto Rican debt crisis and the failure of market discipline. The authors examine the 'Treasury Put' hypothesis, which suggests that the U.S. government implicitly insured Puerto Rican debt, allowing investors to purchase bonds with low risk premiums despite weak macroeconomic fundamentals. The authors use a unique situation where the 'Treasury Put' was extinguished by the non-bailout of Detroit in 2013 to estimate the magnitude of the implicit guarantee. The authors conclude that the 'Treasury Put' was a form of regulatory forbearance that allowed investors to ignore the risks associated with Puerto Rican debt. The document also discusses the challenges faced by Puerto Rico, including a declining population, a high median age, and a lack of fiscal capacity. The authors suggest that institutional reforms are needed to eliminate the 'Treasury Put' and promote market discipline.
