Document title: The Role of Consumer Consent in Open Banking : Financial Inclusion Support Framework
Document description: The document discusses open banking schemes that provide consumers with more choice and new financial products and services through the use of technology, particularly application programming interfaces. Open banking is defined as the sharing and leveraging of customer-permissioned data by banks with third-party developers and firms to build applications and services. The main objective of this paper is to provide guidance on how to implement consumer consent protocols to access bank account data under open banking scenarios. Digital financial services are creating opportunities to accelerate financial inclusion, closing the gap in access that has long existed, especially for low-income and rural consumers. In many instances, new non-bank providers of financial services are entering these markets, leveraging their proximity to previously unbanked customers and the data they have. Open banking was developed to encourage innovation in financial products and services and expand choice for consumers by breaking down barriers to competition arising from unequal access to customer information. The traditional banking system is based on the exclusive use of customer data for payments, investments, and money management generally; only limited types of data, such as repayment of loans, are shared with third parties. Open banking is a model developed in the last decade to allow third parties access to information held by banks with the permission of the customer. The European Union's revised Payment Services Directive and its forerunner, PSD1, are the basis for open banking. In 2016, the Competition and Markets Authority published a report on the United Kingdom's retail banking market that observed that smaller and newer banks found it difficult to grow and access the market, while existing, and particularly larger, banks do not face adequate competition. One of the main legal restrictions on banks' ability to share data with third parties is the existence of bank-secrecy provisions that establish the duty of confidentiality on banks toward their clients. However, these provisions are not absolute and are subject to exemptions—a common exemption relates to the prevention of money laundering and financial terrorism and to the monitoring of credit risk. Another exemption to bank secrecy recognized under the famous Tournier v. Bank of England case is based upon the customer's consent. Open banking also creates an exception to bank-secrecy protections, based upon customer consent, with the objective of benefiting consumers by enabling third-party access to account data held by banks. Since rules under an open-banking scheme are enacted by different authorities, potential conflicts of law may exist. In addition, one of the objectives of enabling open banking is to provide consumers more control over their account information and the possibility to decide with whom they would like to share such data to obtain additional and more convenient and attractive products or services. In such a context, the consumer's consent to allow third parties access to information through application programming interfaces has become a key issue in the formulation of the legal and regulatory framework of open banking.

Document title: Historical Patterns of Inequality and Productivity around Financial Crises
Document description: This paper argues that financial crises are often driven by slow-moving trends in the real economy, specifically rising top income inequality and declining productivity growth, rather than just short-term financial market fluctuations. The author assembles a new dataset covering long-run measures of inequality and productivity for advanced economies to test these hypotheses. The study finds that these two factors are robust predictors of financial crises and that their trend components largely explain the relationship between real economy conditions and instability. Furthermore, the analysis shows that recessions preceded by these negative trends are significantly deeper than those without such pre-existing conditions. The findings suggest that current macrofinancial models need to be updated to account for these lower-frequency fluctuations in inequality and productivity as sources of systemic risk. By excluding capital gains from inequality measures, the author confirms that the predictive power of top income shares is not merely an artifact of asset price movements. The research highlights the importance of considering secular trends alongside traditional cyclical indicators to better understand and predict future financial instability.

Document title: Are Low-Skill Women Being Left Behind? Labor Market Evidence from the UK
Document description: The document discusses the widening wage gap between young and older non-college females in the UK labor market. It examines the contribution of job polarization to this trend and estimates age, period, and cohort effects for the likelihood of employment in different occupations and the wages earned therein. Document title: New Data Show that Economic Growth Was Broadly Shared in 2021
Document description: The document discusses the U.S. economy's strong growth since President Biden entered office, with real gross domestic product growing faster than in any year since 1984. The economy is now 3 percent larger than before the pandemic, with the fastest pandemic growth in the G7. However, the growth has not always been reflected equally across the income spectrum, with those at the top benefiting more than the rest. New data from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, show that the underlying economy is delivering gains to those in the bottom half of the income ladder, even before considering pandemic support. Market incomes grew by 5.6 percent on average in 2021, with growth particularly strong in the bottom half of the income distribution. The data also show that government support during the pandemic protected households, helping them manage the challenges of the pandemic and positioning them today with higher levels of inflation-adjusted disposable income than before the pandemic. The data point to the benefits of the government's response, including the addition of 6.7 million jobs and a reduction in child poverty by almost 40 percent in 2021. However, the gains were not evenly shared, with those between the 50th and 90th percentile seeing their market income grow more slowly than those in the bottom half or the top 10 percent.

Document title: Machine-Learning the Skill of Mutual Fund Managers
Document description: The asset management industry is enormous and growing rapidly, with U.S. mutual funds having $24 trillion in assets under management at the end of 2020. The authors revisit the evidence on the investment performance of actively-traded equity mutual funds using modern techniques and find that fund flows and fund return momentum are the only two characteristics that can meaningfully and robustly help distinguish funds that outperform from those that under-perform. The relative performance of top and bottom performers is particularly large in times of high investor sentiment. The authors use an artificial neural network model to estimate a complex functional relationship among a large set of variables and find that the model predictions generate a large difference in performance out-of-sample. Buying the ten percent of mutual funds with the best predicted performance each month generates a cumulative abnormal return of 72% over the sample period, while buying the ten percent of mutual funds with the worst predicted performance each month produces a cumulative abnormal return of -119%. The results suggest that some investors can detect skill and reallocate their investment towards such skilled managers, and that the flows are gradual and small enough that it takes several periods until the fund runs into zero marginal abnormal returns.

Document title: Labor Market Integration, Local Conditions and Inequalities : Evidence from Refugees in Switzerland
Document description: The document examines the patterns of economic integration of refugees in Switzerland, a country with a long tradition of hosting refugees. It relies on a unique longitudinal dataset consisting of administrative records and social security data for the universe of refugees in Switzerland over 1998-2018. The study documents the patterns of labor-market integration, highlights the heterogeneity by gender and age at arrival, and compares refugees' labor-market performance to natives' and other groups of migrants' labor-market performance. The empirical analysis exploits the government dispersal policy in place since 1998, which consists of the random allocation of refugees across cantons, to identify the causal effects of the local initial conditions. The study finds that higher unemployment rates at arrival slow down the integration process, whereas the existence of a co-ethnic network does not consistently lead to a faster integration. It is shown that in locations where refugees face relatively more hostile attitudes by natives upon arrival, they integrate at a faster pace, probably due to a greater effort undertaken in environments that are more hostile. The results highlight the importance of an early entry in the labor market of the host country and the need to take a longer run perspective when examining the effectiveness of policies. The study also examines the effect of forced displacement on different dimensions of inequalities of refugees' labor-market outcomes and the role of policies and local contexts in affecting the pattern of integration in the receiving society.

Document description: This paper examines the effects of initial labor market conditions on labor market outcomes in Latin America. The authors use harmonized microdata from national household surveys for 15 Latin American countries to build a synthetic panel of cohorts that potentially transition from school to work and observe their labor market outcomes 10 years later. Document title: Heat, Crime, and Punishment
Document description: This document examines the relationship between heat and crime, using administrative criminal records from Texas. The authors find that arrests increase by up to 15 percent on hot days, driven by increases in violent crime. They also find that heat impacts the judicial process, with judges dismissing fewer cases, issuing longer prison sentences, and levying higher fines on hot days. The authors suggest that climate change will increase crime and have substantial distributional consequences, even with adaptation. They also find that the impact of heat on crime varies across different levels of neighborhood adaptation markers, such as income, poverty, and housing stock age. The study uses a unique dataset of over 10 million arrests across the state of Texas from 2010 to 2017, with comprehensive data on the subsequent prosecution and trials of these arrests. The authors examine how heat affects arrests relative to reported crimes and find that temperatures above 65 degrees Fahrenheit lead to increases in crime, driven almost entirely by violent crime. They also find that heat has larger effects on gun-specific charges after January 1, 2016, when Texas made it easier to carry guns in public places.

Document title: Earmarked Paternity Leave and Well-Being
Document description: The document discusses the impact of earmarked paternity leave on parental well-being in Europe. Earmarked paternity leave is a policy where part of the parental leave is exclusively reserved for fathers and cannot be transferred to the mother. The authors analyze the effect of this policy on life satisfaction, job satisfaction, and work-life balance using data from the European Social Survey and data on earmarked paternity leave policies in Europe. They find that earmarked paternity leave increases life satisfaction by 0.18 points, which is equivalent to a 10.8 percentage point increase. The impact on job satisfaction and work-life balance is much smaller and insignificant. The authors also find that the increase in life satisfaction is much stronger for mothers than for fathers. The study contributes to the existing literature on the impact of parental leave policies on outcomes in the work and family domain.

Document title: Virtual banking and beyond
Document description: The document discusses the integration of technology, finance, and services in Asia's banking landscape. The ownership stakes in banks are being taken by big techs and fintech firms, non-bank financial institutions, and incumbent banks. This integration presents opportunities for financial inclusion, but also poses regulatory and competition challenges. The use of the banking system to borrow lags behind the increase in bank accounts worldwide, partly due to the requirement for collateral in conventional bank business loan models. New technology-driven business models exploit data footprints to generate information capital and reduce collateral reliance. Data governance is crucial in this transformation, and a consent-based, granular, open, interoperable, revocable, auditable, and secure data governance system is necessary to respect consumer privacy and market integrity. Virtual banks in Hong Kong and Asia offer a suite of products, leveraging technology to cut transaction costs and service a more diverse range of borrowers. Technology companies are playing an important role in managing modular platforms, data analytics, and risk mitigation.

Document title: Spillovers at the Extremes: The Macroprudential Stance and Vulnerability to the Global Financial Cycle
Document description: This document examines the impact of macroprudential policies on portfolio flows and their sensitivity to the global financial cycle. It finds that tighter macroprudential regulations amplify the impact of risk shocks on bond and equity portfolio investment, increasing outflows during risk-off episodes and increasing inflows during risk-on episodes. The amplification effects are more prominent at the extremes, especially for extreme risk-off periods and for regulations that target specific risks instead of generalized cyclical buffers. The results suggest that macroprudential regulations can shift financial intermediation outside the regulated banking sector to portfolio investors more vulnerable to the global financial cycle. The findings do not imply that macroprudential regulations should be diluted or rolled back, as they may still provide significant benefits by improving the resilience of the domestic banking system. Instead, it is vital to consider the precise macroprudential tools, spillovers, leakages, and corresponding vulnerabilities when designing an optimal policy package.

Document title: How Reliable are Administrative Reports of Paid Work Hours?
Document description: This paper examines the quality of administrative records on paid work hours reported by employers in the State of Washington. The authors subject the administrative records to four trials, all of which suggest the records reliably measure paid hours of work. They compare the distribution of work hours in the Washington administrative data with the hours distribution in the Current Population Survey outgoing rotation groups and find that the Washington data and the CPS are consistent in suggesting that about half of employees work close to 40 hours per week. The authors also assess the ratio of signal to noise in the Washington hours records and find a high ratio of signal-to-noise in the Washington hours data. They construct a measure of hourly wages by dividing quarterly earnings by quarterly hours and show that the distribution of this hourly wage rate exhibits a spike at the Washington minimum wage, and that the spike moves with year-to-year increases in Washington's minimum wage. The findings have implications for any analysis of paid work hours and for economic variables constructed using hours in the denominator, like hourly wage rates and output per hour.

Document title: Labor market integration, local conditions and inequalities: evidence from refugees in Switzerland
Document description: The document examines the economic integration of refugees in Switzerland, a country with a long tradition of hosting refugees. It relies on a unique longitudinal dataset consisting of administrative records and social security data for the universe of refugees in Switzerland over 1998-2018. The study documents the patterns of labor-market integration and highlights the heterogeneity by gender and age at arrival. Refugees' labor-market performance is compared to natives' and other groups of migrants' labor-market performance. The empirical analysis exploits the government dispersal policy in place since 1998, which consists of the random allocation of refugees across cantons, to identify the causal effects of the local initial conditions. The study finds that higher unemployment rates at arrival slow down the integration process, whereas the existence of a co-ethnic network does not consistently lead to a faster integration. It is shown that in locations where refugees face relatively more hostile attitudes by natives upon arrival, they integrate at a faster pace, probably due to a greater effort undertaken in environments that are more hostile. The study aims to provide insights on the effectiveness of policies and the importance of an early entry in the labor market of the host country.

Document description: This working paper argues that the United States terminated the World Trade Organization dispute settlement system in 2019 due to dissatisfaction with rulings that disproportionately restricted the use of trade remedies. The author notes that restoring binding dispute settlement mechanisms faces significant hurdles, including the need to balance policy flexibility for remedy users with market access for exporters. Data from 1995 to 2019 indicates that over forty-five WTO members utilized a wide array of trade remedies, with coverage levels reaching historical highs by the end of that period. While China remains the primary target of these measures, the share of exports from other nations like the European Union and India subject to such restrictions has also risen significantly. The paper highlights that reforms must address the fact that trade remedies often substitute for one another, as countries employ antidumping, countervailing duties, and safeguards in combination. Furthermore, the document suggests that China's unique economic model requires new rules rather than simply restoring old ones, yet no consensus on these rules has been reached. Ultimately, the author concludes that even promising reforms may face practical limitations or political viability issues, making the repair of the trade remedy system a complex challenge.

Document title: Labor Scarcity, Technology Adoption and Innovation: Evidence from the Cholera Pandemics in 19th Century France
Document description: This study examines the impact of labor scarcity on technology adoption and innovation in 19th century France using data from the cholera pandemics in 1832, 1849, and 1854. The results suggest that labor scarcity had a positive and significant effect on technology adoption and innovation in agriculture but a negative and significant impact on technology adoption in industry. The study also finds that the effects of labor scarcity on technology adoption and innovation were quantitatively limited. The positive impact of labor scarcity on human capital accumulation is proposed as an explanation for the main results. The study is related to research on pandemics, income shocks, and economic growth, as well as research on technology adoption during the industrial revolution.

Document title: Agrarian Origins of Individualism and Collectivism
Document description: This study examines the influence of agricultural labor intensity on individualism across U.S. counties. The authors use historical data on crop-specific labor requirements and county-specific crop mix to measure labor intensity. They find that a one standard deviation increase in labor intensity is associated with a reduction of 0.2-0.3 standard deviations in individualism. The authors also document significant changes in individualism over time using within-county changes in labor intensity due to mechanization and the boll weevil. They show that historical agricultural labor intensity continues to influence geographic variation in individualism today. The study provides novel evidence on the roots of individualism in agriculture and contributes to a growing literature on the link between culture and the structure of production.

Document title: Measuring top income shares in the UK
Document description: This paper examines measurement error in the share of income going to the top 1% (and other subgroups) that comes from estimation of the denominator. The authors compare two approaches: the default 'external' approach used in the current literature, which relies on different data sources for the numerator and denominator, and an alternative 'augmented internal' approach that uses the same data source for the denominator as for the numerator, but augments this to fill gaps in coverage. The authors argue that the 'augmented internal' approach is to be preferred, as it satisfies four principled criteria for selecting between these approaches. The authors find that the UK top 1% share is 2 percentage points higher when using the augmented internal approach relative to the external approach. The authors also discuss the implications of their findings for top share measurement and the principles that ought to guide the estimation of any top share series.

Document title: Young Adults and Labor Markets in Africa
Document description: This discussion paper examines the labor market in Africa, focusing on young adults and their job prospects. The authors use the Jobs of the World Database to compare the employment rates of young adults in Africa to those in other low-income regions. They find that young adults in Africa are equally likely to work, but less likely to have a salaried job, especially when the size of their cohort is large. The authors discuss policy priorities for boosting the growth of salaried job creation in the region, including interventions targeting both the demand and supply sides of the labor market. The paper also explores the transformation in the organization of labor as countries develop, and finds that African countries are on average on the same development track as other regions, but with a different age-occupation profile. The authors suggest that the lack of salaried jobs in Africa may be due to the large share of young workers in the population, and propose policies to address this issue.

Document title: WP 22/01 Clemens Fuest, Klaus Gründler, Niklas Potrafke, and Fabian Ruthardt, Tax Policies after Crises
Document description: This document examines how policymakers adjust tax policies in response to national crises. The authors use novel and granular data on tax reforms for 22 developed and emerging economies over the period 1962-2014. They find that governments tend to increase taxes after crises, particularly after financial crises and natural disasters. The tax policy reaction is stronger for tax rates than for tax bases, and the extent of tax increases is not increasing in the pre-crisis level of public debt. The authors also find substantial heterogeneity in post-crisis taxation across tax types, with financial crises often followed by increases in corporate income taxes and value-added taxes, and natural disasters leading to increases in personal income taxes. The study contributes to the literature on fiscal policy and taxation after crises, providing a first empirical evidence on tax policy in the recovery phases of crises.

Document title: Revealing Corruption: Firm and Worker Level Evidence from Brazil
Document description: This document studies the impact of an anti-corruption program in Brazil on firms involved in illegal interactions with the government. The program randomly audits municipal budgets to uncover misuse of federal funds, exposing firms involved in corrupt practices. The authors find that exposed firms experience a 4.8 percent larger increase in size, despite a decrease in procurement contracts. They also find that firms that were victims of corruption or actively involved in corruption cases but provided good quality goods or services to local governments experience an increase in firm size, while poorly performing corrupt firms shrink in size. The authors argue that the revelation of corruption forces exposed firms to change their investment and business practices to compete for private demand. They also find that workers employed by exposed firms experience no significant changes in their probability of being employed or annual labor income. Document description: This discussion paper examines the labor market trends in Africa, focusing on young adults and their job prospects. Document description: This paper studies the impact of the monoline insurance industry's demise on local governments' operations. The author uses a unique data set of local governments' bond issuance, expenditure, and employment to examine the effects of the demise on local governments' ability to issue debt, spend, and hire workers. The author finds that local governments associated with less healthy insurers were able to issue less insured debt and were unable to make up for this shortfall by issuing uninsured bonds. This result shows that insurers' health had a direct effect on local governments' ability to fund themselves. The author also finds that the long-term effects are concentrated among special district governments, which highlights the role of opacity in preventing some local governments from issuing new debt. The disappearance of bond insurance essentially locked some government entities out of the municipal bond market. The author uses an instrumental variable to relax the identifying assumption and finds that the effects are persistent and long-lasting. The paper concludes that bond insurance alleviates information asymmetry problems and that local governments rely on bond insurance to access the municipal bond market.

Document title: Financial frictions : micro vs macro volatility.
Document description: This paper studies the impact of frictional financial intermediation in an incomplete markets model with aggregate and idiosyncratic risk. The authors formulate a heterogeneous agents New Keynesian model where the financial sector provides not only funds for corporate sector investments, but also consumer loans. They show that frictions in intermediation have first-order consequences for welfare that derive from limiting households' ability to insure themselves against idiosyncratic risk. The authors find that the model can replicate empirical regularities such as countercyclical interest rate spreads and procyclical consumer credit. They also show that macro prudential policies may have unwarranted consequences due to reducing household insurance options through borrowing and saving in the face of idiosyncratic income risk. The authors find that bank capital requirements have significant welfare costs across the entire wealth distribution, and that cyclical capital requirements can be used for stabilization policy with small but positive welfare gains for all but the wealthiest households.

Document title: Public Pension Reforms and Retirement Decisions: Narrative Evidence and Aggregate Implications
Document description: This paper examines the impact of public pension reforms on labor market decisions and pension spending. The authors construct a database of public pension policy changes with motivation and implementation information for ten OECD countries. They find that structural pension reforms, depending on whether they come with phase-in periods or not, can have a substantially different impact on the labor decisions of people who are close to retirement. If structural pension retrenchments are implemented immediately, labor force participation rates for groups between the ages of 55 and 64 years rise. However, in response to an announcement about structural pension retrenchment that will be phased in over time, this marginal group of population are more likely to exit the labor market. The authors also find that the decline in the labor force participation rates of people close to retirement in response to a lagged pension retrenchment is particularly strong for reforms that come with exceedingly long lags, in the order of 15 years or longer, and ones that change the fundamental aspects of pension systems.

Document description: The document discusses the obstacles to automation in the telephone industry, specifically in the case of AT&T. Document title: Markups and financial shocks
Document description: This paper investigates the impact of financial frictions on markup adjustments at the firm level. The authors use a rich panel data set that matches information on banking relationships with firm-level data. They find that markup responses to bank-credit supply shocks are heterogeneous across firms, with firms more exposed to liquidity risks raising markups in response to negative bank-loan supply shocks, while less exposed firms generally reduce them. The effects occur only contemporaneously, are driven by more negative financial shocks, and take place mainly during the financial crisis period. The authors also investigate the role of customer market features in driving their results, finding that the effects are generally reinforced in industries where customer market features are more prominent. Additionally, they explore information related to additional firm characteristics, including whether firms change their markups to deplete their inventories, but find this to be less robust in their data.

Document description: The document discusses the adoption of telework during the COVID-19 pandemic and its potential persistence beyond the pandemic. It uses online job postings data from Indeed to analyse the extent and drivers of telework adoption across 20 OECD countries. The results show that the incidence of advertised telework has almost tripled since the beginning of the pandemic, with large differences across sectors and countries. Government restrictions have acted as a catalyst for advertised telework, and digital preparedness plays a crucial role in mediating the response of telework to changes in government restrictions. The increase in advertised telework is most pronounced in skill and digital-intensive sectors, and it is likely to persist even after restrictions are fully lifted. The document suggests that telework is here to stay and may grow even further in highly digitally-prepared countries and sectors. It also highlights the need for governments to adapt to the changing landscape of work and to promote public and private investment in digital and physical infrastructure.

Document title: CP146 – Mortgage Measures Framework Review
Document description: The Central Bank of Ireland introduced mortgage measures in 2015 to increase the resilience of lenders and borrowers to negative economic and financial shocks, and to reduce the risk of a damaging credit-house price feedback loop. The measures have contributed to an improvement in the credit quality of new mortgage loans by guarding against a return to lending at high loan-to-value and loan-to-income ratios. The bank is conducting a review of the mortgage measures framework to ensure its continued appropriateness, given broader changes in the housing and mortgage markets and the wider economy. The review aims to consider the objectives of the mortgage measures, the role of dual or multiple instruments, the choice of income-based instruments, and the use of differential limits by borrower type. The bank will consider the feedback it receives on the questions asked in this consultation paper, which will inform the final conclusions on the design of the framework. The mortgage measures have been successful in improving borrower and bank resilience, but there is a need to consider the broader implications of the measures on the housing market and the economy. The bank's view is that the current lack of an adequate supply of housing at a price appropriate to individuals' incomes is caused predominantly by an imbalance that would be most appropriately addressed through a focus on the level and composition of the supply of housing. The bank will consider the implications for the calibration and implementation of the mortgage measures, taking into account the feedback received and further research and analysis.

Document description: The document discusses the role of firms in wage inequality, presenting comprehensive new evidence on the links between firm performance, wage-setting practices, and wage inequality. Document title: Financial frictions: micro vs macro volatility
Document description: This paper studies the impact of frictional financial intermediation in an incomplete markets model with aggregate and idiosyncratic risk. The authors formulate a heterogeneous agents New Keynesian model where the financial sector provides not only funds for corporate sector investments but also consumer loans. They show that frictions in intermediation have first-order consequences for welfare that derive from limiting households' ability to insure themselves against idiosyncratic risk. The paper finds that the cost of consumer loans typically rises in recessions causing an increase in consumption inequality. The model can replicate this evidence because countercyclical movements in the cost of consumer loans directly affect households' ability to smooth their consumption streams. The authors also consider the extent to which cyclical capital requirements can be used for stabilization policy and find small, but positive, welfare gains for all but the wealthiest households. The paper has important implications for the welfare effects of macro prudential policies and the distributional impact of aggregate shocks.

Document description: The document investigates the performance of cryptocurrency funds and their value as investments. Document title: Individual and Local Effects of Unemployment on Mortgage Defaults
Document description: This document presents a study on the effects of unemployment on mortgage defaults. The authors use data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics to analyze the relationship between unemployment and mortgage defaults. They find that individual unemployment has a relatively large effect on mortgage default rates, with the unemployed experiencing default rates that are 4 percentage points larger than those of the employed. However, when endogeneity is accounted for, the unemployment effect on default rates declines to 3 percentage points. The study also finds that local metrics of unemployment, such as state or county unemployment rates, have a stronger effect on mortgage defaults than individual unemployment. The authors suggest that local metrics of unemployment contain more information than the aggregation of individual effects. The study contributes to the existing literature on mortgage defaults by showing that the effect of local unemployment rates is stronger than the comparable individual effect. The authors also find that various other types of liquidity sources, such as having savings accounts, decrease default rates substantially. The study has implications for policymakers and lenders, as it highlights the importance of considering local economic conditions when assessing mortgage risk.

Document description: The document discusses the relationship between business groups and workers' wages. Document title: Does Paternity Leave Promote Gender Equality within Households?
Document description: This document explores whether paternity leave promotes gender equality within households. The authors consider a non-cooperative model of the household, where the husband and wife decide on parental leave and the allocation of time between child rearing and the labor market. They identify three distinct groups of couples: egalitarian couples with a low gender wage gap, intermediate-gap couples with an intermediate gender wage gap, and high-gap couples with a high gender wage gap. The model predicts that while egalitarian couples never specialize and always share home production, those with intermediate and high gaps do have such an agreement. An expansion in paternity leave reduces the net benefits from the agreement and moves the intermediate-gap couples to their outside option, where women work more and men do more home production. This leads to a reduction in fertility and an increase in the probability of divorce. The authors use Spanish data and a regression discontinuity design to confirm their model's predictions, finding that the introduction of paternity leave in 2007 led to a reduction in fertility by up to 60%, an increase in the probability of divorce by 37%, and an increase in fathers' childcare and housework time by up to 2-3 hours per day.

Document title: The COVID-19 Curtain: Can Past Communist Regimes Explain the Vaccination Divide in Europe?
Document description: The document discusses the relationship between past Communist regimes and vaccination rates in Europe. It presents data from the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) that shows lower COVID-19 vaccine take-up amongst individuals born under a Communist regime in Europe. The authors exploit the quasi-natural experiment provided by the separation and later reunification of Eastern and Western Germany after WWII to establish a causal impact of former institutions on COVID-19 vaccine uptake. They find that exposure to the Communist regime in East Germany decreases one's probability to get vaccinated against COVID-19 and increases the probability of not wanting the vaccine. The authors also identify low social capital as a plausible channel through which past Communist regimes would still affect individuals' preferences for COVID-19 vaccination. Document title: In Vaccines We Trust? The Effects of the CIA's Vaccine Ruse on Immunization in Pakistan
Document description: The document discusses the effects of the CIA's fake vaccine campaign in Pakistan on immunization rates. The disclosure of the information caused uproar in Pakistan and led to the Pakistani Taliban discrediting formal medicine and vaccines. The authors estimate that the disclosure of the vaccine ruse had a substantial effect on vaccination rates, with a one-standard-deviation increase in support for Islamist groups leading to a 9-13 percent larger decline in the likelihood that children received the first dose of several different vaccines. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that the disclosure of the vaccine ruse damaged the reputation of vaccines and formal medicine. The authors also provide evidence that other forms of health-seeking behavior experienced important declines and that the effects were driven by children living in districts where a relatively larger fraction of the population does not trust or consume mainstream media.

Document title: Technology Transfer and Early Industrial Development: Evidence from the Sino-Soviet Alliance
Document description: This paper studies the long-term effects of technology and know-how transfers on structural transformations in China. Document title: Recourse and (strategic) mortgage defaults: Evidence from changes in housing market laws
Document description: This document studies the impact of changes in recourse legislation on mortgage defaults. It presents new evidence on how the provisions of recourse legislation influence default on mortgages. The authors use a large dataset of mortgage loans granted between 2003 and 2016 in Romania to analyze the behavior of borrowers with mortgages issued under a recourse regime after a change in policy limited lender recourse. They find robust evidence that eliminating penalties for default raises the delinquency probability of existing borrowers, particularly those traditionally considered least likely to default. The authors also find that the relationship between borrower and loan characteristics, on the one hand, and mortgage default, on the other hand, is non-monotonic. They observe the strongest effects on non-repayment for less-financially constrained borrowers requesting Datio in Solutum and those with negative equity. These findings are consistent with the idea of strategic default. The authors conclude that the switch from recourse to non-recourse legislation leads to a ten-fold increase in the probability of default for underwater borrowers.

Document description: This document explores the relationship between macroprudential policy and the global financial cycle. Document title: The ECB’s price stability framework : past experience, and current and future challenges.
Document description: The European Central Bank's price stability mandate has been defined by the Treaty, but the Treaty has not spelled out what price stability precisely means. To make the mandate operational, the Governing Council has provided a quantitative definition in 1998 and a clarification in 2003. The landscape has changed notably compared to the time the strategy review was originally designed. At the time, the main concern of the Governing Council was to anchor inflation at low levels in face of the inflationary history of the previous decades. Over the last decade economic conditions have changed dramatically: the persistent low-inflation environment has created the concrete risk of de-anchoring of longer-term inflation expectations. Addressing low inflation is different from addressing high inflation. The ability of the ECB to provide the necessary accommodation to maintain price stability has been tested by the lower bound on nominal interest rates in the context of the secular decline in the equilibrium real interest rate. This report analyses the ECB's performance as measured against its formulation of price stability, whether it is possible to identify a preferred level of steady-state inflation on the basis of optimality considerations, and how to strengthen the ECB's leverage on private-sector expectations for inflation and the ECB's future policy actions so that expectations can act as 'automatic stabilisers' and work alongside the central bank.

Document description: This document presents the results of a laboratory experiment to study decentralized markets where goods are differentiated and information is private. Document title: Community Colleges and Upward Mobility
Document description: The document discusses the impact of community colleges on upward mobility in the United States. It highlights that two-year community colleges enroll nearly half of all first-time undergraduates, but their effects on upward mobility are ambiguous due to low persistence rates and the potential for diverting students from four-year institutions. The paper develops a new instrumental variables approach to identify causal effects along multiple treatment margins and applies it to linked education and earnings registries to disentangle the net impacts of two-year college access. The results show that greater access to two-year colleges boosts educational attainment and earnings on net, but also reveals opposing impacts along two distinct treatment margins: roughly one third of induced two-year entrants are diverted from four-year entry and ultimately complete less education as a result, while the other two thirds of induced two-year entrants would not have otherwise attended college and reap significant gains in educational attainment and earnings. The study also finds that women drive these results with effects of larger magnitude along both margins compared to men, and that two-year access particularly boosts the upward earnings mobility of students from low-income families thanks to their lower likelihood of diversion from four-year entry.

Document title: The Geography of Unemployment
Document description: This paper examines the geography of unemployment and proposes answers to questions about the determinants of spatial unemployment differentials. The author provides new empirical evidence that high local unemployment emerges because of elevated local job losing rates, which are shaped by local employers rather than local workers. The paper also proposes a theory of the location choice of employers with labor market frictions that accounts for spatial differences in job stability. The author estimates the framework on French administrative data and quantifies the local and aggregate welfare gains from place-based policies in general equilibrium. The results show that inefficient location choices by employers amplify spatial unemployment differentials five-fold, and that both real-world and optimal place-based policies can yield sizable local and aggregate welfare gains.

Document title: Furlough and Household Financial Distress during the Covid-19 Pandemic
Document description: This document studies the effects of furlough schemes on household financial distress during the COVID-19 pandemic. Furlough increases the probability of late housing and bill payments by 30% and 9%, respectively. However, the effects are mostly felt by individuals who rent their home, while mortgagees can mitigate financial distress by reducing expenditure during furlough. Furloughed individuals significantly reduce expenditure and spend their savings to offset furlough-induced income reductions. This creates wealth inequality but lowers the probability a furloughed worker experiences financial distress after returning to work. The study finds that a government contribution of 80% of monthly wages stabilizes household income while minimizing the incidence of financial distress and the burden of the scheme on public finances. The research also highlights the differential effects of furlough on financial distress according to whether an individual rents their home or is a mortgagee, and the lasting changes in consumption patterns and savings behavior.

Document title: Fostering Soft Skills in Active Labor Market Programs: Evidence from a Large-Scale RCT
Document description: The document discusses the effectiveness of an Active Labor Market Program (ALMP) implemented in Israel, which aims to foster soft skills among unemployed income-support claimants. The program involves personalized treatment composed of weekly sessions with occupational trainers and motivational group workshops. The study uses a large-scale randomized control trial (RCT) to evaluate the program's effectiveness, with 6,151 individuals allocated to the treated and control groups. The results show that the program increased participants' employment rates by 8 percentage points, lessened their welfare dependency by 11 percentage points, and lowered the share of treated participants reporting to the employment office by 15 percentage points. The impact of the program was greater among high-school dropouts and those with lower labor-force attachment, a longer history of income-support recipiency, or self-reported health limitations. The program also had spillover effects within the household, leading to an increase in labor income of untreated spouses. The analysis of the mechanisms at work shows that the program had positive and significant effects on participants' soft skills, mainly among those with no recent employment spell. The program effects persist in the long run, even during the Covid-19 crisis, about five to six years after its implementation.

Document title: Money Creation in Decentralized Finance: A Dynamic Model of Stablecoin and Crypto Shadow Banking
Document description: This paper provides a dynamic model of stablecoins in continuous time that rationalizes a rich set of strategies common in practice, such as open market operations, dynamic requirement of users' collateral, transaction fees or subsidies, targeted price band, re-pegging, and the issuances of secondary units that function as equity shares of the stablecoin issuer. The model demonstrates a novel mechanism of instability and lends itself to an evaluation of regulatory proposals. The creation of stablecoins resembles money creation in shadow banking, where the issuer transforms risky assets into stablecoins with one-to-one convertibility to fiat currencies. The issuer can debase the stablecoins to avoid liquidation, but this induces an amplification mechanism that generates a bimodal distribution of states. The paper addresses the key questions on the credibility and sustainability of a fixed exchange rate, and it shows that even over-collateralized stablecoins can break the buck when the issuer's reserves fall below a critical threshold.

Document title: Financial crises: A survey
Document description: This document is a survey of financial crises, discussing their large deleterious effects on economic activity. The authors explore how crises are measured, whether they are predictable, and why they are associated with economic contractions. They review the existing literature on financial crises, including historical narrative techniques and quantitative data. The study finds that crises are predictable with growth in credit and elevated asset prices playing an especially important role, and that recent research points convincingly to the importance of behavioral biases in explaining such predictability. The authors also discuss the negative consequences of a crisis, which are due to both the crisis itself and the imbalances that precede it. They conclude that financial crises are a distinct, important, and disastrous type of event, and that understanding their causes and consequences is crucial for policymakers and economists. The study also highlights the importance of investigating the booms that precede financial crises, as these booms can be a key indicator of the likelihood of a crisis. The authors present evidence from various studies that financial crises have large growth costs and are more common than other types of disasters, such as wars and pandemics. They also discuss the importance of considering other types of crises, such as sovereign default crises and currency crises, which are often coincident with financial crises. The study concludes that the economic consequences of a financial crisis are negative and substantial, and that understanding the causes and consequences of these events is crucial for policymakers and economists.

Document title: The 2000s Housing Cycle With 2020 Hindsight: A Neo-Kindlebergerian View
Document description: The document reevaluates the 2000s housing cycle with 2020 hindsight, arguing that it is not a boom-bust cycle but rather a boom-bust-rebound. The authors use a spatial equilibrium regression to show that long-run city-level fundamentals predict not only price and rent growth but also the amplitude of the boom-bust-rebound. They introduce a model of a fundamentally-rooted house price cycle in which belief over-reaction amplifies the boom and a foreclosure spiral exacerbates the bust and discipline the model using simulated method of moments. The authors highlight the role of low interest rates in catalyzing these types of cycles and argue that the 2000s cycle would have been far milder with interest rates closer to their 1980s level.

Document title: Delivering Debt Relief through the Banking Sector: Lessons from the Irish Mortgage Market
Document description: The document discusses the Irish mortgage market's response to the 2008 global financial crisis. The Central Bank of Ireland set expectations for private banks to implement long-term, sustainable mortgage modifications in 2013. The banks were given discretion on how to achieve this, and the document studies how they allocated modifications, the depth of repayment cuts, and the performance of modified loans. Document title: Rational inattention : a review.
Document description: The document discusses the concept of rational inattention, which is the idea that economic decision makers cannot absorb all available information but can choose which pieces of information to process. This theory is motivated by the observation that people often cannot avoid mistakes due to lack of information, but they can choose what to think about, what to pay attention to and to what level of detail. The theory of rational inattention provides a model of how cognitively limited people simplify and summarize available information. It describes behavior that seems error-prone, yet the form of mistakes in final actions is subject to agents' choice; it is driven by agents' preferences and the stochastic properties of the environment. The theory has implications across fields, including macroeconomics, finance, labor economics, behavioral economics, and political economy. It explains why slow adjustment of expectations and actions to some shocks can co-exist with flexible reactions to other shocks. It also predicts how the responses to shocks depend on the environment, in particular on monetary policy. The theory of rational inattention is an active area of research, and many research questions remain open.

Document description: The document discusses the stability of global trade policy arrangements under two regulatory scenarios, with and without Preferential Trade Agreements (PTAs). Document title: CEO Compensation: Evidence from the Field
Document description: This document discusses the design of executive pay, a critical decision for every firm. It surveys non-executive directors and institutional investors on how they set or influence pay, revealing several interesting results. The survey shows that directors view attracting the right CEO as most critical, while investors prioritize designing a structure that motivates the CEO. However, boards feel restricted by far more than the participation and incentive constraints focused on by standard models. They are willing to sacrifice shareholder value to avoid controversy on CEO pay, and this constraint leads to lower pay levels and more one-size-fits-all structures. The survey also suggests that incentive pay may work through different channels to standard models, providing ex-post recognition rather than just consumption incentives. The CEO's intrinsic motivation and personal reputation are seen as most important, yet are absent from nearly all theories. The document also studies the reasons for apparently suboptimal pay practices, such as the limited use of relative performance evaluation and the short-term nature of many pay incentives.

Document title: A Firm-Side Perspective on Parental Leave
Document description: This document discusses the impact of parental leave on firms from a firm-side perspective. The authors use administrative linked employer-employee data from Germany to examine how firms deal with parental leave absences. They find that mothers who are difficult to replace internally take shorter leave and that their firms hire replacements more often. Introducing more generous parental leave benefits erases the link between mothers' internal replaceability and their leave duration. Firms respond by hiring fewer women of childbearing age into occupations where they are difficult to replace internally. The authors also investigate how the introduction of a more generous paid parental leave scheme affects mothers' return to their pre-birth employer and firms' employment. They find that medium- and high-earning mothers substantially delay their return to their pre-birth employers when parental leave benefits are expanded, with no medium- to longer-term impact on the probability of exiting their firm. Firms' employment is negatively affected, implying that firms do not fully compensate the longer absences of mothers. The effects are driven by firms in which fewer internal substitutes are available for the mother-on-leave. The authors also find that firms are less likely to hire women of childbearing age after the reform into occupations in which only few internal substitutes were available in case of a pregnancy.

Document title: Rational inattention: a review
Document description: The document reviews the literature on rational inattention, a theory that assumes economic decision makers cannot absorb all available information but can choose which pieces of information to process. The theory explains how people deal with abundant information and its implications for various fields, including macroeconomics, finance, labor economics, and political economy. Rational inattention predicts that economic behavior will be dampened and delayed, and that agents will make mistakes due to lack of information. The theory also explains how people simplify and summarize available information, and how this affects their decisions. The document surveys the existing applications of the theory and reviews the empirical evidence, highlighting its potential for understanding various economic phenomena. The authors argue that rational inattention is a suitable model for studying how economic actors adjust to cognitive limitations and that it has far-reaching implications for policy.

Document title: Racial Differences in Mortgage Refinancing, Distress, and Housing Wealth Accumulation during COVID-19
Document description: The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated racial disparities in U.S. mortgage markets. Black, Hispanic, and Asian borrowers were significantly more likely than white borrowers to miss payments due to financial distress, and significantly less likely to refinance to take advantage of the large decline in interest rates. The wide-scale forbearance program provided approximately equal payment relief to all distressed borrowers, but Black and Hispanic borrowers were significantly less likely to exit forbearance and resume making payments relative to their Asian and white counterparts. The authors analyze the effects of the pandemic on mortgage outcomes, focusing on racial and ethnic differences. They find that Black and Hispanic borrowers have higher exposure to risk factors such as low credit scores and high loan-to-value ratios, which inhibit refinancing. The authors estimate that Black borrowers were 40 percent less likely than white borrowers to refinance after the pandemic started and interest rates dropped. The evolution of mortgage nonpayment during the pandemic also displays large disparities, with 12.3 percent of Black borrowers past due in October 2020 compared to 1.1 percent for white borrowers. The authors conclude that the typical borrower who missed a mortgage payment is likely to exit forbearance in a financial condition similar to the one they were in before the pandemic, at least as far as their mortgage is concerned.

Document title: The Market for CEOs
Document description: The document studies the market for CEOs of large publicly-traded US firms, analyzing new CEOs' prior connections to the hiring firm. The study reveals that firms hire from a surprisingly small pool of candidates, with more than 80% of new CEOs being insiders. The results show that firms prefer to hire insiders, with 72% of new CEOs being promoted internally and 8.4% being former executives or current or former board members. The study also finds that there are few reallocations of CEOs across firms, with only 3% of new CEOs being poached from another firm. The results suggest that firm-specific human capital and asymmetric learning about CEO ability are key factors in the CEO labor market.

Document title: Personal Bankruptcy and the Accumulation of Shadow Debt
Document description: This document studies the relationship between personal bankruptcy and the accumulation of shadow debt. The authors analyze data from personal bankruptcy filers and find that a significant portion of reported liabilities are shadow debt, which is debt not reported to credit bureaus. They use this data to evaluate how debtor cash flows affect when consumers file for bankruptcy and how much debt they have at bankruptcy. The document finds that filers respond to increases in monthly cash flows by delaying filing and increasing unsecured indebtedness. A large share of the additional debt incurred by delaying filers is shadow debt. The authors also find that borrowers who delay filing increase their shadow debt in particular, with an additional month delay resulting in an average increase of $7,200 in shadow debt per month of filing delay.

Document title: Culture and the Family
Document description: The document discusses the interactions between the family and culture that have significant economic implications. It focuses on how the family's cultural beliefs affect decision-making and outcomes, and how these change and interact over time. The authors argue that understanding the relationship between culture and the family is critical for understanding economic outcomes. They discuss the variation in family institutions around the world and throughout history, and how these institutions have changed over time. The authors also examine how the family transmits culture, leading practices and attitudes to persist, but also provide examples of how culture can change dramatically within relatively short periods. Document title: The Effect of Principal Reduction on Household Distress: Evidence from Mortgage Cramdown
Document description: The document discusses the effects of mortgage cramdown on household distress. Mortgage cramdown is a process where bankruptcy judges can discharge the underwater portion of a mortgage during Chapter 13 bankruptcy. The authors of the paper estimate the causal effect of mortgage cramdown on foreclosure and other economic outcomes using a newly compiled data set. They find that a successful Chapter 13 filing in a cramdown court substantially decreases the five-year foreclosure rate, the propensity to move, and the crime rate. The authors also investigate whether the discharge decisions and the subsequent borrower outcomes depend on the characteristics of the filers for bankruptcy protection. They study whether judges impose differential thresholds on female filers and whether the benefits of bankruptcy protection differ by gender. The authors find beneficial effects of discharge in cramdown courts across different demographic groups, with the benefits being more pronounced for female filers. They also provide a partial-equilibrium back-of-the-envelope calculation of how many foreclosures could have been avoided had the United States allowed mortgage cramdown during the 2008-2013 period.

Document title: Making Entrepreneurs: Returns to Training Youth in Hard Versus Soft Business Skills
Document description: The document discusses the effectiveness of the Skills for Effective Entrepreneurship Development (SEED) program in Uganda, which provides a 3-week mini-MBA program for high school students. Document title: THE EFFECT OF TARIFFS ON SPANISH GOODS EXPORTS
Document description: This paper investigates the impact of trade protectionism in the form of tariff barriers on Spanish goods exports. The Spanish economy has increased its degree of openness, which improves potential economic growth, but also implies a higher exposure to the protectionist shift in the international environment. The authors use data from 1995-2019 to assess the sensitivity of Spanish goods exports to tariff increases. They find that higher tariffs reduce exports levels through both extensive and intensive margins. A 1% tariff increase reduces the probability of exporting to a specific market by nearly 0.08% and exported values by around 1%. The authors also find that the impact of tariffs on real exports is somewhat higher than the long-run exports price elasticity estimated with aggregate real goods exports data. The results are robust to alternative specifications and suggest that the effect of tariffs on quantities exported can be cushioned if sellers partially reduce their price margins.

Document title: Electoral Cycles in Macroeconomic Forecasts
Document description: This paper documents the existence of Political Forecast Cycles, where governments release overly optimistic GDP growth forecasts ahead of elections to increase the reelection probability. The bias arises from lack of commitment if voters are rational and from manipulation of voters' beliefs if they do not expect the incumbent to be biased. Using high-frequency forecaster-level data from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Sweden, the authors document that governments overestimate short-term GDP growth by 10 to 13 percent during campaign periods. The bias is larger when the incumbent government is not term-limited or constrained by a parliament led by the opposition. The authors also find that the election timing and amount of available information determine the size of the bias at different forecast horizons. The theoretical framework adapts the Persson and Tabellini model of political selection by allowing the government to release forecasts for GDP growth to the public. The authors show that the incumbent politician faces a trade-off between the accuracy of the released forecast and the incentive to bias the estimates to increase reelection probability.

Document title: The aftermath of sovereign debt crises: a narrative approach
Document description: This discussion paper explores the aftermath of sovereign debt crises using a narrative approach. The authors analyze a large panel of 50 sovereigns between 1870 and 2010 and find that defaults have spent 18% of time in a state of default since 1820. They estimate the aggregate cost of defaults and find significant and persistent costs starting at 1.6% of GDP and peaking at 3.3% before reverting to trend five years after a debt event. The authors also identify a large heterogeneity of costs by the cause of default, with higher costs associated with defaults initiated by negative supply shocks, political crises, or adverse terms of trade. They use the narrative approach to overcome the endogeneity of sovereign default and find that the effect of crises on GDP is persistent, with GDP only reverting to the pre-crisis level five years after the start of a default.

Document title: Sticky floors or glass ceilings? The role of human capital, working time flexibility and discrimination in the gender wage gap
Document description: The document discusses the gender wage gap in 25 European countries, highlighting that despite changes in social norms and policies, women continue to earn lower hourly earnings than men with similar qualifications and experience. The authors suggest that 'sticky floors' related to social norms, gender stereotyping, and discrimination account for 40% of the gender wage gap, while the 'glass ceiling' related to the motherhood penalty accounts for around 60%. The authors propose policies to address the motherhood penalty, such as promoting flexitime and telework, and supporting early childcare. They also suggest that equal pay and pay transparency laws, measures to address gender stereotyping, and higher wage floors are necessary to reduce the gender wage gap. The authors emphasize the importance of understanding the drivers of the gender wage gap to design effective policies.

Document title: Surviving the Fintech Disruption
Document description: This paper studies how demand for labor reacts to financial technology (fintech) shocks based on comprehensive databases of fintech patents and firm job postings in the U.S. during the past decade. The authors develop a measure of fintech exposure at the occupation level by intersecting the textual information in job task descriptions and fintech patents. They find a significant decline of job postings in the most exposed occupations, and an increase in industry as well as geographical concentration of these occupations. Firms resort to an upskilling strategy in face of the fintech disruption, requiring combo skills, higher education attainments, and longer work experiences in the hiring of fintech-exposed jobs. Financial firms and those with high innovation outputs are able to offset the disruptive effect from the fintech shock. Among innovating firms, however, only inventors experience growth in hiring, sales, investment, and enjoy better returns on assets. The authors also find that fintech innovations are concentrated in four industries: finance, information, manufacturing, and professional, management and administrative services. Firms are not passive players in a wave of disruption, and they adapt to the change by upskilling and changing their recruiting strategies.

Document title: Selecting the Most Effective Nudge: Evidence from a Large-Scale Experiment on Immunization
Document description: This document evaluates a large-scale set of interventions to increase demand for immunization in Haryana, India. The policies under consideration include reminders, incentives, and an intervention inspired by the networks literature. The authors cross-randomize whether individuals receive SMS reminders, incentives for vaccinating their children, or influential individuals are asked to act as ambassadors to spread the word about immunization. The authors develop a new statistical technique to find the best policy from a large set, which also determines which policies are effective and the effect of the best policy. The key outcomes are the number of measles immunizations and the number of immunizations per dollar spent. The policy that has the largest impact increases the number of immunizations by 44% relative to the status quo, and the most cost-effective policy increases the number of immunizations per dollar by 9.1%. The authors use a smart pooling and pruning procedure to select policies, which combines existing techniques from statistics and econometrics for model selection and subsequent inference.

Document title: Fearless Woman: Financial Literacy and Stock Market Participation
Document description: The document explores the relationship between financial literacy and stock market participation, particularly among women. It highlights a pronounced gender gap in financial inclusion, with women having less access to formal financial institutions, credit, and assets. The authors use data from the De Nederlandsche Bank Household Survey to examine the role of confidence in explaining the gender gap in financial literacy and stock market participation. They find that women tend to respond 'do not know' to financial literacy questions, but when this option is unavailable, they often choose the correct answer. The authors estimate a latent class model to predict 'true' financial literacy and find that about one-third of the financial literacy gender gap is due to lower confidence levels. They also show that both financial knowledge and confidence are important for understanding gender differences in stock market participation. The findings suggest that financial education programs tailored to women that boost both knowledge and confidence might be more effective than one-size-fits-all programs.

Document title: Economic Incentives, Childcare and Gender Identity Norms
Document description: This paper investigates the role of gender identity norms in shaping men's and women's time allocation, based on observed behavior following a change in the market penalty for adopting prescriptive norms. The authors study the reallocation of childcare across parents, following changes in their relative take-home pay, exploiting variation from Swedish tax reforms. Document title: Austerity and Elections
Document description: This paper reassesses the conventional wisdom that austerity carries an electoral cost by making important progresses in the identification of the political effects of fiscal austerity. The authors use a real-time narrative dataset of ex-ante austerity plans to analyze the effects of austerity on elections. They find that tax-based austerity carries large electoral costs, while expenditure-based consolidations are neutral on average. An austerity package worth 1% of GDP, carried out mostly through tax hikes, reduces the vote share of the leader's party by about 7%. The authors also investigate whether the timing of austerity in relation to the business cycle matters for its electoral outcomes and find that it does. The electoral cost of austerity—especially tax hikes—is higher (lower) when implemented during bad (good) economic times.

Document title: Will the Economic Impact of COVID-19 Persist? Prognosis from 21st Century Pandemics
Document description: The document discusses the economic impact of COVID-19 and whether its effects will persist. It analyzes the effects of five previous major epidemics in the 21st century and finds that they led to significant and persistent reductions in disposable income, increases in unemployment and income inequality, and increases in public debt-to-GDP ratios. The authors suggest that evidence on the impacts of more recent epidemics, such as SARS, H1N1, MERS, Ebola, and Zika, might be a more useful guide for projections of the lingering impacts of COVID-19 on the economy. They go beyond existing work by examining the impact on a wide range of economic measures, including economic growth, unemployment and public debt, income inequality and poverty, energy use and intensity, and emissions. The authors forecast a persistent decline in the level of economic activity and an increase in poverty due to COVID-19, with an estimated 75 million people falling into poverty by 2025.

Document title: Credit Reversals
Document description: This paper studies episodes where aggregate bank credit contracts alongside expanding economic activity, known as credit reversals. Using data for 179 countries from 1960 to 2017, the paper finds that reversals occur about once every five years and are more prevalent in developing countries. Credit reversals and banking crises appear related, with reversals becoming more likely after banking crises and the likelihood of crises dropping following reversals. The economic costs of credit reversals are substantial, at about one-half of the estimated costs of crises and up to two-thirds after factoring in their relative frequencies. The analysis also explores the relationship between credit reversals and banking crises and the shape of credit cycles, defined by the evolution of the credit-to-GDP gap. The paper provides estimates of the economic costs associated with the presence of credit reversals, comparing them with those attributable to banking crises.

Document title: The Great Depression, banking crisis, and Keynes’ paradox of thrift
Document description: The document discusses the paradox of thrift, a concept formulated by Keynes in the 1930s, which states that an increase in savings does not naturally lead to an increase in investment. The authors analyze data on deposits in savings institutions of 22 countries during the Great Depression and show that Keynes' intuition was right. Banking crises had an impact on economic growth not only through the direct lending channel, but also indirectly through an increase in precautionary savings. The authors find that the surge in savings was usually associated with banking crises, and that the rise in precautionary savings caused by banking crises was an important channel of transmission of the Depression. They also find that the negative effect of precautionary savings on growth was at least as large as the direct effect of the decline in banking activity during the years when the banking crises were most intense. The authors suggest that governments and central banks should respond to the large increase in savings rates by leaving the gold standard and implementing countercyclical policies to foster recovery.

Document title: Welfare Reforms and the Division of Parental Leave
Document description: The document studies the design of parental leave systems through the lens of an estimated model of parents' joint willingness to pay for parental leave. The study uses Danish register data on almost 200,000 births combined with sharp variation in economic incentives created by the parental leave benefit system. The estimated model reproduces the empirical distribution of leave, including bunching at kinks in household budget sets and a large share of fathers taking little or no leave at all. The study provides a menu of counterfactual policy simulations showing substantial interaction effects between earmarked leave, replacement rates, and the duration of leave benefits. The authors discuss the efficiency costs of different policies aimed at increasing the parental leave of fathers and conclude that earmarked parental leave is an efficient way to increase the leave of fathers. The study relates to the empirical literature on parental leave reforms and provides evidence on the effect on household utility, which is a key component in the assessment of the desirability of earmarked leave reforms.

Document title: Crime and Gender Segregation: Evidence from the Bogota "Pico y Genero" Lockdown
Document description: This paper investigates the link between gender and crime using information from a gender-based lockdown policy in Bogota Colombia during the pandemic. The policy, coined Pico y Genero, allowed men to leave their homes on odd-numbered days and women on even-numbered days. The authors compare crime in Bogota to other cities and within Bogota, the gender-based lockdown period to weeks with other lockdown policies. They find that crime rates are higher during the gender-based lockdown policy and that this is driven by more crime involving male victims and on men-only days. There is no evidence that higher crime on men-only days is offset by less crime on women-only days. The authors also find higher sexual crimes on women-only days and an increase in domestic violence on both types of days. The results suggest that gender segregation tends to increase crime.

Document title: Immigration and Regional Specialization in AI
Document description: The document examines the specialization of US commuting zones in AI-related occupations over the 2000 to 2018 period. It defines AI-related jobs based on keywords in Census occupational titles and measures job growth related to AI by weighting employment growth in AI-related occupations by the share of job titles in these occupations that were added after 1990.
