Document title: Can you move to opportunity? Evidence from the Great Migration - Equitable Growth
Document description: This paper examines the impact of the Great Migration on the upward mobility of Black southern families who moved to the northern United States between 1940 and 1970. The study reveals that the influx of Black migrants led to a reduction in upward mobility for Black families, particularly Black men, who earned lower incomes and had lower marriage rates compared to those living in areas less affected by the migration. The research suggests that the negative effects were not due to the selection of negatively selected families but rather changes in the environment, such as increased crime and policing, and segregation. The study also finds that the effects of the migration were not limited to the first generation but persisted through the third generation. The analysis uses a large dataset of census data, local government expenditures, and other sources to estimate the impact of the migration on upward mobility and explores potential mechanisms, including changes in public schools, crime, and incarceration rates. The study provides a nuanced view of the Great Migration and its long-term effects on the lives of Black families.

Document description: This document presents a study on the growth of small retail shops in Indonesia. Document title: An Entertaining Approach to Saving
Document description: This paper investigates the effectiveness of using a Nollywood movie, The Story of Gold, to relay a simple message of 'safe saving and responsible borrowing' through an emotionally-charged storyline to a group of microentrepreneurs in Lagos, Nigeria. The study uses a 2x2 randomized factorial design to exogenously vary exposure to The Story of Gold and access to financial products by offering free 'on-the-spot' micro-savings accounts through a Microfinance Bank at selected screening events. The results show that entrepreneurs in all three treatment arms increase self-reported trust in MFBs, but the treatment arms including The Story of Gold had a larger effect on male self-reported trust. The combination of the movie with the presence of an MFB to help facilitate the opening of a savings account at the time of the screening was substantially more effective at motivating business owners to open an account than the presence of an MFB combined with a placebo screening, and this was most effective for influencing male decisions, increasing savings account sign-up rates from 1% to 11%. However, four months after the event, the study finds limited or no sustained impacts on perceptions of MFBs and intention to borrow and save, and no effect on the likelihood of having a savings account.

Document title: Strengthening the Euro Area : The Role of National Structural Reforms in Building Resilience
Document description: The creation of the euro area has played a central role in boosting European integration, but cross-country differences in economic resilience persist. National structural reforms can help enhance euro area member states' resilience to shocks, including labor and product market regulations and corporate insolvency regimes. The document examines the specific issue of whether and to what extent national structural policies can improve euro area countries' resilience to shocks. It investigates how business cycles in euro area economies have evolved in the post–Bretton Woods era, including compared with other advanced economies. The results suggest that a package of growth-enhancing reforms to labor and product market regulations and corporate insolvency regimes could strengthen economic resilience. Labor market reforms entail measures to ensure that policy instruments such as the labor tax wedge, minimum wages, collective bargaining arrangements, employment protection, and unemployment insurance are appropriately structured and calibrated. Product market reforms include lowering barriers to entrepreneurship, such as administrative burdens on start-ups, regulatory protection of incumbent firms, and licensing and permitting requirements. Insolvency regime reforms include measures to ensure that procedures to restructure or resolve insolvent firms are timely and predictable. The document concludes that national structural policies can improve euro area countries' resilience to shocks, and that a package of growth-enhancing reforms could strengthen economic resilience.

Document title: Research: Over the Top: Why an Annual Wealth Tax for Canada is Unnecessary
Document description: The document discusses the idea of an annual wealth tax in Canada. The authors, Robin Boadway and Pierre Pestieau, argue that wealth taxes add relatively little to the taxes on capital and capital income that are already in place. The authors also mention the administrative challenges in measurement, collection, and coverage for annual wealth taxes. They conclude that annual net wealth taxes are unnecessary since their objectives can be better achieved by suitably designed taxes on capital income and wealth transfers. The document references the work of Thomas Piketty and Elizabeth Warren, who have proposed global and national wealth taxes, respectively. The authors note that several countries have abolished or decreased annual wealth taxes and inheritance taxes. They also mention that taxes on immovable property throughout the OECD represent a small percentage of overall taxation. The document aims to critically evaluate the case for an annual wealth tax as part of Canada's tax system.

Document title: When Dad Can Stay Home: Fathers’ Workplace Flexibility and Maternal Health
Document description: This document examines the impact of workplace flexibility on maternal postpartum health in Sweden. It focuses on a critical period in family life, the months immediately following childbirth, and investigates the effects of paternal access to workplace flexibility on maternal health. The study uses a Regression Discontinuity Difference-in-Differences design and finds that increasing the father's temporal flexibility reduces the risk of the mother experiencing physical postpartum health complications and improves her mental health. The results suggest that mothers bear the burden from a lack of workplace flexibility, not only directly through greater career costs of family formation but also indirectly, as fathers' inability to respond to domestic shocks exacerbates the maternal health costs of childbearing. The study also finds that the reform leads to a reduction in the likelihood of a mother having an inpatient or specialist outpatient visit for childbirth-related complications and an improvement in maternal postpartum mental health.

Document description: This paper investigates the effectiveness of using a Nollywood movie to improve financial behavior. Document title: Financial Crises and Liberalization: Progress or Reversals?
Document description: The document discusses the relationship between financial crises and liberalization. It presents evidence that financial crises can lead to policy reversals, with governments intervening in the financial sector to mitigate the crisis. However, this intervention is often temporary, and countries gradually liberalize their financial markets again in the medium-to-long term. The study uses a comprehensive dataset on financial liberalization across 94 countries for the period between 1973 and 2015. It finds that financial crises lead to a reversal of liberal reforms, but these reforms are only temporary, and countries eventually catch up with others in terms of financial liberalization. The study also explores the dynamic relationship between financial crises and various areas of financial reform, using a flexible methodology estimating the impulse-response functions via local projections. The findings suggest that a banking crisis leads to a rapid reduction in the degree of overall financial liberalization in the first two years after the shock, but governments restart the reform efforts and fully catch up with other countries in a duration of 2-4 years, sometimes even ending up with a more liberalized financial market at the end of a 10-year-long window after a crisis.

Document title: Debt and Depth of Recessions
Document description: This paper investigates the relationship between the speed of private debt buildup and the depth of recessions. The authors differentiate between financial recessions and normal recessions based on the speed of private debt buildup. They find that financial recessions are deeper than normal recessions in advanced economies, and the difference becomes more pronounced when emerging market economies are added to the sample. The authors also find that a buildup in corporate debt is especially damaging for emerging markets during financial recessions. A higher ratio of debt to gross domestic product exacerbates recessions only beyond a certain threshold level, suggesting a nonlinear effect. The authors investigate the role of fiscal space in mitigating the depth of recessions and find that it affects the severity of recessions only after the public debt-GDP ratio reaches a threshold of 57.9%. The findings suggest that private debt buildups can be even more damaging to emerging market economies, which have fewer instruments to smooth consumption.

Document title: Gender-Based Employment Segregation : Understanding Causes and Policy Interventions
Document description: The document discusses employment segregation, which refers to the unequal distribution of female and male workers across and within job types. Document description: The document discusses the effectiveness of financial education in improving financial literacy and behavior. Document title: Trade Wars
Document description: The document discusses the current trade wars and the recent U.S. trade actions that have initiated them. It offers an interpretation of these actions, arguing that the United States is initiating a change from 'rules-based' to 'power-based' tariff bargaining. The authors suggest that the main costs of these trade tactics will arise from the use of the tactics themselves and the damage done to the rules-based multilateral trading system. They also argue that the threat of bargaining tariffs is needed to induce a zero-sum reallocation of the existing spoils from globalization. The document examines the GATT/WTO rules-based multilateral trading system and how recent U.S. trade actions can be seen as an attempt to escape from these constraints. The authors propose a new approach to tariff bargaining, which they argue is more in line with the current global trading system. They also discuss the potential consequences of this new approach, including the potential for a power-based system where countries are free to bargain in a way that is not constrained by any particular set of agreed-upon rules of behavior.

Document title: Effects of extended paternity leave on union stability and fertility
Document description: This study examines the impact of extending the Norwegian paternity leave quota from six to ten weeks on union stability and fertility. The authors use a regression discontinuity design with full population data to compare families who had children just before and just after the reform took effect on July 1, 2009. The results show that the reform significantly increased the amount of leave taken by fathers by approximately three weeks while mothers reduced their leave time. Despite these substantial changes in parental leave uptake, the study found no significant effects on union stability, subsequent fertility, or subsequent earnings for either parents. The findings suggest that while policy-induced father involvement does not automatically stabilize unions or increase fertility, fathers who took extended leave did not face increased earnings penalties. The authors conclude that previous associations between father involvement and positive demographic outcomes may be driven by selection effects rather than causal relationships.

Document title: Macroprudential policy with capital buffers
Document description: This paper studies optimal bank capital requirements in a model of endogenous bank funding conditions. It finds that requirements should be higher during good times to provide a macroprudential buffer. However, whether banks can use buffers to maintain lending during a financial crisis depends on the capital requirement during the subsequent recovery. The paper suggests that regulators should require banks to hold more equity when loan supply is high, but also allow banks to hold very little equity when loan supply is low. It also recommends that banks should be allowed to rebuild equity slowly after loan supply has been low, and that regulators should raise bank future profitability temporarily during the time when banks use a capital buffer to pay out dividends. The paper concludes that optimal regulation requires banks to hold more equity when loan supply is high, but also allows banks to hold very little equity when loan supply is low. It also suggests that regulators should give banks some discretion in calculating risk-weighted assets during times of crisis, and that there should be a buffer on top of market-imposed capital requirements that can be used to stabilize lending when bank equity is low.

Document title: Macroprudential policy with capital buffers / by Josef Schroth.
Document description: This document studies optimal bank capital requirements in a model of endogenous bank funding conditions. The author finds that requirements should be higher during good times to provide a macroprudential buffer. However, the effectiveness of buffers in maintaining lending during a financial crisis depends on the capital requirement during the subsequent recovery. The author concludes that buffers are useful if banks are not required to rebuild them quickly. The paper also develops a model of optimal bank capital regulation and derives implications for bank capital regulation. The main result is that optimal regulation requires banks to hold more equity when loan supply is high, but also allows banks to hold very little equity when loan supply is low. The author suggests that minimum capital requirements should be as low as possible while still discouraging moral hazard. Any additional capital that a regulator wishes banks to hold should take the form of capital buffers, which do not constrain intermediation provided the bank is willing to constrain payouts instead. The author also proposes that capital buffers that banks build up during good times are most effective in stabilizing lending during a financial crisis when banks are allowed to rebuild them slowly during the recovery. The paper's findings have implications for bank regulation and can be compared with recent changes in recommendations for bank regulation under the Basel Accord.

Document title: Collective Emotions and Protest Vote
Document description: This document explores the relationship between collective emotions and protest vote. The authors propose a behavioral theory of protest vote, leveraging findings in social psychology. They argue that individuals develop a feeling of resentment when they experience relative deprivation, and that this feeling is amplified when they identify with a community experiencing the same feeling. The theory predicts higher support for the protest party when individuals identify more strongly with their local community and when a higher share of community members are aggrieved. The authors test this theory using longitudinal data on British households and exploiting the emergence of the UK Independence Party in the 2010 and 2015 national elections. The empirical findings robustly support the theoretical predictions, and the authors show that the emotional channel is distinct from alternative explanations of protest vote.

Document title: Industry Concentration in Europe and North America
Document description: This document presents new evidence on industry concentration trends in Europe and North America. It uses two novel data sources: representative firm-level concentration measures from the OECD MultiProd project, and business-group-level concentration measures using matched Orbis-Worldscope-Zephyr data. The study finds that between 2001 and 2012 the average industry across 10 European economies saw a 2-3-percentage-point increase in the share of the 10% largest companies in industry sales. The increase in industry concentration is observed for both manufacturing and non-financial services and is not driven by digital-intensive sectors. The study also documents a clear increase in industry concentration in Europe as well as in North America between 2000 and 2014 of the order of 4-8 percentage points for the average industry. Industry concentration is related to, but distinct from, the concept of market concentration. Industry concentration measures the extent to which economic activity is concentrated within a small number of large companies or business groups within an industry. Understanding trends in industry concentration is important because they can reflect or have implications for a range of economic phenomena, including technological change, globalisation, and lobbying. Industry concentration is also sometimes seen as a proxy for the degree of competition, which influences a variety of economic outcomes, such as productivity, innovation, and income distribution.

Document description: The document discusses the risks associated with household debt in the US. Document title: Reducing crime through environmental design: evidence from a randomized experiment of street lighting in New York City
Document description: This paper presents experimental evidence that crime can be reduced by changing the situational environment that potential victims and offenders face. The authors focus on street lighting as a ubiquitous but understudied feature of the urban landscape and report the first experimental evidence on the effect of street lighting on crime. They conducted a randomized experiment in New York City, where temporary streetlights were randomly allocated to public housing developments from March through August 2016. The results show that communities assigned more lighting experienced sizable reductions in crime, with a 36 percent reduction in nighttime outdoor index crimes. The authors argue that small changes to the environment can have surprisingly large effects on human behavior and that street lighting can complement traditional deterrence-based strategies to drive down crime. Document title: 1845. The paradox of global thrift
Document description: The document discusses a paradox of global thrift, where low interest rates and monetary policy constrained by the zero lower bound lead to a situation where prudential financial and fiscal policies implemented by governments can backfire and lead to a fall in global output and welfare. The authors develop a tractable framework of a financially integrated world, where equilibrium interest rates are low and monetary policy is occasionally constrained by the zero lower bound. They show that during a global liquidity trap, governments have an incentive to intervene on the current account for prudential reasons, but this can trigger a paradox of global thrift, where the implementation of prudential current account policies by booming countries can aggravate the recession in countries experiencing a liquidity trap. The authors conclude that international cooperation is needed to ensure that current account interventions by booming countries do not impart excessive negative spillovers on the rest of the world.

Document title: Does Paternity Leave Reduce Fertility?
Document description: The document discusses the effects of introducing two weeks of paid paternity leave in Spain in 2007 on fertility rates. The authors find that the introduction of paternity leave led to delays in subsequent fertility, with parents who were eligible for the new leave taking longer to have another child compared to those who were not. The authors also find that older eligible couples were less likely to have an additional child within the following six years after the introduction of the reform. Document description: The document discusses the benefits and costs of Preferential Trade Agreements (PTAs) in the context of global sourcing. Document title: Contingent Debt and Performance Pricing in an Optimal Capital Structure Model with Financial Distress and Reorganization
Document description: The document discusses a dynamic theory of optimal capital structure with financial distress and reorganization. It builds on the trade-off between agency costs and monitoring costs, and assumes that monitoring cannot be applied instantaneously. The firm seeks a monitoring opportunity whenever it is financially distressed, and if a transition to monitoring arrives in time, the manager is dismissed and the capital structure is reorganized. The optimal capital structure consists of equity, long-term debt, contingent long-term debt, and a credit line with performance pricing. Contingent debt is suspended in financial distress, but the interest rate on the credit line is stepped-up, which gives the firm simultaneously debt relief and a steep incentive to improve its financial position. The document provides a new explanation of the role of performance pricing and contingent debt in the firm's capital structure.

Document title: Parental leave benefits, household labor supply, and children's long-run outcomes
Document description: This document studies the effects of parental leave benefit levels on household labor supply, family income, and child outcomes. The authors exploit the Speed Premium in the Swedish leave system, which grants mothers higher benefits for a subsequent child without re-establishing eligibility through market work, if two births occur within a pre-specified interval. The study finds that eligibility to higher PL benefits decreases mothers' labor supply, but has no effect on their total disposable income. The Speed Premium also increases the labor supply of the partners of women in the top third of the earnings distribution. However, the study finds no effects on the new child, who is actually the target of the Speed Premium. The impacts are likely driven by increased maternal time and family financial resources, and by switching from informal to maternal care before the age of two. The authors conclude that the automatic renewal of PL benefits increases inequality in three dimensions: it widens the gender earnings gap within the household, is a regressive scheme that only benefits children to mothers in the top third of the earnings distribution, and widens the birth order gap between siblings.

Document title: Policy in Focus
Document description: Despite progress in education and health worldwide, women continue to face significant obstacles to participate as full citizens in the economy. There are notable differences between men and women in terms of salaries and labor participation. Women also face barriers and lack the necessary assets to become entrepreneurs. These inequalities are still large, persistent, and widespread in many parts of the world. Addressing these gaps is not only a moral imperative, but there is also growing evidence that gender equality can directly promote economic growth and widespread social development. One important aspect of women's economic empowerment is their labor participation, which is the central theme of this special issue of Policy in Focus. However, not all types of work have positive outcomes for women, who face difficulties in securing well-paying and productive jobs that allow them to accumulate assets. The use of women's time will remain limited if the heavy burden of deeply ingrained social conventions, such as domestic chores and childcare responsibilities, is not shared by other family members. There is also evidence of links between greater women's economic empowerment and violence against them. Vulnerable groups are subject to greater gender inequality. When this situation is exacerbated by socioeconomic inequality, the result is a cyclical reproduction and intergenerational transmission of vulnerability and poverty. The articles in this volume examine the conditions under which work can lead to women's empowerment, evaluating recent trends and determinants of women's participation in the labor market, as well as public policies aimed at improving gender equality in the economy.

Document description: This paper updates the database on systemic banking crises presented in Laeven and Valencia (2008, 2013). Document title: Macroeconomic effects of bank capital regulation Discussion paper 44/2018: Sandra Eickmeier, Benedikt Kolb, Esteban Prieto
Document description: The document discusses the macroeconomic effects of bank capital regulation. Since the 2008/2009 financial crisis, advanced economies have introduced new financial stability policy measures, including bank capital-based policy instruments. These instruments aim to enhance financial stability in the long run but may involve costs for the real economy. The authors propose a narrative approach to identify exogenous changes in the aggregate bank capital ratio. They create a narrative index of permanent tightenings in US capital requirements from 1979 to 2008, based on detailed readings of legislative documents. The authors find that a tightening in capital requirements leads to a delayed, permanent increase in the aggregate bank capital ratio. Banks first reduce their assets and then increase capital. The events have significantly negative effects on bank lending and production, which are temporary. Monetary policy also cushions the negative effects of capital requirement tightenings on the economy. The authors detect evidence for anticipation effects, with bank assets, production, and the monetary policy rate adjusting about 6 months before the new rules become effective.

Document title: What works to Prevent Violence Amongst Youth
Document description: This report, commissioned by USAID for the J-PAL Latin America and Caribbean office, evaluates interventions designed to prevent youth violence based on a review of over 264 studies. The authors identify six specific types of programs with strong evidence of effectiveness, including cognitive behavioral therapy, multidimensional therapy, drug courts, focused deterrence, alcohol sales controls, and hot spots policing. While these programs show promise, the report notes that some interventions like hot spots policing require careful consideration regarding potential displacement of crime to surrounding areas. A second category of interventions, such as vocational training and conditional cash transfers, shows modest evidence and offers avenues for innovation through pilot programs. A third group of approaches like environmental design has inconclusive evidence, necessitating thorough assessment before large-scale implementation. Finally, several interventions including boot camps and scared straight programs are found to be ineffective and should be scaled down or replaced. The report emphasizes the need for Mexico to adopt agile innovation in prevention programming while simultaneously strengthening law enforcement and justice institutions to address community violence effectively.

Document title: The macroeconomic effects of macroprudential policy
Document description: The document discusses the macroeconomic effects of macroprudential policy, specifically changes in maximum loan-to-value (LTV) ratios, on output and inflation. The authors use a narrative approach to identify the effects of LTV ratio changes and find that a 10 percentage point reduction in the maximum LTV ratio lowers output by about 1.1% after four years. The authors also test for potential asymmetries and find that the output effect is mainly driven by the negative effects of tightenings in maximum LTV ratios, and not by higher output generated through loosening actions. The results imply that central banks might be able to use macroprudential policies to dampen the financial cycle without risking major interference with their core monetary policy objectives.

Document description: The document discusses the effects of labor demand shocks on local economies, focusing on gender differences in the labor market. It presents a spatial equilibrium model that incorporates gender segmentation and joint mobility frictions for couples. The model predicts that local labor and housing markets respond asymmetrically to equivalent shocks to male and female labor demand. The study uses data from Brazil during the 1991-2010 period to test the model's predictions and finds strong empirical support for the differential migration mechanism. The results show that male demand shocks lead to population growth, increases in female labor supply, and housing demand growth, while equivalent shocks to labor demand for women lead to smaller migration adjustments and effects on the housing and male labor markets. The study also finds that male demand shocks increase the employment and wage gender gaps, while female demand shocks reduce the gender employment gap but not the wage gap. Document title: The Money View Versus the Credit View
Document description: The document discusses a study by Schularick and Taylor that investigates the dynamics of money, credit, and output across a broad sample of countries over the long run. The authors compare the 'money view' and 'credit view' as accounts of macroeconomic outcomes, with the money view associated with Friedman and Schwartz and the credit view emphasizing the significance of movements in credit aggregates. However, the authors' characterization of the money view is faulty, and they misinterpret its implications. The study's results comparing money and credit are undermined by a second flaw in the authors' characterization of the money view. The authors' version of the credit view is one in which credit booms 'go bust,' and they argue against the money view using the result that rapid credit growth is more successful in predicting financial crises than monetary growth. However, this was not the money view expressed by Friedman and Schwartz, who did not predict an automatic relationship between rapid monetary growth and downturns. The authors also show that Schularick and Taylor's data on money have systematic faults, and they have constructed new, more reliable, annual data on money for the countries studied by Schularick and Taylor.

Document title: Convertible bonds and bank risk-taking Discussion paper 24/2018: Natalya Martynova, Enrico Perotti
Document description: The document discusses the effectiveness of contingent convertible capital (CoCo) in reducing bank risk-taking. It studies how CoCo debt affects a bank's incentives to take inefficient risk by choosing speculative assets purely for risk-shifting reasons. The research shows that CoCo debt can be better at reducing ex ante risk than conventional bail-inable debt. Going-concern conversion in high leverage states reduces risk-shifting, while debt bail-in only reallocates losses at default among debtors. The main beneficial effect on risk incentives comes from reduced leverage upon conversion, while any equity dilution has the opposite effect. The document also compares the two main forms of CoCo debt conversion, namely conversion to equity versus principal write-down, and suggests that principal write-down CoCo debt should be preferred as it ensures no equity dilution which has a positive effect on risk incentives. The effectiveness of CoCo conversion on risk incentives critically depends on the precision of the trigger.

Document title: The International Monetary Fund
Document description: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is a multilateral organization focused on the international monetary system. Created in 1946, it has grown to include 189 countries. The IMF has six purposes: promoting international monetary cooperation, expanding the balanced growth of international trade, facilitating exchange rate stability, eliminating restrictions on the international flow of capital, ensuring confidence, and adjusting balance-of-payments imbalances in an orderly manner. The IMF has evolved significantly since its creation, with its role expanding to include the resolution of international financial crises. The United States is the largest financial contributor to the IMF and has veto power over major decisions due to its large voting share. The IMF has provided large loans to countries such as Greece, Ireland, and Portugal. The report evaluates the purpose, membership, financing, and focus of the IMF's activities and discusses the role of Congress in shaping U.S. policy at the IMF. The IMF's origins date back to the Bretton Woods conference in 1944, where representatives of 44 allied nations gathered to create a cooperative and institutional framework for the global economy. The IMF's purpose and contribution to postwar macroeconomic stability were threefold: facilitating trade, creating monetary stability, and providing short-term financing to member countries. The Bretton Woods monetary system, which was in place from 1946 to 1971, ensured IMF members' compliance with a par value exchange rate system. The system was a two-tiered currency regime using gold and the U.S. dollar, with each member country able to define the value of its currency in terms of gold or the U.S. dollar. The IMF has continued to evolve and adapt to changing global economic conditions, with its role expanding to include the resolution of international financial crises.

Document title: 1810. Backing the incumbent in difficult times: the electoral impact of wildfires
Document description: This document studies how voters react to large shocks outside the control of politicians, specifically the electoral impact of wildfires in Spain from 1983 to 2011. The authors find that a large accidental fire up to nine months before a local election increases the incumbent party's vote share by almost 8 percentage points. They argue that this is due to a 'rally' effect, where voters increase their support for the government in response to the disaster, regardless of which party is in office. The authors develop a simple extension of the canonical model of probabilistic voting to formalize this mechanism and find that the effect of a fire on the incumbent's vote share is increasing in the incumbent's vote share in the previous election. They also discuss alternative mechanisms, including blind retrospection and rational updating, but find that they cannot fully explain the results.

Document description: The document examines the effect of the Dunne judgment on mortgage defaults in Ireland. The judgment effectively removed a bank's ability to repossess homes in the event of default, which led to a higher rate of mortgage defaults. The author uses a natural experiment to study the effect of the judgment, comparing the default rates of borrowers who had their repossession risk removed by chance with those who did not. The results show that borrowers who had their repossession risk removed were more likely to default on their mortgages, particularly those who were in negative equity, had lower incomes, and faced higher interest rates. The author argues that the Dunne judgment led to a moral hazard cost, where borrowers were more likely to default on their mortgages because they knew they could not be repossessed. The findings have implications for policymakers who must balance the benefits of reducing repossession risk with the potential moral hazard cost.

Document description: This document discusses the risks in China's financial system, highlighting concerns about high leverage, soaring housing prices, and other sectors in the financial system. Document title: Family, firms and the gender wage gap in France
Document description: This paper explores the gender wage gap in France and its relationship with firm pay policies and parenthood. The authors use a rich matched employer-employee dataset to analyze the bargaining and sorting effects of firms on the gender wage gap. They find that the sorting of women into lower-paying firms and of men into higher-paying firms accounts for 12-15% of the total gender wage gap. This sorting effect is accentuated among parents, and the bargaining effects are close to zero for both parents and non-parents. The authors also find that mothers tend to work in firms closer to their homes and in firms where part-time work is more frequent, which may be at the expense of higher wages and fewer opportunities for promotion. The paper highlights the importance of considering the interaction between firm pay policies and parenthood in understanding the gender wage gap.

Document title: Building Ladders of Opportunity for Young People in the Great Lakes States
Document description: The Great Lakes region, home to 50 million people, faces significant economic and demographic challenges, including a decline in manufacturing employment, rising opioid addiction, and racial segregation. Despite these challenges, the region has strong foundations for future growth, including a diverse economic base, a growing number of skilled workers, and significant assets such as colleges and universities. To build on these strengths and foster the productivity and well-being of everyone in the region, decisionmakers should pursue strategies that invest in people, build ladders of opportunity and economic mobility for young people, especially young people of color, and reform and align civic and budgetary efforts to support future growth and prosperity. The region's future prosperity depends on ensuring that children and young adults are well-equipped to enter the workforce and gain additional skills. Policies and investments that build ladders of opportunity and economic mobility for young people will not only pay dividends for those who grow up in the region but also will encourage more people born there to remain and attract more people from elsewhere to move in. The document recommends five broad strategies to build ladders of opportunity and economic mobility for young people, especially young people of color, in the Great Lakes states, including supporting access to high-quality child development and preschool programs, eliminating gaps in K-12 education, promoting successful transitions to adulthood, higher education, and the workforce, reducing criminal and juvenile justice involvement, and supporting the basic needs of low-income children and parents.

Document description: This paper investigates the macroeconomic effects of UK banking crises over the period 1750 to 1938, using a new annual banking crisis series constructed from bank failure rate data. Document title: 1741. Norms in bargaining: evidence from government formation in Spain
Document description: This document studies bargaining and coalition formation in legislatures, focusing on a norm prescribing that the most voted party should hold the executive position. The authors use data from 2,898 municipal Spanish elections where two parties tied in the number of seats, and find that the party with slightly more votes is roughly 20% more likely to appoint the mayor. This effect is comparable in size to the effect of obtaining an additional seat. The authors also provide evidence from other contexts suggesting that such norms may not be confined to Spain, and that the results are driven by an effect of rank itself and not the increased ability to form coalitions. The study challenges existing theories of legislative bargaining and government formation, which focus on the number of seats held by voting blocks. The authors propose a model where elections play a dual role, aggregating information and disciplining incumbents, and different equilibria (norms) can occur.

Document title: What Are You Voting For? Proximity to Refugee Reception Centres and Voting in the 2016 Italian Constitutional Referendum
Document description: The document discusses the impact of refugee reception centres on voting behaviour in the 2016 Italian constitutional referendum. The authors use Italian municipality data to investigate the effect of proximity to refugee reception centres on voting outcomes. They find that being closer to refugee centres increased the referendum turnout and the proportion of anti-government votes. The study suggests that migration issues can influence voting behaviour even on unrelated subjects. The authors propose a new identification strategy using the decision of another municipality hosting refugees to circumvent endogeneity concerns. The results show that a 1-km reduction in distance to the closest municipality hosting a refugee centre decreases the proportion of people who do not vote and increases the proportion of people voting against the government. The study also investigates potential heterogeneous effects between municipality characteristics and finds larger effects in smaller or less populated municipalities, places with a higher proportion of individuals with at least a high school degree, and poorer municipalities.

Document description: This discussion paper examines gender differences in training opportunities between men and women in the for-profit and non-profit sectors. The study uses Canadian linked employer-employee data to investigate the probability, duration, and intensity of firm-sponsored training. The study also finds that the gender differences in training opportunities between the two sectors can explain a large portion of women's higher probability of employment in the non-profit sector. Furthermore, the study suggests that the gender wage gap in the for-profit sector is partly explained by differences in training opportunities.

Document title: Mortgage-Default Research and the Recent Foreclosure Crisis
Document description: The document reviews recent research on mortgage default, focusing on the relationship of this research to the recent foreclosure crisis. It discusses how research on defaults was advanced both theoretically and empirically before the crisis, but economists have moved the frontier further by improving data sources, building dynamic optimizing models of default, and explicitly addressing reverse causality between rising foreclosures and falling house prices. The document also discusses the foreclosure crisis and how it caused interest in mortgage default to spread from real estate and urban economists to the economics profession at large. It highlights the failure to predict the crisis, which stemmed from analysts' inability to foresee the massive fall in U.S. house prices in the late 2000s. The document also examines the impact of the foreclosure crisis on current research, including the development of new datasets and the use of default models to investigate new questions. It concludes by speculating that a richer model of house-price expectations could be added to the list of explanations for abnormally low default rates.

Document title: Why Some Times Are Different: Macroeconomic Policy and the Aftermath of Financial Crises
Document description: This paper examines the role of macroeconomic policy in explaining the variation in the aftermath of financial crises. The authors use a new measure of financial distress for 24 advanced economies in the postwar period and find that the degree of monetary and fiscal policy space prior to financial distress greatly affects the aftermath of crises. They find that the decline in output following a crisis is less than 1 percent when a country possesses both types of policy space, but almost 10 percent when it has neither. The authors also investigate the mechanisms by which policy space matters and find that countries with space use policy, particularly fiscal policy, much more aggressively. Financial distress itself also appears to be much less persistent in countries with room to use policy.

Document title: Directed Attention and Nonparametric Learning
Document description: This document studies the behavior of an agent who allocates attention across different aspects of a model under ambiguity aversion. The agent chooses to learn most about income dynamics at the very lowest frequencies, which have the greatest effect on utility. This leads to excess sensitivity of consumption to high-frequency components of income, as observed empirically. The agent's consumption growth is positively correlated with the predictable component of income growth at short horizons, violating the permanent income hypothesis. However, the agent neither over- nor under-extrapolates current shocks to income when forecasting long-run future income. The model formalizes the idea that high-frequency mistakes have minimal implications for lifetime utility, while low-frequency mistakes can have substantial effects.

Document title: Strategy-proofness in the Large
Document description: This document proposes a criterion of approximate strategy-proofness called strategy-proofness in the large (SP-L). SP-L weakens strategy-proofness (SP) in two ways: it requires truthful reporting to be approximately optimal in a large enough market, and it evaluates incentives from the interim perspective rather than ex-post. The authors argue that SP-L is a useful second-best to exact strategy-proofness for market design, as it maintains some of the attractive properties of SP, such as robustness and strategic simplicity, while being less restrictive. The document classifies existing non-SP mechanisms into those that are SP-L and those that are not, and suggests that the relevant distinction for practice in markets with a large number of participants is not 'SP vs. not SP', but rather 'SP-L vs. not SP-L'. The authors also identify a precise sense in which, in large markets, SP-L is approximately costless to impose relative to Bayes-Nash incentive compatibility.

Document title: The Dynamics of Gender Earnings Differentials: Evidence from Establishment Data
Document description: The document discusses the dynamics of gender earnings differentials in the United States, using a unique match between the 2000 Decennial Census and the Longitudinal Employer Household Dynamics data. The authors analyze how much of the increase in the gender earnings gap over the lifecycle comes from shifts in the sorting of men and women across high- and low-pay establishments and how much is due to differential earnings growth within establishments. The study finds that for college-educated individuals, the increase in the gender earnings gap is substantial and mainly due to differential earnings growth within establishments. For those with no college education, the relatively small increase in the gender gap can be fully explained by differential moves by gender across establishments. The evidence suggests that the between-establishment component of the increasing wage gap is due almost entirely to those who are married.

Document description: The document discusses the tradeoffs among active mutual funds' characteristics, including fund size, expense ratio, turnover, and portfolio liquidity. Document title: Optimal trend inflation Discussion paper 25/2017: Klaus Adam, Henning Weber
Document description: This discussion paper explores the optimal inflation rate, focusing on firm-level productivity trends and their impact on relative prices. The authors present a sticky-price model incorporating heterogeneous firms and systematic firm-level productivity trends, which delivers different predictions for the optimal inflation rate compared to canonical sticky-price models with homogeneous firms. The model shows that the optimal steady-state inflation rate generally differs from zero and inflation optimally responds to productivity disturbances. The authors use micro data from the US Census Bureau to estimate the inflation-relevant productivity trends at the firm level and quantify the optimal US inflation rate, which is found to be positive and has declined over time. The analysis suggests that structural change and policy can have a prolonged impact on the optimal inflation rate.

Document description: The document discusses the implications of institutional investors on asset prices and informational efficiency. Document description: This document discusses the impact of summer youth employment programs (SYEPs) on criminal justice outcomes, particularly for low-income and non-white youth. Document title: Locus of Control and Investment in Risky Assets
Document description: This discussion paper explores the relationship between a person's internal economic locus of control and their investment decisions in equity. The authors use data from the Dutch National Bank Household Survey to test the hypothesis that individuals with a strong internal economic locus of control are more likely to hold equity and have a larger share of equity in their investment portfolio. The results show that a one standard deviation increase in internal economic locus of control increases the probability of participating in equity by about 2.4 percentage points and increases the portfolio share of equity by 1.3 percentage points. The authors argue that the mechanism behind this positive relation is risk perception, and that individuals with a strong internal economic locus of control perceive less variance in equity, making these investments more attractive. Document title: Globalization and Its (Dis-)Content: Trade Shocks and Voting Behavior
Document description: The document studies the causal effect of trade integration with China and Eastern Europe on voting behavior in Germany from 1987 to 2009. It finds that only extreme-right parties respond significantly to trade integration, with their vote share increasing with import competition and decreasing with export access opportunities. The study uses a unified framework to estimate the effect of trade integration on both changes in voting and local labor market adjustments, and finds that labor markets respond strongly to trade exposure. The study also uses individual-level data from the German Socioeconomic Panel to distinguish between the relative importance of individuals' own trade exposure versus their local labor markets' overall trade exposure in explaining changes in voting behavior. The results suggest that voters adjust their voting behavior in large part because of what they observe in their socio-economic environment rather than voting only based on their own economic situation.

Document title: Does Science Advance One Funeral at a Time?
Document description: The document studies the impact of the death of eminent scientists on the vitality of their areas of scientific inquiry. It examines the entry rates into subfields of 452 academic life scientists who passed away prematurely and finds that the flow of articles by non-collaborators increases by 8.6% on average after the death of a star scientist. This surge in contributions from outsiders is disproportionately likely to be highly cited and draws upon a different scientific corpus. The document suggests that once in control of the commanding heights of their fields, star scientists tend to hold on to their exalted position a bit too long. The study uses a difference-in-differences setup to test Planck's Principle in the context of academic biomedical research and leverages new tools to define scientific subfields. The results provide evidence that the outsiders of today can often turn into the stars of tomorrow, highlighting the importance of caution when drawing welfare implications about the existence of stars writ large.

Document title: Forecasting the equity risk premium with frequency-decomposed predictors
Document description: The document discusses the forecasting of the equity risk premium using frequency-decomposed predictors. The authors show that the out-of-sample forecast of the equity risk premium can be significantly improved by taking into account the frequency-domain relationship between the equity risk premium and several potential predictors. They consider 15 predictors from the existing literature and find that the best result achieved for individual predictors is a monthly out-of-sample R-squared of 2.98% and utility gains of 549 basis points per year for a mean-variance investor. The results are robust for different subsamples, including the Great Moderation period, the Great Financial Crisis period, and periods of bad, normal, and good economic growth. The authors also evaluate the economic significance of the forecasting performance of the frequency-decomposed predictors through an asset allocation analysis and find significant utility gains when making forecasts using the proper set of frequencies of the predictors. The results are robust for different subsamples and the authors document that forecasting during good growth periods using some of the frequency-decomposed predictors also outperforms the historical mean benchmark.

Document title: Bird Flu, the OIE, and National Regulation: The WTO's India–Agricultural Products Dispute
Document description: The document discusses the WTO's India – Agricultural Products dispute, specifically the US challenge to India's regulatory policies for addressing avian influenza (bird flu). The dispute raises important legal, economic, and public policy issues. The US claims that India's import measures applied against avian influenza-infected countries are too restrictive, in light of the World Organisation for Animal Health's standards and guidelines. The document provides a legal-economic assessment of the issues arising in the Panel Report, exploring the relationship between WTO Members, the WTO Agreements, and international standards-setting organizations. The analysis highlights the need to find a balance between a country's right to regulate for health and safety and its participation in a rules-based trading system. The document also discusses the economic markets for poultry and related products, including the potential impact of the policies under dispute. The US is the world's largest producer of poultry, and the country has historically been able to organize politically to overcome the free-rider problem and engage with the office of the US Trade Representative. The dispute involves a number of poultry and livestock-related products that could potentially be affected by avian influenza. The document concludes that the institutional design of the OIE is well-motivated, but there are subtle issues that pose long-term challenges for the multilateral trading system's ability to balance trade rules with public health concerns.

Document title: Patent Value and Citations: Creative Destruction or Strategic Disruption?
Document description: The document discusses the relationship between patent value and citations. It presents a study that uses novel revenue data for tens of thousands of patents held by non-practicing entities to examine the relationship between forward citations and patent value. The study finds that the relationship is not linear and that there is an inverted-U relationship between citations and value. The authors propose a model that explains this relationship by distinguishing between productive and strategic investments in innovation. The model predicts that strategic innovative efforts generate the downslope of the inverted-U relationship. The study also finds that innovators strategically defend against follow-on competitors, which helps to explain the high value-low citation patents. The authors contribute to the innovation literature by providing a more complex and accurate description of the innovative process.

Document title: The Impact of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy on Youth Violence and Dropout in the United States | The Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab
Document description: Researchers evaluated the impact of a cognitive behavioral therapy program, called Becoming a Man (BAM), designed to teach high-risk male students in secondary schools to regulate harmful, automatic behaviors. The program led to a significant drop in arrests, especially for violent crimes, and increased students' chances of graduating on time. Results from two randomized evaluations demonstrated that BAM led to a significant drop in arrests per student, especially for violent crimes, and increased school engagement and high school graduation rates. BAM may have been effective because the program reduced automatic, impulsive behaviors by helping participants slow down their decision-making processes to better assess situations and choose appropriate responses. Students who received BAM were also more engaged in school and scored higher on an index measuring grade point average, attendance, and enrollment. BAM students in one evaluation were 9 percent more likely to graduate high school on time. These effects could be particularly important in the long term as increased school achievement can lead to improvements in lifetime earnings and health. Researchers estimate BAM's overall societal benefits were anywhere from five to 30 times greater than the program's cost, which ranged from US $1,100 to US$1,850 per student per year.

Document title: The Impact of Racial Segregation on College Attainment in Spatial Equilibrium
Document description: This paper explores the impact of racial segregation on college attainment in the St. Louis metro area. The authors build an overlapping-generations spatial-equilibrium model to study the effect of the Black-White wage gap and homophily, which is the preference to live with neighbors of your own race. The model finds that these two forces account for 22 percentage points of the Black-White gap in college attainment, explaining about 80% of the 28 percentage points college gap in the data. The authors also consider a policy reform that equalizes school funding across neighborhoods, which reduces the college gap by almost 10 percentage points. The paper suggests that the presence of the wage gap and homophily generates a college gap and that a policy reform could help reduce this gap. The authors use empirical estimates to calibrate the model and match critical features of the St. Louis MSA. They also validate the model by comparing it with estimates from the literature on the causal effect of neighborhoods on college attainment and the causal effect of segregation on educational attainment.

Document title: Firm Dynamics and Random Search over the Business Cycle - FEDERAL RESERVE BANK of NEW YORK
Document description: This document presents a tractable random search model with firm dynamics, on-the-job search, and aggregate shocks. The model is used to study the business cycle and worker reallocation in Britain. The key features of the model include firm dynamics, a frictional labor market, and aggregate shocks. The model implies that workers have well-defined preferences over firms and that the job ladder is a productivity ladder. The model is calibrated to match a set of moments related to worker mobility and firm dynamics, and it is used to quantify the drivers of worker reallocation in Britain. The results show that most of the fluctuations in labor productivity are driven by worker reallocation, and that the firm component of worker reallocation accounts for 60 percent of the overall drop in worker reallocation after the Great Recession. The model also shows that countercyclical unemployment benefits impact the firm component and interaction component of worker reallocation along the job ladder in opposite directions.

Document title: Immigrants and Native Flight: Geographic Extent and Heterogeneous Preferences
Document description: This document discusses ethnic segregation in Europe, focusing on whether it is driven by native flight or immigrant self-isolation. The authors use a matched panel of individuals and properties in Denmark from 1987 to 2017 to uncover revealed preferences for homophily. They find strong evidence of native flight at both neighborhood and building levels, with flight being stronger among the old and a reaction to the arrival of low-income immigrants. The authors also provide actionable policy targets by identifying the specific demographic patterns of this behavior. They conclude that policies solely operating on immigrant ghettos may not fully succeed unless native behavior is also targeted. The study highlights the importance of understanding the complex relationships between immigration and the native population in European cities.

Document title: Stress/Depression across the COVID-19 Pandemic in Denmark
Document description: The document discusses the mental health of the Danish population during the COVID-19 pandemic. It presents results from a study that tracked trends in the risk of stress and depression across different age groups, genders, and living arrangements from just before the first lockdown in March 2020 to April 2022. The study found that prior to the first lockdown, there was a 'parent gap' in mental health, but this gap closed with the lockdown. However, a gender gap materialized, with women experiencing higher risks of stress and depression than men. Older respondents experienced increasing risks of stress and depression early in the pandemic, while younger respondents experienced decreases. The study also found that longer into the pandemic, risks increased for all age groups and reached levels from before the first lockdown. The authors suggest that the initial improvements to mental health during the first lockdown were short-lived and that two years of pandemic societal restrictions corresponded with deteriorating mental health.

Document title: A Review and Assessment of the Main Business Tax Provisions of the 2025 Reconciliation Act
Document description: The document reviews and assesses the main business tax provisions of the 2025 reconciliation bill, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The bill extends and reinstates several business tax provisions originally enacted under the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, including bonus depreciation, expensing of structures, R&D expensing, interest deduction limitations, and the qualified business income deduction. The document estimates the fiscal cost and likely economic effects of these provisions, particularly their influence on the cost of capital and business investment. The analysis suggests that permanently reinstating 100 percent bonus depreciation, R&D expensing, and the 30 percent EBITDA limit on interest deductions would raise GDP in 2035 by 0.3 percent, increase the capital stock by 0.9 percent, and lift investment by 1.5 percent relative to prior law. The document also discusses the impact of these provisions on the effective marginal tax rate for corporations and pass-through businesses, with the reconciliation bill reducing EMTRs by approximately 6 and 8 percentage points in 2025, respectively.

Document title: A Statistical Decomposition of Nativity Gaps in Criminal Convictions Using Full Population Data from Five Developed Democracies
Document description: The document discusses the relationship between immigration and crime rates in five developed democracies, including Denmark, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, and Sweden. The authors use population-wide administrative data to statistically decompose the correlation between nonwestern immigrant background status and criminal conviction. The results show that differences in conviction rates between immigrants and their children and the majority populations are mostly attributable to gaps in education, labor market status, and income. The authors also highlight the importance of considering the type of migration and the host country's response to it. The study's findings have implications for policymakers seeking to address the perceived consequences of migration for crime and public safety. The authors suggest that investments in labor-market status and education, as well as the circumstances under which children grow, may help to decrease the conviction gaps. The study also notes that the results for New Zealand consistently opposed those for Europe, with lower crime rates among immigrants and their children in New Zealand attributed to selectivity in the types of people likely to migrate to New Zealand relative to Europe. The authors also discuss the theoretical explanations for the difference in results between the US and the EU, including the 'healthy migrant hypothesis', the introduction of new skills and entrepreneurship, and the revitalization of communities and norms.

Document title: Drawing a Line: Comparing the Estimation of Top Incomes Between Tax Data and Household Survey Data
Document description: This research paper compares the estimation of top incomes using household survey data and tax data across the United States, Germany, and France. The authors utilize the Luxembourg Income Study database to align income categories and recipient units between these two distinct data sources. Their analysis reveals that results from both methods correspond extremely well regarding total income, mean income, composition, and income shares above the 90th percentile up to the top one percent. Information available in the United States data allows the authors to investigate the specific determinants of the remaining gap, which is found to be largely due to differences in non-labor incomes, particularly self-employment earnings. The study suggests that discrepancies may stem from tax-induced reclassification of income or the limited ability of surveys to capture the very top of the income distribution. By addressing mechanical differences in income definitions and units of analysis, the paper isolates residual discrepancies caused by household behavior and sampling design. The findings highlight the importance of cross-country analyses to understand where and why these data sources diverge in their measurement of extreme income inequality.

Document title: The Political Economy of Inequality in Rich Democracies
Document description: This working paper investigates the political economy of income inequality in rich democracies, focusing on why the United States has experienced higher inequality levels compared to other nations even before recent trends. The author analyzes data from the 1980s to 2000, finding that while skill-biased technological change and globalization are common explanations for rising inequality, they fail to fully account for the persistent high inequality in the US or explain why some advanced countries have not seen similar rises. The study concludes that political economy factors are more successful predictors of inequality than traditional economic theories. Specifically, the research identifies two key variables: an index of excess earnings for elite professionals and racial diversity as the strongest predictors of income distribution. The paper highlights that top earners in the US are concentrated in heavily regulated sectors like finance, healthcare, and law, rather than in innovative or globalized industries. Additionally, it reviews the historical and political origins of racial inequality, noting how minority oppression limits access to productive occupations and reduces support for public services. Ultimately, the author argues that comprehensive theories of income distribution must integrate political economy considerations to explain patterns in the early twenty-first century.
